sabaoth.etymology: Heb. tseba'oth, pl. of tsaba', an army or host, fr. tsaba', to go forth to war.

sabbatarian.etymology: L. Sabbatarius: cf. F. sabbataire. See Sabbath.

sabbath.etymology: OE. sabat, sabbat, F. sabbat, L. sabbatum, Gr. shabbath, fr. shabath to rest from labor. Cf. Sabbat.

sable.etymology: OF. sable, F. zibeline sable (in sense 4), LL. sabellum; cf. D. sabel, Dan. sabel, zobel, Sw. sabel, sobel, G. zobel; all fr. Russ. sóbole.

saccharify.etymology: L. saccharon sugar + -fy: cf. F. saccharifier.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

saccharine.etymology: F. saccharin, fr. L. saccharob sugar, Gr. çarkara. Cf. Sugar.

saccule.etymology: L. sacculus, dim. of saccus sack.

sacerdotal.etymology: L. sacerdotalis, fr. sacerdos, -otis, a priest, fr.sacer holy, sacred: cf. F. sacerdotal.

sachet.etymology: F., dim. of sac. See Sac.

sack.etymology: OE. seck, F. sec dry (cf. Sp. seco, It secco), from L. siccus dry, harsh; perhaps akin to Gr. sikata sand, Ir. sesc dry, W. hysp. Cf. Desiccate.

sackbut.etymology: F. saquebute, OF. saqueboute a sackbut. earlier, a sort of hook attached to the end of a lance used by foot soldiers to unhorse cavalrymen; prop. meaning, pull and push; fr. saquier, sachier, to pull, draw (perhaps originally, to put into a bag or take out from a bag; see Sack a bag) + bouter to push (see Butt to thrust). The name was given to the musical instrument from its being lengthened and shortened.

sacking.etymology: AS. sæccing, from sæcc sack, bag.

sacque.etymology: Formed after the analogy of the French. See 2d Sack.

sacrament.etymology: L. sacramentum an oath, a sacred thing, a mystery, a sacrament, fr. sacrare to declare as sacred, sacer sacred: cf. F. sacrament. See Sacred.

sacramental.etymology: L. sacramentalis: cf. F. sacramental, sacramentel.

sacred.etymology: Originally p.p. of OE. sacren to consecrate, F. sacrer, fr. L. sacrare, fr. sacer sacred, holy, cursed. Cf. Consecrate, Execrate, Saint, Sextion.

sacrifice.etymology: OE. sacrifise, sacrifice, F. sacrifice, fr. L. sacrificium; sacer sacer + facere to make. See Sacred, and Fact.

sacrilege.etymology: F. sacrilège, L. sacrilegium, from sacrilegus that steals, properly, gathers or picks up, sacred things; sacer sacred + legere to gather, pick up. See Sacred, and Legend.

sacristan.etymology: F. sacristian, LL. sacrista, fr. L. sacer. See Sacred, and cf. Sexton.

sacristy.etymology: F. sacristie, LL. sacristia, fr. L. sacer. See Sacred.

sacrum.etymology: NL., fr. L. sacer sacred, os sacrum the lowest bone of the spine.

sad.etymology: OE. sad sated, tired, satisfied, firm, steadfast, AS. sæd satisfied, sated; akin to D. zat, OS. sad, G. tt, OHG. sat, sa, saddr, Goth. saps, Lith. sotus, L. sat, satis, enough, satur sated, Gr. Assets, Sate, Satiate, Satisfy Satire.

saddle.etymology: OE. sadel, AS. sadol; akin to D. zadel, G. sattel, OHG. satal, satul, Icel. söedhull, Dan. & Sw. sadel; cf. Russ. siedlo; all perh. ultimately from the root of E. sit.

sadducee.etymology: L. Sadducaei, p., Gr. Tsaddukim; -- so called from Tsadok, the founder of the sect.

safe.etymology: OE. sauf, F. sauf, fr. L. salvus, akin to salus health, welfare, safety. Cf. Salute, Salvation, Sage a plant, Save, Salvo an exception.

safflower.etymology: F. safeur, safior, for safran, influenced by fleur flower. See Saffron, and Flower.

saffron.etymology: OE. saffran, F. safran; cf. It. zafferano, Sp. azafran, Pg. açafrao; all fr. Ar. & Per. za' faran.

safranine.etymology: So called because used as a substitute for safranin.

sag.etymology: Akin to Sw. sacka to settle, sink down, LG.sacken, D. zakken. Cf. Sink, v. i.

saga.etymology: Icel., akin to E. saw a saying. See Say, and cf. Saw.

sagacious.etymology: L. sagax, sagacis, akin to sagire to perceive quickly or keenly, and probably to E. seek. See Seek, and cf. Presage.

sage.etymology: OE. sauge, F. sauge, L. salvia, from salvus saved, in allusion to its reputed healing virtues. See Safe.

sagittal.etymology: L. sagitta an arrow: cf. F. saguttal.

sagittarius.etymology: L., literally, an archer, fr. sagittarius belonging to an arrow, fr. sagitta an arrow.

sagittate.etymology: NL. sagittatus, fr. L. sagitta an arrow.

sahib.etymology: Ar. çahib master, lord, fem. çahibah.

sail.etymology: OE. seil, AS. segel, segl; akin to D. zeil, OHG. segal, G. & Sw. segel, Icel. segl, Dan. seil. sq. root 153.

sainfoin.etymology: F., fr. sain wholesome (L. sanus; see Sane.) + foin hay (L. fænum); or perh. fr. saint sacred (L. sanctus; see Saint) + foin hay.

saint.etymology: F., fr. L. santcus sacred, properly p.p. of sancire to render sacred by a religious act, to appoint as sacred; akin to sacer sacred. Cf. Sacred, Sanctity, Sanctum, Sanctus.

sake.etymology: OE. sake cause, also, lawsuit, fault, AS. sacu strife, a cause or suit at law; akin to D. zaak cause, thing, affair, G. sache thing, cause in law, OHG. sahha, Icel. sök, Sw. sak, Dan. sag, Goth. sakj strife, AS. sacan to contend, strive, Goth. sakan, Icel. saka to contend, strive, blame, OHG. sahhan, MHG. sachen, to contend, strive, defend one's right, accuse, charge in a lawsuit, and also to E. seek. Cf. Seek.

saki.etymology: Cf. F. & Pg. saki; probably from the native name.

salacious.etymology: L. salax, -acis, fond of leaping, lustful, fr. salire to leap. See Salient.

salad.etymology: F. salade, OIt. salata, It. insalata, fr. salare to salt, fr. L. sal salt. See Salt, and cf. Slaw.

salamander.etymology: F. salamandre, L. salamandra, Gr. samander, samandel.

sale.etymology: Icel. sala, sal, akin to E.sell. See Sell, v. t.

saleratus.etymology: NL. sal aëratus; -- so called because it is a source of fixed air (carbon dioxide). See Sal, and and Aërated.

salient.etymology: L. saliens, -entis, p.pr. of salire to leap; cf. F. saillant. See Sally, n. & v. i..

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.

salina.etymology: Cf. L. salinae, pl., salt works, from sal salt. See Saline, a.

saline.etymology: F. salin, fr. L. sal salt: cf. L. salinae salt works, salinum saltcellar. See Salt.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

salivary.etymology: L. salivarius slimy, clammy: cf. F. salivaire.

salivate.etymology: L. salivatus, p.p. of salivare to salivate. See Saliva.

sallet.etymology: F. salade, Sp. celada, or It. celata, fr. L. (cassis) caelata, fr. caelare, caelatum, to engrave in relief. So called from the figures engraved upon it.

sallow.etymology: AS. salu; akin to D. zaluw, OHG. salo, Icel. sölr yellow.

sally.etymology: F. saillir, fr. L. salire to leap, spring, akin to gr. Sallient, Assail, Assault, Exult, Insult, Saltation, Saltire.

salmagundi.etymology: F. salmigondis of uncertain origin; perhaps from L. salgama condita, pl.; salgama pickles + condita preserved (see Condite); or from the Countess Salmagondi, lady of honor to Maria de Medici, who is said to have invented it; or cf. It. salame salt meat, and F. salmis a ragout.

salmon.etymology: OE. saumoun, salmon, F. saumon, fr. L. salmo, salmonis perhaps from salire to leap. Cf. Sally, v.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that the substance in the name of which it appears belongs to the series of alcohols or hydroxyl derivatives, as carbinol, glycerol, etc.

saloon.etymology: F. salon (cf. It. salone), fr. F. salle a large room, a hall, of German or Dutch origin; cf. OHG. sal house, hall, G. saal; akin to AS. sæl, sele, D. zaal, Icel. salr, Goth. saljan to dwell, and probably to L. solum ground. Cf. Sole of the foot, Soil ground, earth.

salpa.etymology: NL.: cf. L. salpa a kind of stockfish.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

salsola.etymology: NL., fr. L. salsus salt, because they contain alkaline salts.

salt.etymology: AS. sealt; akin to OS. & OFries. salt, D. zout, G. salz, Icel., Sw., & Dan. salt, L. sal, Gr. sole, Ir. & Gael. salann, W. halen, of unknown origin. Cf. Sal, Salad, Salary, Saline, Sauce, Sausage.

saltcellar.etymology: OE. saltsaler; salt + F. salière saltcellar, from L. sal salt. See Salt, and cf. Salary.

saltire.etymology: F. sautoir, fr. LL. saltatorium a sort of stirrup, fr. L. saltatorius saltatory. See Saltatory, Sally, v.

saltpeter.etymology: F. salpêtre, NL. sal petrae, literally, rock salt, or stone salt; Salt, and Petrify.

saltpetre.etymology: F. salpêtre, NL. sal petrae, literally, rock salt, or stone salt; Salt, and Petrify.

salubrious.etymology: L. salubris, or saluber, fr. salus health; akin to salvus safe, sound, well. See Safe.

salubrity.etymology: L. salubritas: cf. F. salubrité See Salubrious.

salutary.etymology: L. salutaris, from salus, -utis, health safety: cf. F. salutaire. See Salubrious.

salutation.etymology: L. salutatio: cf. F. salutation. See Salute.

salute.etymology: L. salutare, salutatum, from salus, -utis, health, safety. See Salubrious.

salvage.etymology: F. salvage, OF. salver to save, F. sauver, fr. L. salvare. See Save.

salvation.etymology: OE. salvacioun, sauvacion, F. salvation, fr. L. salvatio, fr. salvare to save. See Save.

salve.etymology: L., hail, God save you, imperat. of salvere to be well. Cf. Salvo a volley.

salvific.etymology: L. salficus saving; salvus saved, safe + facere to make.

salvo.etymology: L. salvo jure, literally, the right being reserved. See Safe.

samara.etymology: L. samara, samera, the seed of the elm.

same.etymology: AS. same. adv.; akin to OS. sama, samo, adv., OHG. sam, a., sama, adv., Icel. samr, a., Sw. samme, samma, Dan. samme, Goth. sama, Russ. samui, Gr. sama, Gr. simul at the same time, similis like, and E. some, a., -some. sq. root191. Cf. Anomalous, Assemble, Homeopathy, Homily, Seem, v. i., Semi-, Similar, Some.

roots.meaning: An adjective suffix having primarily the sense of like or same, and indicating a considerable degree of the thing or quality denoted in the first part of the compound; as in mettlesome, full of mettle or spirit; gladsome, full of gladness; winsome, blithesome, etc.
A prefix signifying half, and sometimes partly or imperfectly; as, semiannual, half yearly; semitransparent, imperfectly transparent.

samiel.etymology: Turk. sam-yeli; Ar. samm poison + Turk. yel wind. Cf. Simoom.

samite.etymology: OF. samit, LL. samitum, examitum, from LGr. Six, and cf. Dimity.

samphire.etymology: F. l'herbe de Saint Pierre. See Saint, and Petrel.

sample.etymology: OE. sample, asaumple, OF. essample, example, fr. L. exemplum. See Example, and cf. Ensample, Sampler.

sanctify.etymology: F. sanctifier, L. sanctificare; sanctus holy + - ficare (in comp.) to make. See Saint, and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

sanctimony.etymology: L. sanctimonia, fr. sanctus holy: cf. OF. sanctimonie. See Saint.

sanction.etymology: L. sanctio, from sancire, samctum to render sacred or inviolable, to fix unalternably: cf. F. sanction. See Saint.

sanctity.etymology: L. sanctitas, from sanctus holy. See Saint.

sanctuary.etymology: OE. seintuare, OF. saintuaire, F. sanctuaire, fr. L. sanctuarium, from sanctus sacred, holy. See Saint.

sanctum.etymology: L., p.p. of sanctire to consecrate.

sandal.etymology: F. sandale, L. sandalium, Gr. sandal.

sandalwood.etymology: F. sandal, santal, fr. Ar. çandal, or Gr. sa`ntalon; both ultimately fr. Skr. candana. Cf. Sanders.

sanderling.etymology: Sand + 0ling. So called because it obtains its food by searching the moist sands of the seashore.

sandwich.etymology: Named from the Earl of Sandwich.

sane.etymology: L. sanus; cf. Gr. Sound, a.

sangaree.etymology: Sp. sangria, lit., bleeding, from sangre, blood, L. sanguis.

sanguinary.etymology: L. sanguinarius, fr. sanguis blood: cf. F.sanguinaire.

sanguine.etymology: F. sanguin, L. sanguineus, fr. sanguis blood. Cf. Sanguineous.

sanicle.etymology: F., from L. sanare to heal.

sanious.etymology: L. sanious, fr. sanies: cf. F. sanieux.

sanitary.etymology: L. sanitas health: cf. F. sanitaire. See Sanity.

sanity.etymology: L. saniras, from sanus sound, healthy. See Sane.

sanskrit.etymology: Skr. Samskrsta the Sanskrit language, literally, the perfect, polished, or classical language, fr. samskrsta prepared, wrought, made,excellent, perfect; sam together (akin to E. same) + krsta made. See Same, Create.

sap.etymology: AS. sæp; akin to OHG. saf, G. saft, Icel. safi; of uncertain origin; possibly akin to L. sapere to taste, to be wise, sapa must or new wine boiled thick. Cf. Sapid, Sapient.

sapid.etymology: L. sapidus, fr. sapere to taste: cf. F. sapide. See Sapient, Savor.

sapience.etymology: L. sapientia: cf. F. sapience. See Sapient..

sapient.etymology: L. sapiens, -entis, p.pr. of sapere to taste to have sense, to know. See Sage, a.

sapindus.etymology: NL., fr. L. sapo soap + Indicus Indian.

sapodilla.etymology: Sp. zapote, sapotillo, zapotillo, Mexican cochit-zapotl. Cf. Sapota.

saponaceous.etymology: L. sapo, -onis, soap, of Teutonic origin, and akin to E. soap. See Soap.

saponify.etymology: L. sapo, -onis, soap + -fy: cf. F. saponifier.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

saponin.etymology: L. sapo, -onis soap: cf. F. saponine.

saporous.etymology: L. saporius that relishes well, savory, fr. sapor taste.

sapota.etymology: NL., from Sp. sapote, zapote. See Sapodilla.

sapphire.etymology: OE. saphir, F. saphir, L. sapphirus, Gr. sappir.

sapsago.etymology: G. schabzieger; schaben to shave, to scrape + zieger a sort of hey.

saraband.etymology: F. sarabande, Sp. zarabanda, fr. Per. serbend a song.

saracen.etymology: l. Saracenus perhaps fr. Ar. sharqi, pl. sharqiin, Oriental Eastern, fr. sharaga to rise, said of the sun: cf. F. sarrasin. Cf. Sarcenet, Sarrasin, Sirocco.

sarcenet.etymology: OF. sacenet; cf. LL. saracenium cloth made by Saracens. See Saracen.

sard.etymology: L. sarda, Gr. sarde. Cf. Sardius.

sardius.etymology: L. sardius, lapis sardinus, Gr. Sard.

sardonyx.etymology: L., fr. Gr. Sard, and Onyx.

sarracenia.etymology: NL. So named after a Dr. Sarrazin of Quebec.

sarsaparilla.etymology: Sp. zarzaparrilla; zarza a bramble (perhaps fr. Bisc. zartzia) + parra a vine, or Parillo, a physician said to have discovered it.

sartorius.etymology: NL., fr. L. sartor a patcher, tailor, fr. sarcire, sartum, to patch, mend.

sash.etymology: Pers. shast a sort of girdle.

sassafras.etymology: F. sassafras (cf. It. sassafrasso, sassafras, Sp. sasafras, salsafras, salsifrax, salsifragia, saxifragia), fr. L. saxifraga saxofrage. See Saxifrage.

satan.etymology: Heb. satan an adversary, fr. satan to be adverse, to persecute: cf. GR. Satan, Satanas.

satchel.etymology: OF. sachel, fr. L. saccellus, dim. of saccus. See Sack a bag.

sate.etymology: Probably shortened fr. satiate: cf. L. satus full. See Satiate.

satellite.etymology: F., fr. L. Stelles, -itis, an attendant.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.

satiate.etymology: L. satiatus, p. p. of satiare to satisfy, from sat, satis, enough. See Sad, a., and cf. Sate.

satiety.etymology: L. satietas, from satis, sat, enough: cf. F. satiété.

satin.etymology: F. satin (cf. Pg. setim), fr. It. setino, from seta silk, L. saeta, seta, a thick, stiff hair, a bristle; or possibly ultimately of Chinese origin; cf. Chin. sz-tün, sz-twan. Cf. Sateen.

satire.etymology: L. satira, satura, fr. satura (sc. lanx) a dish filled with various kinds of fruits, food composed of various ingredients, a mixture, a medley, fr. satur full of food, sated, fr. sat, satis, enough: cf. F. satire. See Sate, Sad, a., and cf. Saturate.

satisfaction.etymology: OE. satisfaccioum, F. satisfaction, fr. L. satisfactio, fr. satisfacere to satisfy. See Satisfy.

satisfy.etymology: OF. satisfier; L. satis enough + -ficare (in comp.) to make; cf. F. satisfaire, L. satisfacere. See Sad, a., and Fact.

satrap.etymology: L. satrapes, Gr. khsatrapavan ruler: cf. F. satrape.

saturate.etymology: L. saturatus, p.p. of saturate to saturate, fr. satur full of food, sated. See Satire.

saturday.etymology: OE. Saterday, AS. Sæterdæg, Sæterndæg, Sæternesdæg, literally, Saturn's day, fr. L. Saturnus Saturn + AS. dæg day; cf. L. dies Saturni.

saturn.etymology: L. Saturnus, literally, the saower, fr. serere, satum, to sow. See Season.

saturnine.etymology: L. Saturnus the god Saturn, also, the planet Saturn: cf. F. saturnin of or pertaining to lead (Saturn, in old chemistry, meaning lead),saturnien saturnine, saturnian. See Saturn.

sauce.etymology: F., fr. OF. sausse, LL. salsa, properly, salt pickle, fr. L. salsus salted, salt, p.p. of salire to salt, fr. sal salt. See Salt, and cf. Saucer, Souse pickle, Souse to plunge.

saucer.etymology: F. saucière, from sauce. see Sauce.

sauerkraut.etymology: G., fr. sauer sour + kraut herb, cabbage.

roots.meaning: A New Latin plural combining form or suffix from Gr. foot; as, hexapoda, myriapoda. See -pod.

sausage.etymology: F. saucisse, LL. salcitia, salcicia, fr. salsa. See Sauce.

savage.etymology: F. sauvage, OF. salvage, fr. L. silvaticus belonging to a wood, wild, fr. silva a wood. See Silvan, and cf. Sylvatic.

savanna.etymology: Of American Indian origin; cf. Sp. sabana, F. savane.

savant.etymology: F., fr. savoir to know, L. sapere. See Sage, a.

saveloy.etymology: F. cervelas, It. cervellata, fr. cervello brain, L. cerebellum, dim. of cerebrum brain. See Cerebral.

savin.etymology: OE. saveine, AS. safinæ, savine, L. sabina herba. Cf. Sabine.

savior.etymology: OE. saveour, OF. salveor, F. sauveur, fr. L. salvator to save. See Save, v.

savor.etymology: OE. savour, savor, savur, OF. savor, savour, F. saveur, fr. L. sapor, fr. sapere to taste, savor. See Sage, a., and cf. Sapid, Insipid, Sapor.

savoury.etymology: F. savorée; cf. It. santoreggia, satureja, L. satureia,

savoy.etymology: F. chou de Savoie cabbage of Savoy.

saw.etymology: OE. sawe, AS. sagu; akin to secgan to say. See Say, v. t. and cf. Saga.

sawyer.etymology: Saw + -yer, as in lawyer. Cf. Sawer.

saxatile.etymology: L. saxatilis, fr. saxum a rock: cf. F. saxalite.

saxicoline.etymology: L. saxum a rock + colere to inhabit.

saxifrage.etymology: L. saxifraga, from saxifragus stone- breaking; saxum rock + frangere to break: cf. F. saxifrage. See Fracture, and cf. Sassafras, Saxon.

saxon.etymology: l. Saxo, pl. Saxones, from the Saxon national name; cf. AS. pl. Seaxe, Seaxan, fr. seax a knife, a short sword, a dagger (akin to OHG. sahs, and perhaps to L. saxum rock, stone, knives being originally made of stone); and cf. G. Sachse, pl. Sachsen. Cf. Saxifrage.

scab.etymology: OE. scab, scabbe, shabbe; cf. AS. scæb, sceabb, scebb, Dan. & Sw. skab, and also L. scabies, tr. scabere to scratch, akin to E. shave. See Shave, and cf. Shab, Shabby.

scabbard.etymology: OE. scaubert, scauberk, OF. escaubers, escauberz, pl., scabbards, probably of German or Scan. origin; cf. Icel. skalpr scabbard, and G. bergen to conceal. Cf. Hauberk.

scabious.etymology: L. scabious, from scabies the scab: cf. F. scabieux.

scabrous.etymology: L. scabrosus, fr. scaber rough: cf. F. scabreux.

scaffold.etymology: OF. eschafault, eschafaut, escafaut, escadafaut, F. échafaud; probably oiginally the same word as E. & F. catafalque, It. catafafalco. See Catafalque.

scald.etymology: OF. eschalder, eschauder, escauder, F. échauder, fr. L. excaldare; ex + caldus, calidus, warm, hot. See Ex, and Calderon.

scale.etymology: AS. scale; perhaps influenced by the kindred Icel. skal balance, dish, akin also to D. schaal a scale, bowl, shell, G. schale, OHG. scala, Dan. skaal drinking cup, bowl, dish, and perh. to E. scale of a fish. Cf. Scale of a fish, Skull the brain case.

scallion.etymology: OF. escalone, escaloingne, L. caepa Ascalonius of Ascalon, fr. Ascalo Ascalon, a town in Palestine. Cf. Shallot.

scallop.etymology: OF. escalope a shell, probably of German or Dutch origin, and akin to E. scale of a fish; cf. D. schelp shell. See Scale of a fish, and cf. Escalop.

scalpel.etymology: L scalpellum, dim. of scalprum a knife, akin to scalpere to cut, carve, scrape: cf. F. scalpel.

scamp.etymology: OF. escamper to run away, to make one's escape. originally, one who runs away, a fugitive, a vagabond. See Scamper.

scamper.etymology: OF. escamper to escape, to save one's self; L. ex from + campus the field (sc. of battle). See Camp, and cf. Decamp, Scamp, n., Shamble, v. t.

scan.etymology: L. scandere, scansum, to climb, to scan, akin to Skr. skand to spring, leap: cf. F. scander. Cf. Ascend, Descend, Scale a ladder.

scandal.etymology: F. scandale, fr. L. scandalum, Gr. scandle, OF. escandle. See Slander.

scandalize.etymology: F. scandaliser, L. scandalizare, from Gr. skandali`zein.

scandent.etymology: L. scandens, -entis, p.pr. of scandere to climb.

scandium.etymology: NL. So called because found in Scandinavian minerals

scansion.etymology: L. scansio, fr. scandere, scansum, to climb. See Scan.

scant.etymology: Icel. skamt, neuter of skamr, skammr, short; cf. skamta to dole out, to portion.

scape.etymology: L. scapus shaft, stem, stalk; cf. Gr. scape. Cf. Scepter.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.
A New Latin plural combining form or suffix from Gr. foot; as, hexapoda, myriapoda. See -pod.

scapulary.etymology: F. scapulaire, LL. scapularium, scapulare, fr. L.scapula shoulder blade.

scar.etymology: OF. escare, F. eschare an eschar, a dry slough (cf. It. & Sp. escara), L. eschara, fr. Gr. Eschar.

scaramouch.etymology: F. scaramouche, It.scaramuccio, scaramuccia, originally the name of a celebrated Italian comedian; cf. It. scaramuccia, scaramuccio, F. escarmouche, skirmish. Cf. Skirmish.

scarce.etymology: OE. scars, OF. escars, eschars, LL. scarpsus, for L. excerptus, p. p. of excerpere to pick out, and hence to contract, to shorten; ex (see Ex-) + carpere. See Carpet, and cf. Excerp.

roots.meaning: . A prefix from the latin preposition, ex, akin to Gr. 'ex or 'ek signifying out of, out, proceeding from. Hence, in composition, it signifies out of, as, in exhale, exclude; off, from, or out. as in exscind; beyond, as, in excess, exceed, excel; and sometimes has a privative sense of without, as in exalbuminuos, exsanguinous. In some words, it intensifies the meaning; in others, it has little affect on the signification. It becomes ef- before f, as in effuse. The form e- occurs instead of ex- before b, d, g, l, m, n, r, and v, as in ebullient, emanate, enormous, etc. In words from the French it often appears as es-, sometimes as s- or é-; as, escape, scape, élite. Ex-, prefixed to names implying office, station, condition, denotes that the person formerly held the office, or is out of the office or condition now; as, ex-president, ex-governor, ex-mayor, ex-convict. The Greek form 'ex becomes ex in English, as in exarch; 'ek becomes ec, as in eccentric.

scare.etymology: OE. skerren, skeren, Icel. skirra to bar, prevent, skirrask to shun , shrink from; or fr. OE. skerre, adj., scared, Icel. skjarr; both perhaps akin to E. sheer to turn.

scarlatina.etymology: NL.: cf. F. scarlatine. See Scarlet.

scarlet.etymology: OE. scarlat, scarlet, OF. escarlate, F. écarlate (cf. Pr. escarlat, escarlata, Sp. & Pg. escarlata, It. scarlatto, LL. scarlatum), from Per. sakirlat.

scathe.etymology: Icel. skatha; akin to AS. sceathan, sceth\'eban, Dan. skade, Sw. skada, D. & G. schaden, OHG. scadon, Goth. skaÞjan.

scaup.etymology: See Scalp a bed of oysters or mussels.

scavenger.etymology: OE. scavager an officer with various duties, orginally attending to scavage, fr. OE. & E. scavage. See Scavage, Show, v.

scenic.etymology: L. scaenicus, scenicus, Gr. scénique. See Scene.

scent.etymology: Originally sent, fr. F. sentir to feel, to smell. See Sense.

scepter.etymology: F. sceptre, L. sceptrum, from Gr. shaft. See Shaft, and cf. Scape a stem, shaft.

sceptre.etymology: F. sceptre, L. sceptrum, from Gr. shaft. See Shaft, and cf. Scape a stem, shaft.

schedule.etymology: F. cédule, formerly also spelt schedule, L. schedula, dim. of scheda, scida, a strip of papyrus bark, a leaf of paper; akin to (or perh. from) Gr. scindere to cleave, Gr. Schism, and cf. Cedule.

scheme.etymology: L. schema a rhetorical figure, a shape, figure, manner, Gr. sah to be victorious, to endure, to hold out, AS. sige victory, G. sieg. Cf. Epoch, Hectic, School.

schism.etymology: OE. scisme, OF. cisme, scisme, F. schisme, L. schisma, Gr. scindere, Skr. child, and prob. to E. shed, v.t. (which see); cf. Rescind, Schedule, Zest.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting division or cleavage; as, schizogenesis, reproduction by fission or cell division.
A New Latin plural combining form or suffix from Gr. foot; as, hexapoda, myriapoda. See -pod.

scholar.etymology: OE. scoler, AS. scolere, fr. L. scholaris belonging to a school, fr. schola a school. See School.

scholastic.etymology: L. scholasticus, Gr. scholastique, scolastique. See School.

school.etymology: From Middle English scole , from Old English scōl ( “ place of education ” ) , from Proto-West Germanic *skōlu , from Late Latin schola , scola ( “ learned discussion or dissertation, lecture, school ” ) , from Ancient Greek σχολή ( skholḗ , “ spare time, leisure ” ) , from Proto-Indo-European *seǵʰ- ( “ to hold, have, possess ” ) . Doublet of schola and shul .

schooner.etymology: See the Note below. Cf. Shun.

schottische.etymology: F. schottish, schotisch from G. schottisch Scottish, Scotch.

sciatic.etymology: F. sciatique, LL. sciaticus, from L. inschiadicus, Gr. Ischiadic.

science.etymology: F., fr. L. scientia, fr. sciens, -entis, p.pr. of scire to know. Cf. Conscience, Conscious, Nice.

scientific.etymology: F. scientifique; L. scientia science + facere to make.

scimitar.etymology: F. cimeterre, cf. It. scimitarra, Sp. cimitarra; fr. Biscayan cimetarry with a sharp edge; or corrupted from Per. shimshir.

scintillant.etymology: L. scintillans, p.pr. of scintillare to sparkle. See Scintillate.

scintillate.etymology: L. scintillare, scintillatum, from scintilla a spark. Cf. Stencil.

scion.etymology: OF. cion, F. scion, probably fron scier to saw, fr. L. secare to cut. Cf. Section.

scission.etymology: L. scissio, fr. scindere, scis, to cut, to split: cf. F. scission.

scissors.etymology: OE. sisoures, OF. cisoires (cf. F. ciseaux), probably fr. LL. cisorium a cutting instrument, fr. L. caedere to cut. Cf. Chisel, Concise. The modern spelling is due to a mistaken derivation from L. scissor one who cleaves or divides, fr. scindere, scissum, to cut, spilt.

scissure.etymology: L. scissura, from scindere, scissum, to cut, spilt.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

scoff.etymology: OE. scof; akin to OFries. schof, OHG. scoph, Icel. skaup, and perh. to E. shove.

scold.etymology: Akin to D. schelden, G. schelten, OHG. sceltan, Dan. skielde.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

sconce.etymology: D. schans, OD. schantse, perhaps from OF. esconse a hiding place, akin to esconser to hide, L. absconsus, p. p. of abscondere. See Abscond, and cf. Ensconce, Sconce a candlestick.

scoop.etymology: OE. scope, of Scand. origin; cf. Sw. skopa, akin to D. schop a shovel, G. schüppe, and also to E. shove. See Shovel.

scope.etymology: It. scopo, L. scopos a mark, aim, Gr. skopo`s, a watcher, mark, aim; akin to spy. Cf. Skeptic, Bishop.

scorch.etymology: OE. scorchen, probably akin to scorcnen; cf. Norw. skrokken shrunk up, skrekka, skrökka, to shrink, to become wrinkled up, dial. Sw. skråkkla to wrinkle (see Shrug); but perhaps influenced by OF. escorchier to strip the bark from, to flay, to skin, F. écorcher, LL. excorticare; L. ex from + cortex, -icis, bark (cf. Cork); because the skin falls off when scorched.

score.etymology: AS. scor twenty, fr. sceran, scieran, to shear, cut, divice; or rather the kindred Icel. skor incision, twenty, akin to Dan. skure a notch, Sw. skåra. See Shear.

scorn.etymology: OE. scorn, scarn, scharn, OF. escarn, escharn, eschar, of German origin; cf. OHG. skern mockery, skern to mock; but cf. also OF. escorner to mock.

scorpaenoid.etymology: NL. Scorpaena, a typical genus (see Scorpene) + -oid.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

scorpion.etymology: F., fr. L. scorpio, scorpius, Gr. sharp.

scot.etymology: Cf. L. Skoti, pl., AS. Scotta, pl. Skottas, Sceottas.

scoter.etymology: Cf. Prov. E. scote to plow up.

scots.etymology: For older Scottis Scottish. See Scottish.

scottish.etymology: From Scot a Scotchman: cf. AS. Scyttisc, and E. Scotch, a., Scots, a.

scoundrel.etymology: Probably from Prov. E. & Scotch scunner, scouner, to loathe, to disgust, akin to AS. scunian to shun. See Shun.

scour.etymology: Akin to LG. schüren, D. schuren, schueren, G. scheuern, Dan. skure; Sw. skura; all possibly fr. LL. escurare, fr. L. ex + curare to take care. Cf. Cure.

scourge.etymology: F. escourgée, fr. L. excoriata (sc. scutica) a stripped off (lash or whip), fr. excoriate to strip, to skin. See Excoriate.

scout.etymology: Icel. sk a small craft or cutter.

scowl.etymology: Akin to Dan. skule; cf. Icel. skolla to skulk, LG. schulen to hide one's self, D. schuilen, G. schielen to squint, Dan. skele, Sw. skela, AS. sceolh squinting. Cf. Skulk.

scrabble.etymology: Freq. of scrape. Cf. Scramble, Scrawl, v. t.

scrag.etymology: Cf. dial. Sw. skraka a great dry tree, a long, lean man, Gael. sgreagach dry, shriveled, rocky. See Shrink, and cf. Scrog, Shrag, n.

scramble.etymology: Freq. of Prov. E. scramb to rake together with the hands, or of scramp to snatch at. cf. Scrabble.

scranch.etymology: Cf. D. schransen to eat greedily, G. schranzen. Cf. Crunch, Scrunch.

scrap.etymology: OE. scrappe, fr. Icel. skrap trifle, cracking. See Scrape, v. t.

scrape.etymology: Icel. skrapa; akin to Sw. skrapa, Dan. skrabe, D. schrapen, schrabben, G. schrappen, and prob. to E. sharp.

scratch.etymology: OE. cracchen (perhaps influenced by OE. scratten to scratch); cf. OHG. chrazz, G. kratzen, OD. kratsen, kretsen, D. krassen, Sw. kratsa to scrape, kratta to rake, to scratch, Dan. kradse to scratch, to scrape, Icel. krota to engrave. Cf. Grate to rub.

screak.etymology: Cf. Icel. skrækja to screech. Cf. Creak, v., Screech.

scream.etymology: Icel. skræma to scare, terrify; akin to Sw. skräma, Dan. skræmme. Cf. Screech.

screech.etymology: Also formerly, scritch, OE. skriken, skrichen, schriken, of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. skrækja to shriek, to screech, skrija to titter, Sw. skrika to shriek, Dan. skrige; also Gael. sgreach, sgreuch, W. ysgrechio, Skr. kharj to creak. Cf. Shriek, v., Scream, v.

screed.etymology: Prov. E., a shred, the border of a cap. See Shred.

screen.etymology: OE. scren, OF. escrein, escran, F. écran, of uncertain origin; cf. G. schirm a screen, OHG. scrim, scern a protection, shield, or G. schragen a trestle, a stack of wood, or G. schranne a railing.

screw.etymology: OE. scrue, OF. escroue, escroe, female screw, F. écrou, L. scrobis a ditch, trench, in LL., the hole made by swine in rooting; cf. D. schroef a screw, G. schraube, Icel. skr.

scribe.etymology: L. scriba, fr. scribere to write; cf. Gr. scarify. Cf. Ascribe, Describe, Script, Scrivener, Scrutoire.

scrimmage.etymology: A corruption of skirmish. "Sore scrymmishe." Ld. Berners.

scrimp.etymology: Cf. Dan. skrumpe, G. schrumpfen, D. krimpen. Cf. Shrimp, Shrine.

scrip.etymology: OE. scrippe, probably of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. & OSw. skreppa, and also LL. scrippum, OF. esquerpe, escrepe, F. écharpe scarf. Cf. Scarp, Scarf a piece of dress.

script.etymology: OE. scrit, L. scriptum something written, fr. scribere, scriptum to write: cf. OF. escript, , F. écrit. See Scribe, and cf. Scrip a writing.

scripture.etymology: L. scriptura, fr. scribere, scriptum, to write: cf. OF. escripture, escriture, F. écriture. See Scribe.

scrivener.etymology: From older scrivein, OF. escrivain, F. écrivain, LL. scribanus, from L. scribere to write. See Scribe.

scrofula.etymology: L. scrofulae, fr. scrofa a breeding sow, because swine were supposed to be subject to such a complaint, or by a fanciful comparison of the glandular swellings to little pigs; perhaps akin to Gr. scrofules. Cf. Scroyle.

scroll.etymology: A dim. of OE. scroue, scrowe (whence E. escrow), OF. escroe, escroue, F. écrou entry in the jail book, LL. scroa scroll, probably of Teutonic origin; cf. OD. schroode a strip, shred, slip of paper, akin to E. shred. Cf. Shred, Escrow.

scrophularia.etymology: NL. So called because it was reputed to be remedy for scrofula.

scrub.etymology: OE. scrobben, probably of Dutch or Scand. origin; cf. Dan. sckrubbe, Sw. skrubba, D. schrobben, LG. schrubben.

scruple.etymology: L. scrupulus a small sharp or pointed stone, the twenty-fourth part of an ounce, a scruple, uneasiness, doubt, dim. of scrupus a rough or sharp stone, anxiety, uneasiness; perh. akin to Gr. kshura: cf. F. scrupule.

scrutiny.etymology: L. scrutinium, fr. scrutari to search carefuly, originally, to search even to the rags, fr. scruta trash, trumpery; perhaps akin to E. shred: cf. AS. scrudnian to make scrutiny.

scud.etymology: Dan. skyde to shoot, shove, push, akin to skud shot, gunshot, a shoot, young bough, and to E. shoot. sq. root159. See Shoot.

scuff.etymology: Cf. D. schoft shoulder, Goth. skuft hair of the head. Cf. Scruff.

scuffle.etymology: Freq. of scuff, v.i.; cf. Sw. skuffa to push, shove, skuff a push, Dan. skuffe a drawer, a shovel, and E. shuffle, shove. See Shove, and cf. Shuffle.

scullery.etymology: Probably originally, a place for washing dishes, and for swillery, fr. OE. swilen to wash, AS. swilian (see Swill to wash, to drink), but influenced either by Icel. skola, skyla, Dan. skylle, or by OF. escuelier a place for keeping dishes, fr. escuele a dish, F. écuelle, fr. L. scutella a salver, waiter (cf. Scuttle a basket); or perhaps the English word is immediately from the OF. escuelier; cf. OE. squyllare a dishwasher.

scullion.etymology: OF. escouillon (Cot.) a dishclout, apparently for escouvillon, F. écouvillon a swab; cf. also OF. souillon a servant employed for base offices. Cf. Scovel.

sculptor.etymology: L. sculptor, fr. sculpere, sculptum, to carve; cf. scalpere to cut, carve, scratch, and Gr. sculpteur.

scum.etymology: Of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. & Sw. skum, Icel. sk, LG. schum, D. schuim, OHG. sc, G. schaum; probably from a root meaning, to cover. sq. root158. Cf. Hide skin, Meerschaum, Skim, v., Sky.

scupper.etymology: OF. escopir, escupir, to spit, perhaps for escospir, L. ex + conspuere to spit upon; pref. con- + spuere to spit. Cf. Spit, v.

roots.meaning: - (cum, signifying with, together, etc. See Com-.

scurf.etymology: AS. scurf, sceorf, or from Scand.; cf. Sw. skorf, Dan. skurv, Icel. skurfur, D. schurft, G. schorf; all akin to AS. scurf, and to AS. sceorfan to scrape, to gnaw, G. schürfen to scrape, and probably also to E. scrape. Cf. Scurvy.

scut.etymology: Cf. Icel. skott a fox's tail. sq. root 159.

scute.etymology: L. scutum a shield, a buckler. See Scudo.

scuttle.etymology: AS. scutel a dish, platter; cf. Icel. skutill; both fr. L. scutella, dim. of scutra, scuta, a dish or platter; cf. scutum a shield. Cf. Skillet.

scythe.etymology: OE. sithe, AS. si\'ebe, sigthe; akin to Icel. sigthr a sickle, LG. segd, seged, seed, seid, OHG. segansa sickle, scythe, G. sense scythe, and to E. saw a cutting instrument. See Saw.

sea.etymology: OE. see, AS. sæ; akin to D. zee, OS. & OHG. seo, G. see, OFries. se, Dan. sö, Sw. sjö, Icel. sær, Goth. saiws, and perhaps to L. saevus firce, savage. sq. root 151 a.

seal.etymology: OE. sele, AS. seolh; akin to OHG. selah, Dan. sæl, Sw. själ, Icel. selr.

seamstress.etymology: From older seamster, properly fem., AS. seámestre. See Seam.

seance.etymology: F., fr. L. sedens, -entis, p.pr. of sedere to sit. See Sit.

sear.etymology: OE.seeren, AS. seárian. See Sear, a.

search.etymology: OE. serchen, cerchen, OF. cerchier, F. chercher, L. circare to go about, fr. L. circum, circa, around. See Circle.

season.etymology: OE. sesoun, F. saison, properly, the sowing time, fr. L. satio a sowing, a planting, fr. serere, satum, to sow, plant; akin to E. sow, v., to scatter, as seed.

seat.etymology: OE. sete, Icel. sæti; akin to Sw. säte, Dan. sæde, MHG. saze, AS. set, setl, and E. sit. sq. root154. See Sit, and cf. Settle, n.

sebaceous.etymology: NL. sebaceus, from L. sebum tallow, grease.

secant.etymology: L. secans, -antis, p.pr. of secare to cut. See Section.

secede.etymology: L. secedere, secessum; pref se- aside + cedere to go, move. See Cede.

secession.etymology: L. secessio: cf. F. sécession. See Secede.

seclude.etymology: L. secludere, seclusum pref. se- aside + claudere to shut. See Close, v. t.

second.etymology: F., fr. L. secundus second, properly, following, fr. sequi to follow. See Sue to follow, and cf. Secund.

secondary.etymology: Cf. F. secondaire, L. secundaire. See Second, a.

secret.etymology: F. secret (cf. Sp.& Pg. secreto, It. secreto, segreto), fr. L. secretus, p.p. of secrernere to put apart, to separate. See Certain, and cf. Secrete, Secern.

secretary.etymology: F. secrétaire (cf. Pr. secretari, Sp. & Pg. secretario, It. secretario, segretario) LL. secretarius, originally, a confidant, one intrusted with secrets, from L. secretum a secret. See Secret, a. & n.

secrete.etymology: L. secretus separated, secret, hidden, p. p. of secernere. See Secret, and cf. Discrete, Discreet.

section.etymology: L. sectio, fr. secare, sectum, to cut; akin to E. saw a cutting instrument: cf. F. section. See Saw, and cf. Scion, Dissect, Insect, Secant, Segment.

sector.etymology: L., properly, a cutter, fr. secare, sectum, to cut: cf. F. secteur. See Section.

secular.etymology: OE. secular, seculer. L. saecularis, fr. saeculum a race, generation, age, the times, the world; perhaps akin to E. soul: cf. F. séculier.

secure.etymology: L. securus; pref. se- without + cura care. See Cure care, and cf. Sure, a.

security.etymology: L. securitas: cf. F. sécurité. See Secure, and cf. Surety.

sedan.etymology: Said to be named from Sedan, in France, where it was first made, and whence it was introduced into England in the time of King Charles I.

sedate.etymology: L. sedatus, p. p. of sedare, sedatum, to allay, calm, causative of sedere to sit. See Sit.

sedentary.etymology: L. sedentarius, fr. sedere to sit: cf. F. seédentaire. See Sedent.

sedge.etymology: OE. segge, AS. secg; akin to LG. segge; -- probably named from its bladelike appearance, and akin to L. secare to cut, E. saw a cutting instrument; cf. Ir. seisg, W. hesg. Cf. Hassock, Saw the instrument.

sediment.etymology: F. sédiment, L. sedimentum a settling, fr. sedere to sit, to settle. See Sit.

sedition.etymology: OE. sedicioun, OF. sedition, F. sédition, fr. L. seditio, originally, a going aside; hence, an insurrectionary separation; pref. se-, sed-, aside + itio a going, fr. ire, itum, to go. Cf. Issue.

seduce.etymology: L. seducere, seductum; pref. se- aside + ducere to lead. See Duke.

seduction.etymology: L. seductio: cf. F. séduction. See Seduce.

sedulous.etymology: L. sedulus, perhaps from sedere to sit, and so akin to E. sit.

sedum.etymology: NL., fr. L. sedere to sit; so called in allusion to the manner in which the plants attach themselves to rocks and walls.

see.etymology: OE. se, see, OF. se, sed, sied, fr. L. sedes a seat, or the kindred sedere to sit. See Sit, and cf. Siege.

seed.etymology: OE. seed, sed, AS. s, fr. sawan to sow; akin to D. zaad seed, G. saat, Icel. sa, s, Goth. manas seed of men. world. See Sow to scatter seed, and cf. Colza.

seek.etymology: OE, seken, AS. s, s; akin to OS. s, LG. söken, D. zoeken, OHG. suohhan, G. suchen, Icel. s, Sw. söka, Dan. söge, Goth. s, and E. sake. Cf. Beseech, Ransack, Sagacious, Sake, Soc.

seel.etymology: F.siller, ciller, fr. cil an eyelash, L. cilium.

seem.etymology: OE. semen to seem, to become, befit, AS. s to satisfy, pacify; akin to Icel. s to honor, to bear with, conform to, s becoming, fit, s to beseem, to befit, sama to beseem, semja to arrange, settle, put right, Goth. samjan to please, and to E. same. The sense is probably due to the adj. seemly. sq. root191. See Same, a., and cf. Seemly.

seemly.etymology: Icel. s, fr. s becoming, fit; akin to samr same, E. same; the sense being properly, the same or like, hence, fitting. See Seem, v. i.

seesaw.etymology: Probably a reduplication of saw, to express the alternate motion to and fro, as in the act of sawing.

seethe.etymology: OE. sethen, AS. seó; akin to D. sieden, OHG. siodan, G. sieden, Icel. sj, Sw. sjuda, Dan. syde, Goth. saubs a burnt offering. Cf. Sod, n., Sodden, Suds.

segment.etymology: L. segmentum, fr. secare to cut, cut off: cf. F. segment. See Saw a cutting instrument.

segregate.etymology: L. segregatus, p. p. of segregare to separate; pref. se- aside + grex, gregis, a flock or herd. See Gregarious.

seignior.etymology: OF. seignor, F. seigneur, cf. It. signore, Sp. señor from an objective case of L. senier elder. See Senior.

seigniory.etymology: OE. seignorie, OF. seigneurie, F. seigneurie; cf. It. signoria.

roots.meaning: A suffix indicating something drawn or written, a drawing, writing; -- as, monogram, telegram, chronogram.
A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.
A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

seize.etymology: OE. seisen, saisen, OF. seisir, saisir, F. saisir, of Teutonic origin, and akin to E. set. The meaning is properly, to set, put, place, hence, to put in possession of. See Set, v. t.

selaginella.etymology: NL., fr. L. selago, -inis, a kind of plant.

seldom.etymology: AS. seldan, seldon, seldum, fr. seld rare; akin to OFries. sielden, D. zelden, G. selten, OHG. seltan, Icel. sjaldan, Dan. sielden, Sw. sällan, Goth. sildaleiks marvelous.

select.etymology: L. selectus, p. p. of seligere to select; pref. se- aside + levere to gather. See Legend.

selenium.etymology: NL., from Gr. tellurium (from L. tellus the earth), being, as it were, a companion to it.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

self.etymology: AS. self, seolf, sylf; akin to OS. self, OFries. self, D. zelf, G. selb, selber, selbst, Dan. selv. Sw. sjelf, Icel. sjalfr, Goth. silba. Cf. Selavage.

sell.etymology: F. selle, L. sella, akin to sedere to sit. See Sit.

selvage.etymology: Self + edge, i. e., its own proper edge; cf. OD. selfegge.

selvedge.etymology: Self + edge, i. e., its own proper edge; cf. OD. selfegge.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

semen.etymology: L., from the root of serere, satum, to sow. See Sow to scatter seed.

semester.etymology: G., from L. semestris half-yearly; sex six + mensis a month.

semibreve.etymology: Pref. semi- + breve: cf. F. semi-breve, It. semibreve.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying half, and sometimes partly or imperfectly; as, semiannual, half yearly; semitransparent, imperfectly transparent.

seminal.etymology: L. seminalis, fr. semen, seminis, seed, akin to serere to sow: cf. F. seminal. See Sow to scatter seed.

seminary.etymology: L. seminarium, fr. seminarius belonging to seed, fr. semon, seminis, seed. See Seminal.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.

semiology.etymology: Gr. shmei^on a mark, a sign + -logy.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

semiotic.etymology: Gr. shmei^on a mark, a sign.

roots.meaning: A prefix signifying half, and sometimes partly or imperfectly; as, semiannual, half yearly; semitransparent, imperfectly transparent.

semolina.etymology: It. semolino, from semola bran, L. simila the finest wheat flour. Cf. Semoule, Simnel.

sempiternal.etymology: L. sempiternus, fr. semper always: cf. F. sempiternel.

senate.etymology: OE. senat, F. sénat, fr. L. senatus, fr. senex, gen. senis, old, an old man. See Senior, Sir.

senator.etymology: OE. senatour, OF. senatour, F. sénateur, fr. L. senator.

send.etymology: AS. sendan; akin to OS. sendian, D. zenden, G. senden, OHG. senten, Icel. senda, Sw. sända, Dan. sende, Goth. sandjan, and to Goth. sinp a time (properly, a going), gasinpa companion, OHG. sind journey, AS. si, Icel. sinni a walk, journey, a time. W. hynt a way, journey, OIr. s. Cf. Sense.

senecio.etymology: L., groundsel, lit., an old man. So called in allusion to the hoary appearance of the pappus.

senescent.etymology: L. senescent, p. pr. of senescere to grow old, incho. fr. senere to be old.

seneschal.etymology: OF. seneschal, LL. seniscalcus, of Teutonic origin; cf. Goth. sineigs old, skalks, OHG. scalch, AS. scealc. Cf. Senior, Marshal.

senile.etymology: L. senilis, from senex, gen. senis, old, an old man: cf. F. sénile. See Senior.

senior.etymology: L. senior, compar. of senex, gen. senis, old. See Sir.

senna.etymology: Cf. It. & Sp. sena, Pg. sene, F. séné; all fr. Ar. sana.

sense.etymology: L. sensus, from sentire, sensum, to perceive, to feel, from the same root as E. send; cf. OHG. sin sense, mind, sinnan to go, to journey, G. sinnen to meditate, to think: cf. F. sens. For the change of meaning cf. See, v. t. See Send, and cf. Assent, Consent, Scent, v. t., Sentence, Sentient.

sensible.etymology: F., fr. L. sensibilis, fr. sensus sense.

sensorium.etymology: L., fr. sentire, sensum, to discern or perceive by the senses.

sensual.etymology: L. sensualis, from sensus sense: cf. F. sensuel.

sensuality.etymology: CF. F. sensualité, L. sensualitas sensibility, capacity for sensation.

sentence.etymology: F., from L. sententia, for sentientia, from sentire to discern by the senses and the mind, to feel, to think. See Sense, n., and cf. Sentiensi.

sentient.etymology: L. sentiens, -entis, p. pr. of sentire to discern or perceive by the senses. See Sense.

sentiment.etymology: OE. sentement, OF. sentement, F. sentiment, fr. L. sentire to perceive by the senses and mind, to feel, to think. See Sentient, a.

sentinel.etymology: F. sentinelle (cf. It. sentinella); probably originally, a litle path, the sentinel's beat,, and a dim. of a word meaning, path; cf. F. sente path. L. semita; and OF. sentine, sentele, senteret, diminutive words. Cf. Sentry.

sentry.etymology: Probably from OF. senteret a little patch; cf. F. sentier path, and OF. sente. See Sentinel.

sepal.etymology: NL. sepalum, formed in imitation of NL. petalum, petal, to denote one of the divisions of the calyx: cf. F. sépale.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

separate.etymology: From Middle English separaten ( “ to separate ” ) , from separat ( “ separated ” ) +‎ -en , from Latin sēparātus , perfect passive participle of sēparō ( “ to separate ” ) (see -ate ( verb-forming suffix ) ), from sē- ( “ apart ” ) +‎ parō ( “ prepare ” ) , ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *per- ( “ produce, procure, bring forward, bring forth ” ) . Displaced Middle English scheden , from Old English scēadan (whence English shed ).

roots.meaning: Combining forms fr. Gr. li`qos a stone; -- used chiefly in naming minerals and rocks.

september.etymology: L., fr. septem seven, as being the seventh month of the Roman year, which began with March: cf. F. septembre. See Seven.

septenary.etymology: L. septenairus, from septeni seven each, septem seven: cf. F. septénaire. See Seven.

septet.etymology: From L. septem seven, like duet, from L. duo.

septette.etymology: From L. septem seven, like duet, from L. duo.

roots.meaning: A combining form meaning seven; as, septifolious, seven-leaved; septi-lateral, seven-sided.

A suffix, denoting that the element indicated enters into certain compounds with its highest valence, or with a valence relatively higher than in compounds where the name of the element ends in -ous; as, ferric, sulphuric. It is also used in the general sense of pertaining to; as, hydric, sodic, calcic.

septillion.etymology: F. septilion, formed fr. L. septem seven, in imitation of million.

septuagesima.etymology: NL., fr. L. septuagesimus the seventieth, fr. septuaginta seventy.

septum.etymology: L. septum, saeptum, an inclosure, hedge, fence, fr. sepire, saepire, to hedge in, inclose.

septuple.etymology: LL. septuplus; cf. Gr. septuple. Cf. Double, Quadruple.

sepulcher.etymology: OE. sepulcre, OF. sepulcre, F. sépulcre, fr. L. sepulcrum, sepulchrum, fr. sepelire to bury.

sepulchre.etymology: OE. sepulcre, OF. sepulcre, F. sépulcre, fr. L. sepulcrum, sepulchrum, fr. sepelire to bury.

sepulture.etymology: F. sépulture, L. sepultura, fr. sepelire, sepultum, to bury.

sequel.etymology: L. sequela, fr. sequit to follow: cf. F. séquelle a following. See Sue to follow.

sequela.etymology: L., a follower, a result, from sequit to follow.

sequence.etymology: F. séquence, L. sequentia, fr. sequens. See Sequent.

sequent.etymology: L. sequens, -entis, p. pr. of sequi to follow. See Sue to follow.

sequester.etymology: F. séquestrer, L. sequestrare to give up for safe keeping, from sequester a depositary or trustee in whose hands the thing contested was placed until the dispute was settled. Cf. Sequestrate.

sequin.etymology: F. sequin, It. zecchino, from zecca the mint, fr. Ar. sekkah, sikkah, a die, a stamp. Cf. Zechin.

sequoia.etymology: NL. So called by Dr. Endlicher in honor of Sequoyah, who invented the Cherokee alphabet.

seraglio.etymology: It. serraglio, originally, an inclosure of palisades, afterwards also, a palace, seraglio (by confusion with Per. sera\'8ba a palace, an entirely different word), fr. serrare to shut, fr. LL. serra a bar for fastening doors, L. sera. See Serry, Series.

serenade.etymology: F. sérénade, It. serenata, probably fr. L. serenus serene (cf. Serene), misunderstood as a derivative fr. L. serus late. Cf. Soirée.

serf.etymology: F., fr. L. serus servant, slave; akin to servare to protect, preserve, observe, and perhaps originally, a client, a man under one's protection. Cf. Serve, v. t.

serge.etymology: F. serge, sarge, originally, a silken stuff, fr. L. serica, f. or neut. pl. of sericus silken. See Sericeous, Silk.

sergeant.etymology: F. sergent, fr. L. serviens, -entis, p. pr. of servire to serve. See Serve, and cf. Servant.

sericeous.etymology: L. sericus silken, sericum Seric stuff, silk, fr. Sericus belonging to the Seres, Gr. Silk, Serge a woolen stuff.

series.etymology: L. series, fr. serere, sertum, to join or bind together; cf. Gr. sarit thread. Cf. Assert, Desert a solitude, Exert, Insert, Seraglio.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.

serious.etymology: L. serius: cf. F. sérieux, LL. seriosus.

sermon.etymology: OE. sermoun, sermun, F. sermon, fr. L. sermo, - onis, a speaking, discourse, probably fr. serer, sertum, to join, connect; hence, a connected speech. See Series.

serotine.etymology: F. sérotine, fr. L. serotinus that comes or happens late.

serpent.etymology: F., fr. L. serpens, -entis (sc. bestia), fr. serpens, p. pr. of serpere to creep; akin to Gr. sarp, and perhaps to L. repere, E. reptile. Cf. Herpes.

serrate.etymology: L. serratus, fr. serra a saw; perhaps akin to secare to cut, E. saw a cutting instrument. Cf. Sierra.

serrated.etymology: L. serratus, fr. serra a saw; perhaps akin to secare to cut, E. saw a cutting instrument. Cf. Sierra.

serrulate.etymology: L. serrula a lttle saw, dim. of serra a saw.

sertularia.etymology: NL., dim. fr. L. serta a garland.

serum.etymology: L., akin to Gr. sara curd.

servant.etymology: OE. servant, servaunt, F. servant, a & p. pr. of servir to serve, L. servire. See Serve, and cf. Sergeant.

serve.etymology: OE. serven, servien, OF. & F. servir, fr. L. servire; akin to servus a servant or slave, servare to protect, preserve, observe; cf. Zend har to protect, haurva protecting. Cf. Conserve, Desert merit, Dessert, Observe, Serf, Sergeant.

service.etymology: Properly, the tree which bears serve, OE. serves, pl., service berries, AS. syrfe service tree; akin to L. sorbus.

servile.etymology: L. servile, fr. servus a servant or slave: cf. F. servile. See Serve.

servitor.etymology: L., fr. servire to serve: cf. F. serviteur.

sesquipedalian.etymology: Sesqui- + pedal: cf. F. sesquipédal, L. sesquipedalis.

roots.meaning: A combining form (also used adjectively) denoting that three atoms or equivalents of the substance to the name of which it is prefixed are combined with two of some other element or radical; as, sesquibromide, sesquicarbonate, sesquichloride, sesquioxide.

sess.etymology: Aphetic form of assess. See Assess, Cess.

sessile.etymology: L. sessilis low, dwarf, from sedere, sessum, to sit: cf. F. sessile.

session.etymology: L. sessio, fr. sedere, sessum, to sit: cf. F. session. See Sit.

sestet.etymology: It. sestetto, fr. sesto sixth, L. sextus, fr. sex six.

set.etymology: OE. setten, AS. setton; akin to OS. settian, OFries. setta, D. zetten, OHG. sezzen, G. setzen, Icel. setja, Sw. sätta, Dan. s, Goth. satjan; causative from the root of E. sit. Sit, and cf. Seize.

setaceous.etymology: L. seta a bristle: cf. F. sétacé.

seton.etymology: F. séton (cf. It. setone), from L. seta a thick, stiff hair, a bristle.

setose.etymology: L. setosus, saetosus, from seta, saeta, bristle: cf. F. séteux.

settee.etymology: From Set; cf. Settle a seat.

settle.etymology: OE. setel, setil, a seat, AS. setl: akin to OHG. sezzal, G. sessel, Goth. sitls, and E. sit. sq. root154. See Sit.

seven.etymology: OE. seven, seoven, seofen, AS. seofon, seofan, seofen; akin to D. zeven, OS., Goth., & OHG. sibun, G. sieben, Icel. sjau, sjö, Sw. sju, Dan. syv, Lith. septyni, Russ. seme, W. saith, Gael. seachd, Ir. seacht, L. septem, Gr. saptan. sq. root305. Cf. Hebdomad, Heptagon, September.

seventeen.etymology: OE. seventene, AS. seofontyne, i. e., seven- ten. Cf. Seventy.

seventeenth.etymology: From Seventeen: cf. AS. seofonteóedha, seofonteogeedha.

seventy.etymology: AS. hund-seofontig. See Seven, and Ten, and cf. Seventeen, Sixty.

sever.etymology: OF. sevrer, severer, to separate, F. sevrer to wean, fr. L. separare. See Separate, and cf. Several.

several.etymology: OF., fr. LL. separalis, fr. L. separ separate, different. See Sever, Separate.

severe.etymology: L. severus; perhaps akin to Gr. swikns innocent, chaste: cf. F. sévère. Cf. Asseverate, Persevere.

sewer.etymology: OF. sewiere, seuwiere, ultimately fr. L. ex out + a derivative of aqua water; cf. OF. essevour a drain, essever, esseuwer, essiaver, to cause to flow, to drain, to flow, LL. exaquatorium a channel through which water runs off. Cf. Ewer, Aquarium.

sext.etymology: L. sexta, fem. of sextus sixtt, fr. sex six: cf. F. sexte.

sextant.etymology: L. sextans, -antis, the sixth part of an as, fr. sextus sixth, sex six. See Six.

sextillion.etymology: Formed (in imitation of million) fr. L. sextus sixth, sex six: cf. F. sextilion.

sextuple.etymology: Formed (in imitation of quadruple) fr. L. sextus sixth: cf. F. sextuple.

sexual.etymology: L. sexualis, fr. sexus sex: cf. F. sexuel.

sforzando.etymology: It. sforzando, p. pr., and sforzato, p. p. of sforzare to force.

shabby.etymology: See Shab, n., Scabby, and Scab.

shack.etymology: Prov. E., to shake, to shed. See Shake.

shad.etymology: AS. sceadda a kind of fish, akin to Prov. G. schade; cf. Ir. & Gael. sgadan a herring, W. ysgadan herrings; all perhaps akin to E. skate a fish.

shaddock.etymology: Said to be so called from a Captain Shaddock, who first brought this fruit from the East Indies.

shade.etymology: OE. shade, shadewe, schadewe, AS. sceadu, scead; akin to OS. skado, D. schaduw, OHG. scato, (gen. scatewes), G. schatten, Goth. skadus, Ir. & Gael. sgath, and probably to Gr. Shadow, Shed a hat.

shadow.etymology: Originally the same word as shade. sq. root162. See Shade.

shaft.etymology: OE. shaft, schaft, AS. sceaft; akin to D. schacht, OHG. scaft, G. schaft, Dan. & Sw. skaft handle, haft, Icel. skapt, and probably to L. scapus, Gr. Scape, Scepter, Shave.

shag.etymology: AS. sceacga a bush of hair; akin to Icel. skegg the beard, Sw. skägg, Dan. skj. Cf. Schock of hair.

shah.etymology: Per. shah a king, sovereign, prince. Cf. Checkmate, Chess, Pasha.

shake.etymology: OE. shaken, schaken, AS. scacan, sceacan; akin to Icel. & Sw. skaka, OS. skakan, to depart, to flee. sq. root161. Cf. Shock, v.

shako.etymology: Hung. csákó: cf. F. shako, schako.

shale.etymology: AS. scealy, scalu. See Scalme, and cf. Shell.

shallot.etymology: OF. eschalote (for escalone), F. échalote. See Scallion, and cf. Eschalot.

shallow.etymology: OE. schalowe, probably originally, sloping or shelving; cf. Icel. skjalgr wry, squinting, AS. sceolh, D. & G. scheel, OHG. schelah. Cf. Shelve to slope, Shoal shallow.

sham.etymology: Originally the same word as shame, hence, a disgrace, a trick. See Shame, n.

shamble.etymology: OE. schamel a bench, stool, AS. scamel, sceamol, a bench, form, stool, fr. L. scamellum, dim. of scamnum a bench, stool.

shame.etymology: OE. shame, schame, AS. scamu, sceamu; akin to OS. & OHG. scama, G. scham, Icel. skömm, shkamm, Sw. & Dan. skam, D. & G. schande, Goth. skanda shame, skaman sik to be ashamed; perhaps from a root skam meaning to cover, and akin to the root (kam) of G. hemd shirt, E. chemise. Cf. Sham.

shamefaced.etymology: For shamefast; AS. scamf. See Shame, n., and Fast firm.

shammy.etymology: F. chamious a chamois, shammy leather. See Chamois.

shampoo.etymology: Hind. champna to press, to squeeze.

shamrock.etymology: L. seamrog, seamar, trefoil, white clover, white honeysuckle; akin to Gael. seamrag.

shank.etymology: OE. shanke, schanke, schonke, AS. scanca, sceanca, sconca, sceonca; akin to D. schonk a bone, G. schenkel thigh, shank, schinken ham, OHG. scincha shank, Dan. & Sw. skank. sq. root161. Cf. Skink, v.

shanty.etymology: Said to be fr. Ir. sean old + tig. a house.

shape.etymology: OE. shapen, schapen, AS. sceapian. The p. p. shapen is from the strong verb, AS. scieppan, scyppan, sceppan, p. p. sceapen. See Shape, n.

shard.etymology: AS. sceard, properly a p. p. from the root of scearn to shear, to cut; akin to D. schaard a fragment, G. scharte a notch, Icel. skar. See Shear, and cf. Sherd.

share.etymology: OE. schar, AS. scear; akin to OHG. scaro, G. schar, pflugshar, and E. shear, v. See Shear.

shark.etymology: Of uncertain origin; perhaps through OF. fr. carcharus a kind of dogfish, Gr. Shark, v. t.&i.); cf. Corn. scarceas.

sharp.etymology: OE. sharp, scharp, scarp, AS. scearp; akin to OS. skarp, LG. scharp, D. scherp, G. scharf, Dan. & Sw. skarp, Icel. skarpr. Cf. Escarp, Scrape, Scorpion.

shatter.etymology: OE. schateren, scateren, to scatter, to dash, AS. scateran; cf. D. schateren to crack, to make a great noise, OD. schetteren to scatter, to burst, to crack. Cf. Scatter.

shave.etymology: OE. shaven, schaven, AS. scafan, sceafan; akin to D. schaven, G. schaben, Icel. skafa, Sw. skafva, Dan. skave, Goth. scaban, Russ. kopate to dig, Gr. scabere to scratch, to scrape. Cf. Scab, Shaft, Shape.

shaw.etymology: OE. schawe, scha, thicket, grove, AS. scaga; akin to Dan. skov, Sw. skog, Icel. sk.

shawl.etymology: Per. & Hind. shal: cf. F. châle.

shawm.etymology: OE. shalmie, OF. chalemie; cf. F. chalumeau shawm, chaume haulm, stalk; all fr. L. calamus a reed, reed pipe. See Haulm, and cf. Calumet.

sheaf.etymology: OE. sheef, shef, schef, AS. sceáf; akin to D. schoof, OHG. scoub, G. schaub, Icel. skauf a fox's brush, and E. shove. See Shove.

shear.etymology: OE. sheren, scheren, to shear, cut, shave, AS. sceran, scieran, scyran; akin to D. & G. scheren, Icel. skera, Dan. ski, Gr. Jeer, Score, Shard, Share, Sheer to turn aside.

shears.etymology: Formerly used also in the singular. See Shear, n.,1.

shearwater.etymology: Shear + water; cf. G. wassersherer; -- so called from its running lightly along the surface of the water.

sheatfish.etymology: Cf. dial. G. scheid, schaid, schaiden.

sheath.etymology: OE. schethe, AS. scæedh, sceáedh, sceedh; akin to OS. skeedhia, D. scheede, G. scheide, OHG. sceida, Sw. skida, Dan. skede, Icel. skeiedhir, pl., and to E. shed, v.t., originally meaning, to separate, to part. See Shed.

shebeen.etymology: Of Irish origin; cf. Ir. seapa a shop.

shed.etymology: The same word as shade. See Shade.

sheen.etymology: OE. sehene, AS. sciéne, sc, sc, splendid, beautiful; akin to OFries. sk, sk, OS. sc, D. schoon, G. schön, OHG. sc, Goth, skanus, and E. shew; the original meaning being probably, visible, worth seeing. It is not akin to E. shine. See Shew, v. t.

sheep.etymology: OE. shep, scheep, AS. sc, sceáp; akin to OFries. sk, LG. & D. schaap, G. schaf, OHG. scaf, Skr. chaga. sq. root295. Cf. Sheepherd.

sheepshead.etymology: So called because of the fancied resemblance of its head and front teeth to those of a sheep.

sheer.etymology: OE. shere, skere, pure, bright, Icel. sk; akin to skirr, AS. scir, OS. skiri, MHG. schir, G. schier, Dan. sk, Sw. skär, Goth. skeirs clear, and E. shine. sq. root157. See Shine, v. i.

sheet.etymology: OE. shete, schete, AS. sc, sc, fr. sceát a projecting corner, a fold in a garment (akin to D. schoot sheet, bosom, lap, G. schoss bosom, lap, flap of a coat, Icel. skaut, Goth. skauts the hem of a garment); originally, that which shoots out, from the root of AS. sceótan to shoot. sq. root159. See Shoot, v. t.

sheik.etymology: Ar. sheikh, shaykh, a venerable old man, a chief, fr. shakha to grow or be old.

shekel.etymology: Heb. shegel, fr. shagal to weigh.

shelf.etymology: OE. shelfe, schelfe, AS. scylfe; akin to G. schelfe, Icel. skjalf. In senses 2 & 3, perhaps a different word (cf. Shelve, v. i.).

shell.etymology: OE. shelle, schelle, AS. scell, scyll; akin to D. shel, Icel. skel, Goth. skalja a tile, and E. skill. Cf. Scale of fishes, Shale, Skill.

shellac.etymology: Shell + lac a resinous substance; cf. D. shellak, G. schellack.

shelter.etymology: Cf. OE. scheltrun, shiltroun, schelltrome, scheldtrome, a guard, squadron, AS. scildtruma a troop of men with shields; scild shield + truma a band of men. See Shield, n.

shelve.etymology: Perhapss originally from the same source as shallow, but influenced by shelf a ledge, a platform.

shepherd.etymology: OE. schepherde, schephirde, AS. sceáphyrde; sceáp sheep + hyrde, hirde, heorde, a herd, a guardian. See Sheep, and Herd.

sherbet.etymology: Ar. sherbet, shorbet, sharbat, properly, one drink or sip, a draught, beverage, from shariba to drink. Cf. Sorbet, Sirup, Shrub a drink.

sheriff.etymology: OE. shereve, AS. scir-ger; scir a shire + ger a reeve. See Shire, and Reeve, and cf. Shrievalty.

sherry.etymology: So called from Xeres, a Spanish town near Cadiz, x in Spanish having been formerly pronounced like sh in English.

shiah.etymology: Ar. shi'aia follower of the sect of Ali, fr. shi'at, shi'ah, a multitude following one another in pursuit of the same object, the sect of Ali, fr. sha'a to follow.

shibboleth.etymology: Heb. shibboleth an ear of corn, or a stream, a flood.

shield.etymology: OE. sheld, scheld, AS. scield, scild, sceld, scyld; akin to OS. scild, OFries. skeld, D. & G. schild, OHG. scilt, Icel. skjöldr, Sw. sköld, Dan. skiold, Goth. skildus; of uncertain origin. Cf. Sheldrake.

shift.etymology: OE. shiften, schiften, to divide, change, remove. AS. sciftan to divide; akin to LG. & D. schiften to divide, distinguish, part Icel. skipta to divide, to part, to shift, to change, Dan skifte, Sw. skifta, and probably to Icel. skifa to cut into slices, as n., a slice, and to E. shive, sheave, n., shiver, n.

shiite.etymology: Ar. shi'aia follower of the sect of Ali, fr. shi'at, shi'ah, a multitude following one another in pursuit of the same object, the sect of Ali, fr. sha'a to follow.

shilling.etymology: OE. shilling, schilling, AS. scilling; akin to D. schelling, OS. & OHG. scilling, G. schilling, Sw. & Dan. skilling, Icel. skillingr, Goth. skilliggs, and perh. to OHG. scellan to sound, G. schallen.

shiloh.etymology: Heb. shiloh, literally, quiet, rest, fr. shalah to rest.

shimmer.etymology: OE. schimeren, AS. scimerian; akin to scimian, sciman, to glitter, D. schemeren, G. schimmern, Dan. skimre, Sw. skimra, AS. scima a light, brightness, Icel. skima, Goth. skeima a torch, a lantern, and E. shine. sq. root157. See Shine, v. i.

shin.etymology: OE. shine, schine, AS. scina; akin to D. scheen, OHG. scina, G. schiene, schienbein, Dan. skinnebeen, Sw. skenben. Cf. Chine.

shine.etymology: OE. shinen, schinen, AS. scinan; akin to D. schijnen, OFries. skina, OS. & OHG. scinan, G. scheinen, Icel.skina, Sw. skina, Dan. skinne, Goth. skeinan, and perh. to Gr. Sheer pure, and Shimmer.

shingle.etymology: Prob. from Norw. singl, singling, coarse gravel, small round stones.

shingles.etymology: OF. cengle a girth, F. sangle, fr. L. cingulum a girdle, fr. cingere to gird. Cf. Cincture, Cingle, Surcingle.

shinto.etymology: Chin. shin god + tao way, doctrine.

shipper.etymology: See Ship, n., and cf. Skipper.

shire.etymology: AS. scire, scir, a division, province, county. Cf. Sheriff.

shirk.etymology: Probably the same word as shark. See Shark, v. t.

shirt.etymology: OE. schirte, sherte, schurte; akin to Icel. skyrta, Dan. skiorte, Sw. skjorta, Dan. skiört a petticoat, D. schort a petticoat, an argon, G. schurz, schürze, an argon; all probably from the root of E. short, as being originally a short garment. See Short, and cf. Skirt.

shiver.etymology: OE. schivere, fr. shive; cf. G. schifer a splinter, slate, OHG. scivere a splinter, Dan. & Sw. skifer a slate. See Shive, and cf. Skever.

shoal.etymology: AS. scolu, sceolu, a company, multitude, crowd, akin to OS. skola; probably originally, a division, and akin to Icel. skilja to part, divide. See Skill, and cf. School. of fishes.

shock.etymology: OE. schokke; cf. OD schocke, G. schock a heap, quantity, threescore, MHG. schoc, Sw. skok, and also G. hocke a heap of hay, Lith. kugis.

shoddy.etymology: Perhaps fr. Shed, v. t.; as meaning originally, waste stuff shedor thrown off.

shoe.etymology: OE. sho, scho, AS. sc, sceóh; akin to OFries. sk, OS. sk, D. schoe, schoen, G. schuh, OHG. scuoh, Icel. sk, Dan. & Sw. sko, Goth. sk; of unknown origin.

shogun.etymology: Chin. tsiang kiÜn commander in chief.

shoo.etymology: Cf. G. scheuchen to scare, drive away.

shook.etymology: Cf. Shock a bundle of sheaves.

shoot.etymology: F. chute. See Chute. Confused with shoot to let fly.

shop.etymology: OE. shoppe, schoppe, AS. sceoppa a treasury, a storehouse, stall, booth; akin to scypen a shed, LG. schup a shed, G. schoppen, schuppen, a shed, a coachhouse, OHG. scopf.

shoplifter.etymology: Shop + lift. See Lift to steal.

shore.etymology: OE. schore; akin to LG. schore, D. schoor, OD. schoore, Icel. skor, and perhaps to E. shear, as being a piece cut off.

short.etymology: OE. short, schort, AS. scort, sceort; akin to OHG. scurz, Icel. skorta to be short of, to lack, and perhaps to E. shear, v. t. Cf. Shirt.

shot.etymology: AS. scot, sceot, fr. sceótan to shoot; akin to D. sschot, Icel. skot. sq. root159. See Scot a share, Shoot, v. t., and cf. Shot a shooting.

shote.etymology: AS. sceóta a darting fish, a trout, fr. sceótan. See Shoot, v. t.

shoulder.etymology: OE. shulder, shuldre, schutder, AS. sculdor; akin to D. schoulder, G. schulter, OHG. scultarra, Dan. skulder, Sw. skuldra.

shout.etymology: OE. shouten, of unknown origin; perhaps akin to shoot; cf. Icel. sk, sk, a taunt.

shove.etymology: OE. shoven, AS. scofian, fr. sc; akin to OFries. sk, D. schuiven, G. schieben, OHG. scioban, Icel. sk, sk, Sw. skuffa, Dan. skuffe, Goth. afskiuban to put away, cast away; cf. Skr. kshubh to become agitated, to quake, Lith. skubrus quick, skubinti to hasten. sq. root160. Cf. Sheaf a bundle of stalks, Scoop, Scuffle.

shovel.etymology: OE. shovele, schovele, AS. scoft, sceoft; akin to D. schoffel, G. schaufel, OHG. sc, Dan. skovl, Sw. skofvel, skyffel, and to E. shove. sq. root160. See Shove, v. t.

show.etymology: OE. schowen, shewen, schewen, shawen, AS. sceáwian, to look, see, view; akin to OS. scaw, OFries. skawia, D. schouwen, OHG. scouw, G. schauen, Dan. skue, Sw. sk, Icel. sko, Goth. usskawjan to waken, skuggwa a mirror, Icel. skuggy shade, shadow, L. cavere to be on one's guard, Gr. kavi wise. Cf. Caution, Scavenger, Sheen.

shower.etymology: OE. shour, schour, AS. se; akin to D. schoer, G. schauer, OHG. sc, Icel. sk, Sw. skur, Goth. sk a storm of wind; of uncertain origin.

shred.etymology: OE. shrede, schrede, AS. screáde; akin to OD. schroode, G. schrot a piece cut off, Icel. skrjothr a shred, and to E. shroud. Cf. Screed, Scroll, Scrutiny.

shrewd.etymology: Originally the p. p. of shrew, v.t.

shriek.etymology: OE. shriken, originallythe same word as E. screech. See Screech, and cf. Screak.

shrift.etymology: OE. shrift, schrift, AS. scrift, fr. scrifan to shrive. See Shrive.

shrike.etymology: Akin to Icel. skrikja a shrieker, the shrike, and E. shriek; cf. AS. scric a thrush. See Shriek, v. i.

shrill.etymology: OE. shril, schril; akin to LG. schrell, G. schrill. See Shrill,v. i.

shrimp.etymology: Cf. AS. scrimman to dry up, wither, MHG. schrimpfen to shrink, G. schrumpfen, Dan. skrumpe, skrumpes, Da. & Sw. skrumpen shriveled. Cf. Scrimp, Shrink, Shrivel.

shrine.etymology: OE. schrin, AS. scrin, from L. scrinium a case, chest, box.

shrink.etymology: OE. shrinken, schrinken, AS. scrincan; akin to OD. schrincken, and probably to Sw. skrynka a wrinkle, skrynkla to wrinkle, to rumple, and E. shrimp, n. & v., scrimp. CF. Shrimp.

shrive.etymology: OE. shriven, schriven, AS. scrivan to shrive, to impose penance or punishment; akin to OFries. skriva to impose punishment; cf. OS. biskriban to be troubled. Cf. Shrift, Shrovetide.

shrivel.etymology: Probably akin to shrimp, shrink; cf. dial. AS. screpa to pine away, Norw. skrypa to waste, skryp, skryv, transitory, frail, Sw. skröpling feeble, Dan. skröbelig, Icel. skrj brittle, frail.

shroud.etymology: OE. shroud, shrud, schrud, AS. scr a garment, clothing; akin to Icel. skru the shrouds of a ship, furniture of a church, a kind of stuff, Sw. skrud dress, attire, and E. shred. See Shred, and cf. Shrood.

shrovetide.etymology: From shrive to take a confession (OE. imp. shrof, AS. scraf) + tide.

shrub.etymology: Ar. shirb, shurb, a drink, beverage, fr. shariba to drink. Cf. Sirup, Sherbet.

shrug.etymology: Probably akin to shrink, p. p. shrunk; cf. Dan. skrugge, skrukke, to stoop, dial. Sw. skrukka, skruga, to crouch.

shuck.etymology: Perhaps akin to G. shote a husk, pod, shell.

shudder.etymology: OE. shoderen, schuderen; akin to LG. schuddern, D. schudden to shake, OS. skuddian, G. schaudern to shudder, schütteln to shake, schütten to pour, to shed, OHG. scutten, scuten, to shake.

shuffle.etymology: Originally the same word as scuffle, and properly a freq. of shove. See Shove, and Scuffle.

shun.etymology: OE. shunien, schunien, schonien, AS. scunian, sceonian; cf. D. schuinen to slepe, schuin oblique, sloping, Icel. skunda, skynda, to hasten. Cf. Schooner, Scoundrel, Shunt.

shunt.etymology: Prov. E., to move from, to put off, fr. OE. shunten, schunten, schounten; cf. D. schuinte a slant, slope, Icel. skunda to hasten. Cf. Shun.

shut.etymology: OE. shutten, schutten, shetten, schitten, AS. scyttan to shut or lock up (akin to D. schutten, G. schützen to protect), properly, to fasten with a bolt or bar shot across, fr. AS. sceótan to shoot. sq. root159. See Shoot.

shuttle.etymology: Also shittle, OE. schitel, scytyl, schetyl; cf. OE. schitel a bolt of a door, AS. scyttes; all from AS. sceótan to shoot; akin to Dan. skyttel, skytte, shuttle, dial. Sw. skyttel, sköttel. sq. root159. See Shoot, and cf. Shittle, Skittles.

shy.etymology: OE. schey, skey, sceouh, AS. sceóh; akin to Dan. sky, Sw. skygg, D. schuw, MHG. schiech, G. scheu, OHG. sciuhen to be or make timid. Cf. Eschew.

sib.etymology: AS. sibb alliance, gesib a relative. sq. root289. See Gossip.

sibilant.etymology: L. sibilans, -antis, p. pr. of sibilare to hiss: cf. F. sibilant.

sick.etymology: OE. sek, sik, ill, AS. seóc; akin to OS. siok, seoc, OFries. siak, D. ziek, G. siech, OHG. sioh, Icel. sj, Sw. sjuk, Dan. syg, Goth. siuks ill, siukan to be ill.

sickle.etymology: OE. sikel, AS. sicol; akin to D. sikkel, G. sichel, OHG. sihhila, Dan. segel, segl, L. secula, fr. secare to cut; or perhaps from L. secula. See Saw a cutting instrument.

side.etymology: AS. side; akin to D. zijde, G. seite, OHG. sita, Icel. si, Dan. side, Sw. sida; cf. AS. sid large, spacious, Icel. si long, hanging.

sidereal.etymology: L. sidereus, from sidus, sideris, a constellation, a star. Cf. Sideral, Consider, Desire.

siege.etymology: OE. sege, OF. siege, F. siège a seat, a siege; cf. It. seggia, seggio, zedio, a seat, asseggio, assedio, a siege, F. assiéger to besiege, It. & LL. assediare, L. obsidium a siege, besieging; all ultimately fr. L. sedere to sit. See Sit, and cf. See, n.

sienna.etymology: It. terra di Siena, fr. Siena in Italy.

sierra.etymology: Sp., properly, a saw, fr. L. serra a saw. See Serrate.

siesta.etymology: Sp., probably fr. L. sessitare to sit much or long, v. freq. of sedere, sessum, to sit. See Sit.

sieve.etymology: OE. sive, AS. sife; akin to D. zeef, zift, OHG. sib, G. sieb. sq. root151a. Cf. Sift.

sift.etymology: AS. siftan, from sife sieve. sq. root151a. See Sieve.

sigh.etymology: OE. sighen, si; cf. also OE. siken, AS. sican, and OE. sighten, si, sichten, AS. siccettan; all, perhaps, of imitative origin.

sight.etymology: OE. sight, si, siht, AS. siht, gesiht, gesih, gesieh, gesyh; akin to D. gezicht, G. sicht, gesicht, Dan. sigte, Sw. sigt, from the root of E. see. See See, v. t.

sign.etymology: F. signe, L. signum; cf. AS. segen, segn, a sign, standard, banner, also fr. L. signum. Cf. Ensign, Resign, Seal a stamp, Signal, Signet.

signal.etymology: F., fr. LL. signale, fr. L. signum. See Sign, n.

signature.etymology: F. (cf. It. signatura, segnatura, Sp. & LL. signatura), from L. signare, signatum. See Sign, v. t.

signet.etymology: OF. signet a signet, F., a bookmark, dim. of signe. See Sign, n., and cf. Sennet.

significant.etymology: L. significans, -antis, p. pr. of significare. See Signify.

signify.etymology: F. signifier, L. significare; signum a sign + - ficare (in comp.) to make. See Sign, n., and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

silence.etymology: F., fr. L. silentium. See Silent.

silene.etymology: NL., fr. L. Silenus, the attendant of Bacchus.

silent.etymology: L. silens, -entis, p. pr. of silere to be silent; akin to Goth. ana-silan.

silenus.etymology: L. Silenus the tutor and attendant of Bacchus.

silhouette.etymology: F.; -- so called from Etienne de Silhoutte, a French minister of finance in 1759, whise diversion it was to make such portraits on the walls of his apartments.

silica.etymology: NL., from L. silex, silics, a flint.

siliceous.etymology: L. siliceus, fr. silex, silicis, a flint.

silicle.etymology: L. silicula, dim. of siliqua a pod or husk: cf. F. silicule.

silique.etymology: L. siliqua a pod or husk, a very small weight or measure: cf. F. silique.

silk.etymology: OE. silk, selk, AS. seolc, seoloc; akin to Icel. silki, SW. & Dan. silke; prob. through Slavic from an Oriental source; cf. Lith. szilkai, Russ. shelk', and also L. sericum Seric stuff, silk. Cf. Sericeous. Serge a woolen stuff.

sill.etymology: OE. sille, sylle, AS. syl, syll; akin to G. schwelle, OHG. swelli, Icel. syll, svill, Sw. syll, Dan. syld, Goth. gasuljan to lay a foundation, to found.

sillabub.etymology: Cf. sile to strain, and bub liquor, also Prov. E. sillibauk.

silly.etymology: OE. seely, sely, AS. s, ges, happy, good, fr. s, s, good, happy, s good fortune, happines; akin to OS. salig, a, good, happy, D. zalig blessed, G. selig, OHG. salig, Icel. s, Sw. säll, Dan. salig, Goth. s good, kind, and perh. also to L. sollus whole, entire, Gr. sarva. Cf. Seel, n.

silt.etymology: OE. silte gravel, fr. silen to drain, E. sile; probably of Scand. origin; cf. Sw. sila, prob. akin to AS. seón to filter, sigan to fall, sink, cause to sink, G. seihen to strain, to filter, OHG. sihan, Icel.sia, Skr. sic to pour; cf. Gr. Sig, Sile.

silurian.etymology: From L. Silures, a people who anciently inhabited a part of England and Wales.

silvan.etymology: L. silva, less correctly sylva, a wood or grove, perh. akin to Gr. "y`lh; cf. L. Silvanus Silvanus the god of woods: cf. F. sylvain silvan. Cf. Savage.

silver.etymology: OE. silver, selver, seolver, AS. seolfor, siolfur, siolufr, silofr, sylofr; akin to OS. silubar, OFries. selover, D. zilver, LG. sulver, OHG. silabar, silbar, G. silber, Icel. silfr, Sw. silfver, Dan. sölv, Goth. silubr, Russ. serebro, Lith. sidabras; of unknown origin.

similar.etymology: F. similaire, fr. L. similis like, similar. See Same, a., and cf. Simulate.

similitude.etymology: F. similitude, L. similitudo, from similis similar. See Similar.

simmer.etymology: Prov. E. also simper; -- an onomatopoetic word.

simnel.etymology: OF. simenel cake or bread of wheat flour, LL. simenellus wheat bread, fr. L. simila the finest wheat flour. Cf. Semolina.

simony.etymology: F. simonie, LL. simonia, fr. Simon Magus, who wished to purchase the power of conferring the Holy Spirit. Acts viii.

simoom.etymology: Ar. sam, fr. samma to poison. Cf. Samiel.

simoon.etymology: Ar. sam, fr. samma to poison. Cf. Samiel.

simper.etymology: Cf. Norw. semper fine, smart, dial. Dan. semper, simper, affected, coy, prudish, OSw. semper one who affectedly refrains from eating, Sw. sipp finical, prim, LG. sipp.

simple.etymology: F., fr. L. simplus, or simplex, gen. simplicis. The first part of the Latin words is probably akin to E. same, and the sense, one, one and the same; cf. L. semel once, singuli one to each, single. Cg. Single, a., Same, a., and for the last part of the word cf. Double, Complex.

simplicity.etymology: F. simplicité, L. simplicitas. See Simple.

simplify.etymology: Cf. F. simplifier, LL. simplificare. See Simple, and -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

simulate.etymology: L. simulatus, p. p. of simulare to simulate; akin to simul at the same time, together, similis like. See Similar, and cf. Dissemble, Semblance.

simultaneous.etymology: LL. simultim at the same time, fr. L. simul. See Simulate.

sin.etymology: OE. sinne, AS. synn, syn; akin to D. zonde, OS. sundia, OHG. sunta, G. sünde, Icel., Dan. & Sw. synd, L. sons, sontis, guilty, perhaps originally from the p. pr. of the verb signifying, to be, and meaning, the one who it is. Cf. Authentic, Sooth.

sincere.etymology: L. sincerus, of uncertain origin; the first part perhaps akin to sin- in singuli (see Single), and the second to cernere to separate (cf. Discern): cf. F. sincère.
