sinciput.etymology: L., half a head; semihalf + caput the head.

sine.etymology: LL. sinus a sine, L. sinus bosom, used in translating the Ar. jaib, properly, bosom, but probably read by mistake (the consonants being the same) for an original jiba sine, from Skr. jiva bowstring, chord of an arc, sine.

sinecure.etymology: L. sine without + cura care, LL., a cure. See Cure.

sinew.etymology: OE. sinewe, senewe, AS. sinu, seonu; akin to D. zenuw, OHG. senawa, G. sehne, Icel. sin, Sw. sena, Dan. sene; cf. Skr. snava. sq. root290.

sing.etymology: AS. singan; akin to D. zingen, OS. & OHG. singan, G. singen, Icel. syngja, Sw. sjunga, Dan. synge, Goth. siggwan, and perhaps to E. say, v.t., or cf. Gr. Singe, Song.

singe.etymology: OE. sengen, AS. sengan in besengan (akin to D. zengen, G. sengen), originally, to cause to sing, fr. AS. singan to sing, in allusion to the singing or hissing sound often produced when a substance is singed, or slightly burned. See Sing.

single.etymology: L. singulus, a dim. from the root in simplex simple; cf. OE. & OF. sengle, fr. L. singulus. See Simple, and cf. Singular.

singular.etymology: OE. singuler, F. singulier, fr. L. singularius, singularis, fr. singulus single. See Single, a.

sinister.etymology: Accented on the middle syllable by the older poets, as Shakespeare, Milton, Dryden.

sinistrorsal.etymology: L.sinistrorsus, sinistroversus, turned toward the left side; sinister left + vertere, vortere, versum, vorsum, to turn.

sink.etymology: OE. sinken, AS. sincan; akin to D. zinken, OS. sincan, G. sinken, Icel. sökkva, Dan. synke, Sw. sjunka, Goth. siggan, and probably to E. silt. Cf. Silt.

sinuate.etymology: L. sinuatus, p. p. of sinuare to wind, bend, fr. sinus a bend.

sinuous.etymology: L. sinuosus, fr. sinus a bent surface, a curve: cf. F. sinueux. See Sinus.

sinus.etymology: L., a bent surface, a curve, the folds or bosom of a garment, etc., a bay. Cf. Sine, n.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

sip.etymology: OE. sippen; akin to OD. sippen, and AS. s to sip, suck up, drink. See Sup, v. t.

sir.etymology: OE. sire, F. sire, contr. from the nominative L. senior an elder, elderly person, compar. of senex,senis, an aged person; akin to Gr. sana, Goth. sineigs old, sinista eldest, Ir. & Gael. sean old, W. hen. Cf. Seignior, Senate, Seneschal, Senior, Senor, Signor, Sire, Sirrah.

sirdar.etymology: Hind. & Per. sardar a chief, general; sar the head, top + dar holding, possessing.

sire.etymology: F. sire, originally, an older person. See Sir.

siriasis.etymology: L., fr. Gr. (Med.) (a) A sunstroke. (b) The act of exposing to a sun bath. [Obs.

sirloin.etymology: A corruption of surloin. Not so called because this cut of beaf was once jocosely knighted (dubbed Sir Loin) by an English king, as according to a popular story.

sirocco.etymology: It. sirocco, scirocco, Ar. shorug, fr. sharq the rising of the sun, the east, fr, sharaca to rise as the sun. Cf. Saracen.

sirrah.etymology: Probably from Icel. sira, fr. F. sire. See Sir.

sirup.etymology: F. sirop (cf. It. siroppo, Sp. jarabe, jarope, LL. siruppus, syrupus), fr. Ar. sharab a drink, wine, coffee, sirup. Cf. Sherbet.

siskin.etymology: Dan. sisgen; cf. Sw. siska, G. zeisig, D. sijsje; of Slav. origin; cf. Pol. czy.

siss.etymology: Of imitative origin; cf. D. sissen, G. zischen.

sister.etymology: OE. sister, fr. Icel. systir; also suster, from AS. sweostor, sweoster, swuster, akin to OFries. sweester, suster, LG. süster, suster, D. zuster, OS. & OHG. swestar, G. schwester, Icel. systir, Sw. syster, Dan. söster, Goth. swistar, Lith. ses, Russ. sestra, Pol. siostra, L. soror, Skr. svasr. sq. root298. Cf. Cousin.

sit.etymology: OE. sitten, AS. sittan; akin to OS. sittian, OFries. sitta, D. zitten, G. sitzen, OHG. sizzen, Icel. sitja, SW. sitta, Dan. sidde, Goth. sitan, Russ. sidiete, L. sedere, Gr. sad. sq. root154. Cf. Assess,Assize, Cathedral, Chair, Dissident, Excise, Insidious, Possess, Reside, Sanhedrim, Seance, Seat, n., Sedate, 4th Sell, Siege, Session, Set, v. t., Sizar, Size, Subsidy.

site.etymology: L. situs, fr. sinere, situm, to let, p. p. situs placed, lying, situate: cf. F. site. Cf. Position.

situate.etymology: LL. situatus, from situare to place, fr. L. situs situation, site. See Site.

situated.etymology: LL. situatus, from situare to place, fr. L. situs situation, site. See Site.

six.etymology: AS. six, seox, siex; akin to OFries. sex, D. zes, OS. & OHG. sehs, G. sechs, Icel., Sw., & Dan. sex, Goth. saíhs, Lith. szeszi, Russ. sheste, Gael. & Ir. se, W. chwech, L. sex, Gr. shesh, Skr. shash. sq. root304. Cf. Hexagon, Hexameter, Samite, Senary, Sextant, Sice.

sixteen.etymology: AS. sixt, sixt. See Six, and Ten, and cf. Sixty.

sixth.etymology: From Six: cf. AS. sixta, siexta.

sixty.etymology: AS. siextig; akin to G. sechzig, Goth. saíhs tigjus. See Six, Ten, and cf. Sixteen.

skeg.etymology: Prov. E., also a stump of a branch, a wooden peg; cf. Icel. sk a wood, Sw. skog. Cf. Shaw.

skein.etymology: OE. skeyne, OF. escaigne, F. écagne, probably of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. sgainne, Gael. sgeinnidh thread, small twine; or perhaps the English word is immediately from Celtic.

skep.etymology: Icel. skeppa a measure, bushel; cf. Gael. sgeap a basket, a beehive.

skeptic.etymology: Gr. skeptiko`s thoughtful, reflective, fr. ske`ptesqai to look carefully or about, to view, consider: cf. L. scepticus, F. sceptique. See Scope.

sketch.etymology: D. schets, fr. It. schizzo a sketch, a splash (whence also F. esquisse; cf. Esquisse.); cf. It. schizzare to splash, to sketch.

skew.etymology: Cf. D. scheef. Dan. ski, Sw. skef, Icel. skeifr, G. schief, also E. shy, a. & v. i.

skewer.etymology: Probably of Scand, origin; cf. Sw. & Dan. skifer a slate. Cf. Shuver a fragment.

skid.etymology: Icel. ski a billet of wood. See Shide.

skiff.etymology: F. esquif, fr. OHG. skif, G. schiff. See Ship.

skill.etymology: Icel. skil a distinction, discernment; akin to skilja to separate, divide, distinguish, Sw. skilja,. skille to separate, skiel reason, right, justice, Sw. skäl reason, Lith. skelli to cleave. Cf. Shell, Shoal, a multitude.

skillet.etymology: OF. escuelette, dim. of escuelle a porringer, F. ecuelle, fr. L. scutella, dim. of scutra, scuta, a dish. Cf. Scuttle a basket.

skim.etymology: Cf. Sw. skymma to darken. sq. root158. See Scum.

skin.etymology: Icel. skinn; akin to Sw. skinn, Dan. skind, AS. scinn, G. schined to skin.

skipper.etymology: D. schipper. See Shipper, and Ship.

skirl.etymology: Of Scand. origin, and originally the same word as E. shrill.

skirmish.etymology: OE. skirmishen, scarmishen, OF. escremir, eskermir, to fence, fight, F. escrimer, of German origin; cf. OHG. scirmen to protect, defend, G. schirmen, OHG. scirm, scerm, protection, shield, G. schirm; perhaps akin to Gr. Scaramouch, Scrimmage.

skirret.etymology: A corrupted form equivalent to sugarwort.

skirt.etymology: OE. skyrt, of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. skyrta a shirt, Sw. skört a skirt, skjorta a shirt. See Shirt.

skit.etymology: Prov. E. skitto slide, as adj., hasty, precipitate, of Scand. origin, and akin to E. shoot, v.t.; cf. Icel. skyti, skytja, skytta, a marksman, shooter, skjota to shoot, skuta a taunt. sq. root159. See Shoot.

skittles.etymology: Of Scand. origin. sq. root159. See Shoot, v. t., and cf. Shuttle, Skit, v. t.

skive.etymology: Cf. Icel. skifa a shaving, slice, E. shive, sheave.

skulk.etymology: Of Scand. origin; cf. Dan. skulke to spare or save one's self, to play the truant, Sw. skolka to be at leisure, to shirk, Icel. skolla. Cf. Scowl.

skunk.etymology: Contr. from the Abenaki (American Indian) seganku.

sky.etymology: OE. skie a cloud, Icel. sk; akin to Sw. & Dan. sky; cf. AS. sc, sc, shadow, Icel. skuggi; probably from the same root as E. scum. sq. root158. See Scum, and cf. Hide skin, Obscure.

slab.etymology: OE. slabbe, of uncertain origin; perhaps originally meaning, a smooth piece, and akin to slape, Icel. sleipr slippery, and E. slip, v. i.

slabber.etymology: OE. slaberen; akin to LG. & D. slabbern, G. schlabbern, LG. & D. slabben, G. schlabben, Icel. slafra. Cf. Slaver, Slobber, Slubber.

slag.etymology: Sw. slagg, or LG. slacke, whence G. schlacke; originally, perhaps, the splinters struck off from the metal by hammering. See Slay, v. t.

slake.etymology: OE. slaken to render slack, to slake, AS. sleacian, fr. sleac slack. See Slack, v. & a.

slam.etymology: Of Scand. origin; cf. Icel. slamra, slambra, sl, Norw. slemba, slemma, dial. Sw. slämma.

slander.etymology: OE. sclandere, OF. esclandre, esclandle, escandre, F. esclandre, fr. L. scandalum, Gr. skand to spring, leap. See Scan, and cf. Scandal.

slant.etymology: OE. slenten to slope, slide; cf. Sw. slinta to slide.

slap.etymology: OE. slappe; akin to LG. slappe, G. schlappe; probably of imitative origin.

slash.etymology: OE. slaschen, of uncertain origin; cf. OF. esclachier to break, esclechier, esclichier, to break, and E. slate, slice, slit, v. t.

slate.etymology: OE. slat, OF. esclat a shiver, splinter, F. éclat, fr. OF. esclater to shiver, to chip, F. éclater, fr. OHG. sliezen to tear, slit, split, fr. slizan to slit, G. schleissen. See Slit, v. t., and cf. Eclat.

slaughter.etymology: OE. slautir, slaughter, slaghter, Icel. slatr slain flesh, modified by OE. slaught, slaht, slaughter, fr. AS. sleaht a stroke, blow; both from the root of E. slay. See Slay, v. t., and cf. Onslaught.

slav.etymology: A word originally meaning, intelligible, and used to contrast the people so called with foreigners who spoke languages unintelligible to the Slavs; akin to OSlav. slovo a word, slava fame, Skr. çru to hear. Cf. Loud.

slave.etymology: Cf. F. esclave, D. slaaf, Dan. slave, sclave, Sw. slaf, all fr. G. sklave, MHG. also slave, from the national name of the Slavonians, or Sclavonians (in LL. Slavi or Sclavi), who were frequently made slaves by the Germans. See Slav.

slaw.etymology: D. sla, contr. fr. salade, OD. salaet, salad. See Salad.

slay.etymology: OE. slan, sl, sleen, slee, AS. sleán to strike, beat, slay; akin to OFries. sla, D. slaan, OS. & OHG. slahan, G. schlagen, Icel. sla, Dan. slaae, Sw. sl, Goth. slahan; perhaps akin to L. lacerare to tear to pieces, Gr. lacerate. Cf. Slaughter, Sledge a hammer, Sley.

sleazy.etymology: Cf. G. schleissig worn out, threadbare, from schleissen to slit, split, decay, or E. leasy.

sled.etymology: Akin to D. slede, G. schlitten, OHG. slito, Icel. sle, Sw. släde, Dan. sl, and E. slide, v. See Slide, and cf. Sledge a vehicle, Sleigh.

sledge.etymology: Perhaps from sleds, pl. of sled, confused with sledge a hammer. See Sled, n.

sleek.etymology: OE. slik; akin to Icel. slikr, and OE. sliken to glide, slide, G. schleichen, OHG. slihhan, D. slik, slijk, mud, slime, and E. slink. Cf. Slick, Slink.

sleep.etymology: OE. slepen, AS. sl; akin to OFries. sl, OS. slapan, D. slapen, OHG. slafan, G. schlafen, Goth. sl, and G. schlaff slack, loose, and L. labi to glide, slide, labare to totter. Cf. Lapse.

sleeper.etymology: Cf. Norw. sleip a sleeper (a timber), as adj., slippery, smooth. See Slape.

sleet.etymology: OE. sleet; akin to MHG. sl, sl hailstone, G. schlosse; of uncertain origin.

sleeve.etymology: OE. sleeve, sleve, AS. sl, sl; akin to sl to put on, to clothe; cf. OD. sloove the turning up of anything, sloven to turn up one's sleeves, sleve a sleeve, G. schlaube a husk, pod.

sleigh.etymology: Cf. D. & LG. slede, slee, Icel. sle. See Sled.

sleight.etymology: OE. sleighte, sleihte, sleithe, Icel. sl (for sl) slyness, cunning, fr. sl (for sl) sly, cunning. See Sly.

slender.etymology: OE. slendre, sclendre, fr. OD. slinder thin, slender, perhaps through a French form; cf. OD. slinderen, slidderen, to creep; perh. akin to E. slide.

sleuth.etymology: Icel. sloedh. See Slot a track.

slice.etymology: OE. slice, sclice, OF. esclice, from esclicier, esclichier, to break to pieces, of German origin; cf. OHG. slizan to split, slit, tear, G. schleissen to slit. See Slit, v. t.

slide.etymology: OE. sliden, AS. slidan; akin to MHG. sliten, also to AS. slidor slippery, E. sled, Lith. slidus slippery. Cf. Sled.

slight.etymology: Cf. D. slechten to level, to demolish.

slim.etymology: Formerly, bad, worthless, weak, slight, awry, fr. D. slim; akin to G. schlimm, MHG. slimp oblique, awry; of uncertain origin. The meaning of the English word seems to have been influenced by slender.

slime.etymology: OE. slim, AS. slim; akin to D. slijm, G. schleim, MHG. slimen to make smooth, Icel. slim slime, Dan. sliim; cf. L. limare to file, polish, levis smooth, Gr. limus mud.

sling.etymology: OE. slinge; akin to OD. slinge, D. slinger, OHG. slinga; cf. OF. eslingue, of German origin. See Sling, v. t.

slink.etymology: AS. slincan; probably akin to G. schleichen, E. sleek. See Sleek, a.

slip.etymology: OE. slippen; akin to LG. & D. slippen, MHG. slipfen (cf. Dan. slippe, Sw. slippa, Icel. sleppa), and fr. OE. slipen, AS. slipan (in comp.), akin to G. schleifen to slide, glide, drag, whet, OHG. slifan to slide, glide, make smooth, Icel. slipa to whet; cf. also AS. sl, Goth. sliupan, OS. slopian, OHG. sliofan, G. schliefen, schl, which seem to come from a somewhat different root form. Cf. Slope, n.

slit.etymology: OE. slitten, fr. sliten, AS. stitan to tear; akin to D. slijten to wear out, G. schleissen to slit, split, OHG. slizan to split, tear, wear out, Icel. stita to break, tear, wear out, Sw. slita, Dan. slide. Cf. Eclat, Slate, n., Slice.

slither.etymology: Cf. G. schlittern, LG. schliddern. See Slide.

sloe.etymology: OE. slo, AS. sla; akin to D. slee, G. schlehe, OHG. sl$ha, Dan. slaaen, Sw. sl, perhaps originally, that which blunts the teeth, or sets them on edge (cf. Slow); cf. Lith. sliwa a plum, Russ. sliva.

slogan.etymology: Gael. sluagh-ghairm, i.e., an army cry; sluagh army + gairm a call, calling.

sloop.etymology: D. sloep, of uncertain origin. Cf. Shallop.

slop.etymology: OE. sloppe a pool; akin to As. sloppe, slyppe, the sloppy droppings of a cow; cf. AS. sl to slip, and E. slip, v.i. Cf. Cowslip.

slope.etymology: Formed (like abode fr. abide) from OE. slipen. See Slip, v. i.

slot.etymology: LG. & D. slot a lock, from a verb meaning to close., to shut, D. sluiten; akin to G. schliessen, OHG. sliozan, OFries. sl, and probably to L. claudere. Cf. Close, Sluice.

sloth.etymology: OE. slouthe, sleuthe, AS. sl, fr. slaw slow. See Slow.

slouch.etymology: Cf. Icel. sla slouching felloew, and E. slack, slug, a lazy fellow.

slough.etymology: OE. slugh, slouh; cf. MHG. sl the skin of a serpent, G. schlauch a skin, a leather bag or bottle.

sloven.etymology: D. slaf careless, negligent, a sloven; akin to LG. sluf slovenly.

slow.etymology: OE. slow, slaw, AS. slaw; akin to OS. sl blunt, dull, D. sleeuw, slee, sour, OHG. sl blunt, dull, Icel. sl, sl, Dan. slöv, Sw. slö. Cf. Sloe, and Sloth.

slowworm.etymology: AS. slawyrm; the first part is probably akin to sleán to strike, the reptile being supposed to be very poisonous. See Slay, v. t., and Worm.

slue.etymology: Prov. E. slew to turn round, Scot. to lean or incline to a side; cf. Icel. sn to turn, bend.

slug.etymology: OE. slugge slothful, sluggen to be slothful; cf. LG. slukk low-spirited, sad, E. slack, slouch, D. slak, slek, a snail.

roots.meaning: The termination of many English words; as, coward, reynard, drunkard, mostly from the French, in which language this ending is of German origin, being orig. the same word as English hard. It usually has the sense of one who has to a high or excessive degree the quality expressed by the root; as, braggart, sluggard.

sluice.etymology: OF. escluse, F. écluse, LL. exclusa, sclusa, from L. excludere, exclusum, to shut out: cf. D. sluis sluice, from the Old French. See Exclude.

slumber.etymology: OE. slombren, slumberen, slumeren, AS. slumerian, fr. sluma slumber; akin to D. sluimeren to slumber, MHG. slummern, slumen, G. schlummern, Dan. slumre, Sw. slumra, Goth. slawan to be silent.

slump.etymology: Cf. D. slomp a mass, heap, Dan. slump a quantity, and E. slump, v.t.

slur.etymology: Cf. OE. sloor mud, clay, Icel. sl, slo, to trail or drag one's self along, D. sleuren, sloren, to train, to drag, to do negligently and slovenly, D. sloor, sloerie, a sluttish girl.

slush.etymology: Cf. Sw. slaska to paddle in water, slask wet, filth.

slut.etymology: OE. slutte; cf. OD. slodde a slut, Icel. slöttr a heavy, loglike fellow, slota to droop.

sly.etymology: OE. sli, slegh, sleih, Icel sl, for sl; akin to Sw. slug, Dan. slu, LG. slou, G. schlau; probably to E. slay, v.t.; cf. G. verschlagen sly. See Slay, v. t., and cf. Sleight.

smack.etymology: D. smak; akin to LG. smack, smak, Dan. smakke, G. schmacke, F. semaque.

smart.etymology: OE. smarten, AS. smeortan; akin to D. smarten, smerten, G. schmerzen, OHG. smerzan, Dan. smerte, SW. smärta, D. smart, smert, a pain, G. schmerz, Ohg. smerzo, and probably to L. mordere to bite; cf. Gr. m to rub, crush. Cf. Morsel.

smash.etymology: Cf. Sw. smisk a blow, stroke, smiska to strike, dial. Sw. smaske to kiss with a noise, and E. smack a loud kiss, a slap.

smatter.etymology: OE. smateren to make a noise; cf. Sw. smattra to clatter, to crackle, G. schmettern to dash, crash, to warble, quaver.

smear.etymology: OE. smeren, smerien, AS. smierwan, smyrwan, fr. smeoru fat, grease; akin to D. smeren, OHG. smirwen, G. schmieren, Icel. smyrja to anoint. See Smear, n.

smell.etymology: OE. smellen, smillen, smullen; cf. LG. smellen, smelen, smölen, schmelen, to smoke, to reek, D. smeulen to smolder, and E. smolder. Cf. Smell, n.

smelt.etymology: AS. smelt, smylt; akin to Dan. smelt.

smile.etymology: OE. smilen; akin to Dan. smile, Sw. smila, MHG. smielen, smieren, L. mirari to wonder at, Skr. smi to smile; and probably to E. smicker. sq. root173. Cf. Admire, Marvel, Smirk.

smirk.etymology: OE. smirken, ASS. smercian, smearcian; cf. MHG. smieren, smielen, to smile. See Smile, v. i.

smite.etymology: AS. smitan to smite, to soil, pollute; akin to OFries. smita to smite, LG. smiten, D. smijten, G. schmeissen, OHG. smizan to smear, stroke, OSw. & dial. Sw. smita to smite, Dan. smiide to throw, Goth. bismeitan, to anoint, besmear; cf. Skr. m to be fat. The original sense seems to have been, to daub on, to smear. Cf. Smut.

smithy.etymology: AS. smi, fr. smi; akin to D. smidse, smids, OHG. smitta, G. schmiede, Icel. smi. See Smith, n.

smock.etymology: AS. smoc; akin to OHG. smocho, Icel. smokkr, and from the root of AS. sm to creep, akin to G. schmiegen to cling to, press close. MHG. smiegen, Icel. smj to creep through, to put on a garment which has a hole to put the head through; cf. Lith. smukti to glide. Cf. Smug, Smuggle.

smoke.etymology: AS. smoca, fr. smeócan to smoke; akin to LG. & D. smook smoke, Dan. smög, G. schmauch, and perh. to Gr. smaugti to choke.

smolder.etymology: OE. smolderen; cf. Prov. G. smölen, smelen, D. smeulen. Cf. Smell.

smooth.etymology: OE. smothe, smethe, AS. smeedhe, smoeedte, where e, oe, come from an older o; cf. LG. smöde, smöe, smödig; of uncertain origin.

smother.etymology: OE. smotheren; akin to E. smoor. See Smoor.

smoulder.etymology: OE. smolderen; cf. Prov. G. smölen, smelen, D. smeulen. Cf. Smell.

smudge.etymology: Cf. Dan. smuds smut, E. smutch, or smoke.

smug.etymology: Of. Scand. or Low German origin; cf. LG. smuck, G. schmuck, Dan. smuk, OSw. smuck, smöck, and E. smock, smuggle; cf. G. schmuck ornament. See Smock.

smuggle.etymology: Of Low German or Scand. origin; cf. LG. smuggeln, D. smokkelen, G. schmuggeln, Dan. smugle, Sw. smyga to introduce or convey secretly, Dan. i smug secretly, D. smuigen to eat in secret, AS. smgan to creep. See Smock.

smut.etymology: Akin to Sw. smuts, Dan. smuds, MHG. smuz, G. schmutz, D. smet a spot or stain, smoddig, smodsig, smodderig, dirty, smodderen to smut; and probably to E. smite. See Smite, v. t., and cf. Smitt, Smutch.

smutch.etymology: Prob. for smuts. See Smut, n.

snaffle.etymology: D. snavel a beak, bill, snout; akin to G. schnabel, OHG. snabul,. sneb, snebbe, OFries. snavel mouth, Dan. & Sw. snabel beak, bill, Lith. snapas, and to E. snap, v. See Snap, and cf. Neb.

snag.etymology: Prov. E., n., a lump on a tree where a branch has been cut off; v., to cut off the twigs and small branches from a tree, of Celtic origin; cf. Gael. snaigh, snaidh, to cut down, to prune, to sharpen, p. p. snaighte, snaidhte, cut off, lopped, Ir. snaigh a hewing, cutting.

snail.etymology: OE. snaile, AS. sn, snegel, sn; akin to G. schnecke, OHG. snecko, Dan. snegl, Icel. snigill.

snake.etymology: AS. snaca; akin to LG. snake, schnake, Icel. snakr, sn, Dan. snog, Sw. snok; of uncertain origin.

snakebird.etymology: So named from its snakelike neck.

snap.etymology: LG. or D. snappen to snap up, to snatch; akin to G. schnappen, MHG. snaben, Dan. snappe, and to D. snavel beak, bill. Cf. Neb, Snaffle, n.

snare.etymology: AS. sneara cord, a string; akin to D. snoer, G. schnur, OHG. snour a cord, snarahha a noose, Dan. snare, Sw. & Icel. snara, Goth. sn a basket; and probably also to E. needle. See Needle, and cf. Snarl to entangle.

snatch.etymology: OE. snachen, snechen; akin to D. snakken to gasp, to long (for), to desire. Cf. Snack, n., Sneck.

sneak.etymology: OE. sniken, AS. snican to creep; akin to Dan. snige sig; cf. Icel. snikja to hanker after.

sneer.etymology: OE. sneren, Dan. sn to snarl or grin (like a dog); cf. Prov. E. sneer to grin, sner to snort, snert to sneer at. See Snore, v. i.

sneeze.etymology: OE. snesen; of uncertain origin; cf. D. snuse to sniff, E. neese, and AS. fneósan.

snick.etymology: Prov. E. snick a notch; cf. Icel. snikka nick, cut.

snicker.etymology: Cf. D. snikken to sob, to sigh.

sniff.etymology: OE. sneven; akin to snivel, snuff; cf. Dan. snive to sniff. See Snuff, v. t.

snip.etymology: D. snippen; akin to G. schnippen.

snipe.etymology: OE. snipe; akin to D. snep, snip, LG. sneppe, snippe, G. schnepfe, Icel. snipa (in comp.), Dan. sneppe, Sw. snäppa a sanpiper, and possibly to E. snap. See Snap, Snaffle.

snivel.etymology: OE. snivelen, snevelen, snuvelen, freg. of sneven. See Sniff, and cf. Snuffle.

snob.etymology: Icel. snapr a dolt, impostor, charlatan. Cf. Snub.

snook.etymology: Prov. E. snook to search out, to follow by the scent; cf. Sw. snoka to lurk, LG. snöggen, snuckern, snökern, to snuffle, to smell about, to search for.

snooze.etymology: Scot. snooze to sleep; cf. Dan. & Sw. snus snuff.

snore.etymology: OE. snoren, AS. snora a snoring; akin to LG. snoren, snorken, snurken, to snore, D. snorken, G. schnarchen to snore, schnarren to rattle, MHG. snarren, Sw. snarka to snore, Icel. snarka to sputter, fizzle. Cf. Snarl to growl, Sneer, Snort. See Snoring.

snort.etymology: OE. snorten; akin to snoren. See Snore.

snot.etymology: AS. snot; akin to D. snot, LG. snotte, Dan. snot, and to E. snout. See Snout.

snout.etymology: OE. snoute, probably of Scand, or Low German origin; cf. LG. snute, D. snuit, G. schnauze, Sw. snut, snyte, Dan. snude, Icel. sn to blow the nose; probably akin to E. snuff, v.t. Cf. Snite, Snot, Snuff.

snow.etymology: LG. snaue, or D. snaauw, from LG. snau a snout, a beak.

snub.etymology: Cf. D. snuiven to snort, to pant, G. schnauben, MHG. snuben, Prov. G. schnupfen, to sob, and E. snuff, v.t.

snuff.etymology: Cf. G. schnuppe candle snuff, schnuppen to snuff a candle (see Snuff, v. t., to snuff a candle), or cf. Snub, v. t.

snuffle.etymology: Freq. of snuff, v.i.; akin to LG. snuffeln, G. schnüffeln, D. snuffeln, Dan. snövle. Cf. Sniffle.

snug.etymology: Prov. E. snug tight, handsome; cf. Icel. snöggr smooth, ODan. snög neat, Sw. snugg.

soak.etymology: OE. soken, AS. socian to sioak, steep, fr. s, s, to suck. See Suck.

soap.etymology: OE. sope, AS. sape; akin to D. zeep, G. seife, OHG. seifa, Icel. sapa, Sw. s, Dan. s, and perhaps to AS. sipan to drip, MHG. sifen, and L. sebum tallow. Cf. Saponaceous.

sober.etymology: OE. sobre, F. sobre, from L. sobrius, probably from a prefix so- expressing separation + ebrius drunken. Cf. Ebriety.

sobriety.etymology: L. sobrietas: cf. F. sobriété. See Sober.

sobriquet.etymology: F. sobriquet, OF. soubzbriquet, soubriquet, a chuck under the chin, hence, an affront, a nickname; of uncertain origin; cf. It. sottobecco a chuck under the chin.

sociable.etymology: F., fr. L. sociabilis, fr. sociare to associate, fr. socius a companion. See Social.

social.etymology: L. socialis, from socius a companion; akin to sequi to follow: cf. F. social. See Sue to follow.

society.etymology: L. societas, fr. socius a companion: cf. F. société. See Social.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

sock.etymology: F. soc, LL. soccus, perhaps of Celtic origin.

socket.etymology: OE. soket, a dim. through OF. fr. L. soccus. See Sock a covering for the foot.

socle.etymology: F., fr. L. socculus, dim. of soccus. See Sock a covering for the foot. Cf. Zocco.

sod.etymology: Akin to LG. sode, D. zode, OD. sode, soode, OFries. satha, and E. seethe. So named from its sodden state in wet weather. See Seethe.

soda.etymology: It., soda, in OIt., ashes used in making glass, fr. L. solida, fem. of solidus solid; solida having probably been a name of glasswort. See Solid.

roots.meaning: Combining forms fr. Gr. li`qos a stone; -- used chiefly in naming minerals and rocks.

sodality.etymology: L. sodalitas, fr. sodalis a comrade.

sodomy.etymology: From Sodom. a country mentioned in the Bible: cf. F. sodomite.

sofa.etymology: Ar. soffah, from saffa to dispose in order: cf. F. sofa, It.sofà.

soffit.etymology: It. soffitta, soffitto, fr. soffiggere to hide, properly, to fix or fasten under, L. suffigere to fasten beneath or below; sub under, beneath + figere to fix, faste: cf. F. soffite.

soft.etymology: OE. softe, AS. s, properly adv. of s, adj.; akin to OS. safto, adv., D. zacht, OHG. samfto, adv., semfti, adj., G. sanft, LG. sacht; of uncertain origin.

soggy.etymology: Cf. Icel. söggr damp, wet, or E. soak.

soil.etymology: OF. saoler, saouler, to satiate, F. soûler, L. satullare, fr. satullus, dim. of satur sated. See Satire.

soilure.etymology: OF. soillure, F. souillure. See Soil to make dirty.

soiree.etymology: F., fr. soir evening, fr. L. serus late, serum late time. Cf. Serenade.

sojourn.etymology: OE. sojornen, sojournen, OF. sojorner, sejorner, F. séjourner, fr. L. sub under, about + diurnus belonging to the day. See Journal, Diurnal.

solace.etymology: OF. solas, ssoulaz, L. solacium, solatium, fr. solari to comfort, console. Cf. Console, v. t.

solar.etymology: OE. soler, AS. solere, L. solarium, from sol the sun. See Solar, a.

sold.etymology: F. solde. See Soldier, and cf. Sou.

solder.etymology: Formerly soder; F. soudure, OF. soudeure, fr. OF. & F. souder to solder, L. solidare to fasten, to make solid. See Solid, and cf. Sawder.

soldier.etymology: OE. souldier, soudiour, souder, OF. soldier, soldoier, soldeier, sodoier, soudoier, soudier, fr. L. solidus a piece of money (hence applied to the pay of a soldier), fr. solidus solid. See Solid, and cf. Sold, n.

sole.etymology: F. sole, L. solea; -- so named from its flat shape. See Sole of the foot.

solecism.etymology: F. solécisme, L. soloecismus, Gr. soloikismo`s, fr. soloiki`zein to speak or write incorrectly, fr. so`loikos speaking incorrectly, from the corruption of the Attic dialect among the Athenian colonists of So`loi in Cilicia.

solemn.etymology: OE. solempne, OF. solempne, L. solemnis, solennis, sollemnis, sollennis; sollus all, entire + annus a year; properly, that takes place every year; -- used especially of religious solemnities. Cf. Silly, Annual.

solemnity.etymology: L. solemnitas, solennitas: cf. F. solennité, solemnité, OF. also sollempnité.

roots.meaning: A suffix or combining form meaning like, resembling, in the form of; as in anthropoid, asteroid, spheroid.

solicit.etymology: F. sollicier, L. sollicitare, solicitare, -atum, fr. sollicitus wholly (i. e., violently) moved; sollus whole + citus, p. p. of ciere to move, excite. See Solemn, Cite.

solicitous.etymology: L. sollicitus, solicitus. See Solicit, v. t.

solid.etymology: L. solidus, probably akin to sollus whole, entire, Gr. solide. Cf. Consolidate,Soda, Solder, Soldier, Solemn.

solidago.etymology: NL., fr. L. solidare to strengthen, unite; -- so called in allusion to its reputed healing qualities.

solidarity.etymology: F. solidarité, fr. solide. See Solid.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

soliloquy.etymology: L. soliloquium; solus alone + loqui to speak. See Sole ly, and Loquacious.

solitary.etymology: L. solitarius, fr. solus alone: cf. F. solitaire. See Sole, a., and cf. Solitaire.

solitude.etymology: F., from L. solitudo, solus alone. See Sole, a.

solleret.etymology: F. soleretim. fr. OF. soler shoe.

solmization.etymology: F. solmisation, fr. solmiser to sol-fa; -- called from the musical notes sol, mi. See Sol-fa.

solo.etymology: It., from L. solus alone. See Sole, a.

solstice.etymology: L. solstitium; sol the sun + sistere to cause to stand, akin to stare to stand: cf. F. solstice. See Solar, a., Stand, v. i.

soluble.etymology: L. solubilis, fr. solvere, solutum, to loosen, to dissolve: cf. F. soluble. See Solve, and cf. Solvable.

solute.etymology: L. solutus, p.p. of solvere to loosen. See Solve.

solution.etymology: OE. solucion, OF. solucion, F. solution, fr. L. solutio, fr. solvere, solutum, to loosen, dissolve. See Solve.

solvable.etymology: F. solvable. See Solve, and cf. Soluble, Solvible.

solve.etymology: L. solvere, solutum; from a prefix so- expressing separation (cf. Sober) + luere to loosen; cf. OF. soldre, soudre. See Loose, and cf. Absolve.

solvent.etymology: L. solvens, p.pr. of solvere. See Solvable.

somber.etymology: F. sombre; cf. Sp. sombra, shade, prob. from LL. subumbrare to put in the shade; L. sub under + umbra shade. See Umbrage.

sombre.etymology: F. sombre; cf. Sp. sombra, shade, prob. from LL. subumbrare to put in the shade; L. sub under + umbra shade. See Umbrage.

sombrero.etymology: Sp., from sombra shade. See Sombre.

some.etymology: OE. som, sum, AS. sum; akin to OS., OFries., & OHG. sum, OD. som, D. sommig, Icel. sumr, Dan. somme (pl.), Sw. somlige (pl.), Goth. sums, and E. same. sq. root191. See Same, a., and cf. - some.

somersault.etymology: F. soubresaut a jump, leap, OF. soubresault, It. soprassalto an overleap, fr. L. supra over + saltus a leap, fr. salire to leap; or the French may be from Sp. sobresalto a sudden asault, a surprise. See Supra, and Salient.

somerset.etymology: F. soubresaut a jump, leap, OF. soubresault, It. soprassalto an overleap, fr. L. supra over + saltus a leap, fr. salire to leap; or the French may be from Sp. sobresalto a sudden asault, a surprise. See Supra, and Salient.

sometimes.etymology: Sometime + adverbial ending -s, as in - wards.

somnambulation.etymology: L. somnus sleep + ambulatio a walking about, from ambulare to walk. See Somnolent, Amble.

somniferous.etymology: L. somnifer; somnus sleep + ferre to bring.

somnific.etymology: L. somnificus; somnus sleep + facere to make.

somnolent.etymology: F. somnolent, L. somnolentus, from somnus sleep, akin to Gr. svapna sleep, dream, svap to sleep, Icel. sofa, AS. swefn sleep. Cf. Hypnotic, Somnambulism, Soporific.

son.etymology: OE. sone, sune, AS. sunu; akin to D. zoon, OS., OFries., & OHG. sunu, G. sohn, Icel. sonr, Sw. son, Dan. sön, Goth. sunus, Lith. sunus, Russ. suin', Skr. sunu (from su to beget, to bear), and Gr. Sow, n.

sonant.etymology: L. sonans, -antis, p.pr. of sonare to sound. See Sound a noise.

sonata.etymology: It., fr. It. & L. sonare to sound. See Sound a noise.

song.etymology: AS. song, sang, fr. singan to sing; akin to D. zang, G. sang, Icel. söngr, Goeth. sagws. See Sing.

roots.meaning: A suffix used to form feminine nouns; as, actress, deaconess, songstress.

sonnet.etymology: F., fr. It. sonetto, fr. suono a sound, a song, fr. L. sonus a sound. See Sound noise.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

sonorous.etymology: L. sonorus, fr. sonor, -oris, a sound, akin to sonus a sound. See Sound.

sonsy.etymology: Scot. sonce, sons, prosperity, happiness, fr. Gael. & Ir. sonas.

sontag.etymology: So called from from Mme. Henriette Sontag, a famous singer.

soon.etymology: OE. sone, AS. s; cf. OFries. s, OS. sana, sano, OHG. sar, Goth. suns.

soot.etymology: OE. sot, AS. s; akin to Icel. s, Sw. sot, Dan. sod, OD. soet, Lith. s; cf. Gael. suith, Ir. suth.

sooth.etymology: OE. soth, AS. s, for san; akin to OS. s, OHG. sand, Icel. sannr, Sw. sann, Dan. sand, Skr. sat, sant, real, genuine, present, being; properly p. pr. from a root meaning, to be, Skr. as, L. esse; also akin to Goth. sunjis true, Gr. satya. Absent, Am, Essence, Is, Soothe, Sutee.

soothe.etymology: Originally, to assent to as true; OE. so to verify, AS. ges to prove the truth of, to bear witness. See Sooth, a.

sop.etymology: OE. sop, soppe; akin to AS. s to sup, to sip, to drink, D. sop sop, G. suppe soup, Icel. soppa sop. See Sup, v. t., and cf. Soup.

sophist.etymology: F. sophiste, L. sophistes, fr. Gr. Sophism.

sophisticate.etymology: LL. sophisticatus, p.p. of sophisticare to sophisticate.

sophomore.etymology: Probably fr. soph or sophister + Gr. Soph-Mor as "the next distinctive appellation to Freshman," but the term has now almost ceased to be known at the English university from whence it came.

soporiferous.etymology: L. soparifer; sopor a heavy sleep + ferere to bring.

soporific.etymology: L. sopor a heavy sleep (akin to somnus sleep) + facere to make. See Somnolent, Fact.

soprano.etymology: It., fr. soprano superior, highest, fr. sopra above, L. supra. See Sovereign.

sorb.etymology: L. sorbus the tree, sorbum the fruit; cf. F. sorbe. See Service tree.

sorbefacient.etymology: L. sorbere to suck in, absorb + faciens, p.pr. of facere to make.

sorbent.etymology: L. sorbens, p.pr. of sorbere to suck in, to absorb.

sorbet.etymology: F. sorbet or It. sorbetto or Sp. sorbete, from the same source as E. sherbet. See Sherbet.

sorcery.etymology: OE. sorcerie, OF. sorcerie, fr. OF. & F. sorcier a sorcerer, LL. sortiarius, fr. L. sors, sortis, a lot, decision by lot, fate, destiny. See Sort, n.

sordid.etymology: L. sordidus, fr. sordere to be filthy or dirty; probably akin to E. swart: cf. F. sordide. See Swart, a.

sore.etymology: F. saure, sore, sor; faucon sor a sore falcon. See Sorrel, n.

sororal.etymology: L. soror sister: cf. F. sororal.

sorrel.etymology: F. saur, saure, OF. sor, sore, probably of Teutonic origin; cf. D. zoor dry, LG. soor; the meaning probably coming from the color of dry leaves. See Sear, a., and cf. Sorel.

sorrow.etymology: OE. sorwe, sorewe, sor, AS. sorg, sorh; akin to D. zorg care, anxiety, OS. sorga, OHG. sorga, soraga, suorga, G. sorge, Icel., Sw., & Dan. sorg, Goth. saúrga; of unknown origin.

sorry.etymology: OE. sory, sary, AS. sarig, fr. sar, n., sore. See Sore, n. & a. The original sense was, painful; hence. miserable, sad.

sort.etymology: F. sorl, L. sors, sortis. See Sort kind.

sortie.etymology: F., fr. sortir to go out, to issue, probably fr. L. sortus, for surrectus, p.p. of surgere to raise up, to rise up. See Source.

sortition.etymology: L. sortitio, from sortiri to draw or cast lots, fr. sors, sortis, a lot.

sot.etymology: F., fr. LL. sottus; of unknown origin, cf. Ir. sotal pride, soithir proud, or Chald. & NHeb. shoten foolish.

roots.meaning: A combining form denoting a discourse, treatise, doctrine, theory, science; as, theology, geology, biology, mineralogy.

sou.etymology: F. sou, OF. sol, from L. solidus a gold coin, in LL., a coin of less value. See Sold, n., Solid, and and cf. Sol, Soldo.

souchong.etymology: Chin. seou chong little plant or sort.

soul.etymology: F. soûler to satiate. See Soil to feed.

sound.etymology: AS. sund a swimming, akin to E. swim. See Swim.

soup.etymology: F. soupe, OF. sope, supe, soupe, perhaps originally, a piece of bread; probably of Teutonic origin; cf. D. sop sop, G. suppe soup. See Sop something dipped in a liquid, and cf. Supper.

sour.etymology: OE. sour, sur, AS. s; akin to D. zuur, G. sauer, OHG. s, Icel. s, Sw. sur, Dan. suur, Lith. suras salt, Russ. surovui harsh, rough. Cf. Sorrel, the plant.

source.etymology: OE. sours, OF. sourse, surse, sorse, F. source, fr. OF. sors, p.p. of OF. sordre, surdre, sourdre, to spring forth or up, F. sourdre, fr. L. surgere to lift or raise up, to spring up. See Surge, and cf. Souse to plunge or swoop as a bird upon its prey.

soutane.etymology: F., fr. Sp. sotana, or It. sottana, LL. subtana, fr. L. subtus below, beneath, fr. sub under.

south.etymology: OE. south, suþ, AS. suedh for sunedh; akin to D. zuid, OHG. sund, G. süd, süden, Icel. suedhr, sunnr, Dan. syd, sönden, Sw. syd, söder, sunnan; all probably akin to E. sun, meaning, the side towards the sun. sq. root297. See Sun.

souvenir.etymology: F., fr. souvenir to remember, fr. L. subvenire to come up, come to mind; sub under + venire to come, akin to E. come. See Come, and cf. Subvention.

sovereign.etymology: OE. soverain, sovereyn, OF. soverain, suvrain, F. souverain, LL. superanus, fr. L. superus that is above, upper, higher, fr. super above. See Over, Super, and cf. Soprano. The modern spelling is due to a supposed connection with reign.

sovereignty.etymology: OE. soverainetee, OF. sovraineté, F. souveraineté.

sow.etymology: OE. sowe, suwe, AS. sugu, akin to su, D. zog, zeug, OHG. su, G. sau, Icel. syr, Dan. so, Sw. sugga, so, L. sus. Gr. "y^s, sy^s, Zend. hu boar; probably from the root seen in Skr. su to beget, to bear; the animal being named in allusion to its fecundity. sq. root294. Cf. Hyena, Soil to stain, Son, Swine.

space.etymology: OE. space, F. espace, from L. spatium space; cf. Gr. span. Cf. Expatiate.

spacious.etymology: L. spatiousus: cf. F. spacieux. See Space, n.

spall.etymology: OF. espaule; cf. It. spalla. See Epaule.

span.etymology: AS. spann; akin to D. span, OHG. spanna, G. spanne, Icel. spönn. sq. root170. See Span, v. t.

spang.etymology: AS. spange a clasp or fastening; akin to D. spang, G. spange, OHG. spanga, Icel. spöng a spangle.

spangle.etymology: OE. spangel, dim. of AS. spange. See Spang a spangle.

spaniel.etymology: OF. espagneul, F. épagneul, espagnol Spanish, Sp. españnol, fr. España Spain, from L. Hispania.

spank.etymology: Of unknown origin; cf. LG. spakken, spenkern, to run and spring about quickly.

spar.etymology: AS. spær in spærstan chalkstone; akin to MHG. spar, G. sparkalk plaster.

spare.etymology: AS. sparian, fr. spær spare, sparing, saving; akin to D. & G. sparen, OHG. spar, Icel. & Sw. spara, Dan. spare See Spare, a.

spark.etymology: OE. sparke, AS. spearca; akin to D. spark, sperk; cf. Icel. spraka to crackle, Lith. spragëti, Gr. sph to crackle, to thunder. Cf. Speak.

sparling.etymology: Akin to G. spierling, spiering, D. spiering: cf. F. éperlan.

sparrow.etymology: OE. sparwe, AS. spearwa; akin to OHG. sparo, G. sperling, Icel. spörr, Dan. spurv, spurre, Sw. sparf, Goth. sparwa; - - originally, probably, the quiverer or flutterer, and akin to E. spurn. See Spurn, and cf. Spavin.

sparse.etymology: L. sparsus, p.p. of spargere to strew, scatter. Cf. Asperse, Disperse.

spasm.etymology: F. spasme, L. spasmus, Gr. Span, v. t.

spastic.etymology: L. spasticus, Gr. spastique. See Spasm.

spat.etymology: From the root of spit; hence, literally, that which is ejected.

spate.etymology: Of Celtic origin; cf. Ir. speid.

spathe.etymology: L. spatha, Gr. spathe. See Spade for digging.

spatter.etymology: From the root of spit salvia.

spatula.etymology: L. spatula, spathula, dim. of spatha a spatula: F. spatule. See Spade for digging.

spavin.etymology: OE. spaveyne, OF. esparvain, F. éparvin; akin to OF. espervier a sparrow hawk, F. épervier, fr. OHG. sparwari (G. sperber), fr. OHG. sparo sparrow, because this disease makes the horse raise the infirm leg in the manner of a sparrow hawk or sparrow. See Sparrow.

spawl.etymology: Cf. AS. spatl, fr. spætan to spit; probably akin to spiwan, E. spew. Cf. Spew.

spawn.etymology: OE. spanen, OF. espandre, properly, to shed, spread, L. expandere to spread out. See Expand.

spay.etymology: Cf. Spade a spay, Spay, v. t.

speak.etymology: OE. speken, AS. specan, sprecan; akin to OF.ries. spreka, D. spreken, OS. spreken, G. sprechen, OHG. sprehhan, and perhaps to Skr. sphurj to crackle, to thunder. Cf. Spark of fire, Speech.

spear.etymology: OE. spere, AS. spere; akin to D. & G. speer, OS. & OHS. sper, Icel. spjör, pl., Dan. spær, L. sparus.

spearmint.etymology: So named from its spiry, not capitate, inflorescence. Dr. Prior.

special.etymology: L. specialis, fr. species a particular sort, kind, or quality: cf. F. spécial. See Species, and cf. Especial.

specie.etymology: Formed as a singular from species, in sense 5.

species.etymology: L., a sight, outward appearance, shape, form, a particular sort, kind, or quality, a species. See Spice, n., and cf. Specie, Special.

specific.etymology: F. spécifique, or NL. cpesificus; L. species a particular sort or kind + facere to make. Cf. Specify.

specify.etymology: F. spécifier, or OF. especifier, fr. LL. specificare. See Species, -fy.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

specimen.etymology: L., fr. specere to look, to behold. See Spy.

specious.etymology: L. speciosusgood-looking, beautiful, specious, fr. species look, show, appearance; cf. F. spécoeux. See Species.

speck.etymology: Cf. Icel. spik blubber, AS. spic, D. spek, G. speck.

speckle.etymology: Dim. of speck; cf. D. spikkel.

spectacle.etymology: F., fr. L. spectaculum, fr. spectare to look at, to behold, v. intens. fr. specere. See Spy.

spectator.etymology: L. spectator: cf. F. spectateur. See Spectacle.

specter.etymology: F. spectre, fr. L. spectrum an appearance, image, specter, fr. specere to look. See Spy, and cf. Spectrum.

spectre.etymology: F. spectre, fr. L. spectrum an appearance, image, specter, fr. specere to look. See Spy, and cf. Spectrum.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.
A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.

specular.etymology: L. specularis (cf., from the same root, specula a lookout, watchtower): cf. F. spéculaire. See Speculum.

speculate.etymology: L. speculatus, p.p. of speculari to spy out, observe, fr. specula a lookout, fr. specere to look. See Spy.

speculation.etymology: L. speculatio a spying out, observation: cf. F. spéculation.

speculator.etymology: L., a spy, explorer, investigator: cf. F. spéculateur.

speculum.etymology: L., fr. specere to look, behold. See Spy.

speech.etymology: OE. speche, AS. sp, spr, fr. specan, sprecan, to speak; akin to D. spraak speech, OHG. sprahha, G. sprache, Sw. spr, Dan. sprog. See Speak.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

speed.etymology: AS. sp success, swiftness, from sp to succeed; akin to D. spoedd, OHG. spuot success, spuot to succees, Skr. spha to increase, grow fat. sq. root170b.

spell.etymology: OE. speld, AS. speld a spill to light a candle with; akin to D. speld a pin, OD. spelle, G. spalten to split, OHG. spaltan, MHG. spelte a splinter, Icel. spjald a square tablet, Goth. spilda a writing tablet. Cf. Spillsplinter, roll of paper, Spell to tell the letters of.

spelter.etymology: Cf. LG. spialter, G. & D. spiauter. Cf. Pewter.

spencer.etymology: OF. despensier. See Spence, and cf. Dispenser.

spend.etymology: AS. spendan (in comp.), fr. L. expendere or dispendere to weigh out, to expend, dispense. See Pendant, and cf. Dispend, Expend, Spence, Spencer.

sperm.etymology: F. sperme, L. sperma, Gr. Spore.

spermaceti.etymology: L. sperma sperm + cetus,gen. ceti, any large sea animal, a whale, Gr. Sperm, Cetaceous.

spermatic.etymology: L. spermaticus, Gr. spermatique. See Sperm.

roots.meaning: Combining forms from Gr. seed, sperm, semen (of plants or animals); as, spermatoblast, spermoblast.

spew.etymology: OE. spewen, speowen, AS. spiwan;n to D. spuwen to spit. OS & OHG. spiwan, G. speien, Icel. sp to spew, Sw. spy, Dan. spye, Goth. spiewan, th. spjauti, L. spuere to split, Gr. shtiv, shthiv. Cf. Pyke, Spit.

sphacelate.etymology: NL. sphacelare, sphacelatum, mortify: cf. F. sphacéler. See Sphacelus.

spheroid.etymology: L. spheroides ball-like, spherical, Gr. sphéroïde.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

sphinx.etymology: L., from Gr. sfi`gx, usually derived from sfi`ggein to bind tight or together, as if the Throttler.

spica.etymology: L., an ear, as of corn.

spicate.etymology: L. spicatus, p. p. of spicare furnish with spikes, or ears, fr. spica a spike, or ear.

spiccato.etymology: It., p. p. of spicare to detach, to separate.

spice.etymology: OE. spice, spece, spice, species, OF. espice, espece, F. épice spice, espèce species, fr. L. species particular sort or kind, a species, a sight, appearance, show, LL., spices, drugs, etc., of the same sort, fr. L. specere to look. See Spy, and cf. Species.

spick.etymology: Cf. Sw. spik. See Spike a nail.

spicule.etymology: L. spiculum a little point, a dart.

spider.etymology: OE. spi, fr. AS. spinnan to spin; -- so named from spinning its web; cf. D. spin a spider, G. spinne, Sw. spindel. Seee Spin.

spigot.etymology: From spick,or spike; cf. Ir. & Gael. spiocaid a spigot, Ir. spice a spike. See Spike.

spike.etymology: Akin to LG. spiker, spieker, a large nail, D. spijker, Sw. spik, Dan. spiger, Icel. spik; all perhaps from L. spica a point, an ear of grain; but in the sense of nail more likely akin to E. spoke of a wheel. Cf. Spine.

spikenard.etymology: For spiked nard; cf. G. spieknarde, NL. spica nardi. See Spike an ear, and Nard.

spile.etymology: Cf. LG. spile, dial. G. speil, speiler, D. spijl. *170.

spill.etymology: sq. root170. Cf. Spell a splinter.

spin.etymology: AS. spinnan; akin to D. & G. spinnen, Icel. & Sw. spinna, Dan. spinde, Goth. spinnan, and probably to E. span. sq. root170. Cf. Span, v. t., Spider.

spinach.etymology: OF. espinache, espinoche, F. épinard; cf. F. spinace, Sp. espinaca; all fr. Ar. isfanaj, isfinaj, aspanakh, probably of Persian origin.

spinal.etymology: L. spinalis, fr. spina the spine: cf. F. spinal. See Spine.

spindle.etymology: AS. spinal, fr. spinnan to spin; akin to D. spil, G. spille, spindel, OHG. spinnala. sq. root170. See Spin.

spine.etymology: L. spina thorn, the spine; akin to spica a point: cf. OF. espine, F. épine. Cf. Spike, Spinet a musical instrument, Spinny.

spinel.etymology: F. spinelle, or LL. spinellus, perhaps from L. spina a thorn, a prickle, in allusion to its pointed crystals.

spinet.etymology: OF. espinete, F. épinette (cf. It. spinetta), fr. L. spina a thorn; -- so called because its quills resemble thorns. See Spine.

spinose.etymology: L. spinosus, from spina a thorn.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting the agent (originally a woman), especially a person who does something with skill or as an occupation; as in spinster (originally, a woman who spins), songster, baxter (= bakester), youngster.

spiracle.etymology: L. spiraculum, fr. spirare to breathe: cf. F. spiracule. See Spirit.

spiral.etymology: Cf. F. spiral. See Spire a winding line.

spirant.etymology: L. spirans, -antis, p. pr. of spirare to breathe. See Spirit.

spire.etymology: L. spirare to breathe. See Spirit.

spirillum.etymology: NL., dim. of L. spira a coil.

spirit.etymology: OF. espirit, esperit, F. esprit, L. spiritus, from spirare to breathe, to blow. Cf. Conspire, Expire, Esprit, Sprite.

spiritual.etymology: L. spiritualis: cf. F. spirituel. See Spirit.

spirituous.etymology: Cf. (for sense 2) F. spiritueux. Cf. Spiritous.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying something written, a writing; also, a writer; as autograph, crystograph, telegraph, photograph.
A suffix denoting that by which anything is measured; as, barometer, chronometer, dynamometer.

spirula.etymology: NL., dim. of L. spira a coil.

spit.etymology: OE. spite, AS. spitu; akin to D. spit, G. spiess, OHG. spiz, Dan. spid. Sw. spett, and to G. spitz pointed. sq. root170.

spitter.etymology: See Spit to eject from the mouth.

spleen.etymology: L. splen, Gr. lien, plihan, plihan.

splendid.etymology: L. splendidus, fr. splendere shine; cf. Lith. splendëti: cf. F. splendide.

splendor.etymology: L. fr. splendere to shine: cf. F. splendeur.

splenetic.etymology: L. spleneticus: cf. F. splénétique. See Spleen.

splice.etymology: D. splitsen, splitten; akin to G. splissen, Sw. splissa, Dan. splisse, and E. split; -- from the dividing or splitting the ends into separate strands. See Split, v. t.

splint.etymology: Akin to D. splinter,G. splinter, splitter, Dan. splint, Sw. splint a kind of spike, a forelock (in nautical use), Sw. splintato splint, splinter, Dan. splinte, and E. split. See Split, v. t., and cf. Splent.

splinter.etymology: Cf. LG. splittern, splinteren. See Splint, n., Split.

split.etymology: Probably of Scand. or Low german origin; cf. Dan. splitte, LG. splitten, OD. splitten, spletten, D. splijten, G. spleissen, MHG. splizen. Cf. Splice, Splint, Splinter.

splutter.etymology: Prov. E. splutter, eqivalent to sputter. Cf. Sputter.

spodumene.etymology: Gr. spodo`s ashes; cf. F. spodumène.

spoil.etymology: F. spolier, OF. espoilelier, fr. L. spoliare, fr. spolium spoil. Cf. Despoil, Spoliation.

spoke.etymology: OE. spoke, spake, AS, spaca; akin to D. speek, LG. speke, OHG. speihha, G. speiche. sq. root170. Cf. Spike a nail.

spoliation.etymology: L. spoliatio; cf. F. spoliation. See Spoil, v. t.

spondee.etymology: L. spondeus, Gr. spondée. So called because at libations slow, solemn melodies were used, chiefly in this meter.

sponge.etymology: OF. esponge, F. éponge, L. spongia, Gr. Fungus, Spunk.

sponsor.etymology: L., from spondere, sponsum, to engage one's self. See Spose.

spontaneous.etymology: L. spontaneus, fr. sponte of free will, voluntarily.

spook.etymology: D. spook; akin to G. spuk, Sw. spöke, Dan. spögelse a specter, spöge to play, sport, joke, spög a play, joke.

spool.etymology: OE. spole, OD. spoele, D. spoel; akin to G. spule, OHG. spuola, Dan. & Sw. spole.

spoon.etymology: OE. spon, AS. sp, a chip; akin to D. spaan, G. span, Dan. spaan, Sw. spån, Icel. spánn, spónn, a chip, a spoon. sq. root170. Cf. Span-new.

spoor.etymology: D. spoor; akin to AS. spor, G. spur, and from the root of E. spur. sq. root171. See Spur.

spot.etymology: Cf. Scot. & D. spat, Dan. spette, Sw. spott spittle, slaver; from the root of E. spit. See Spit to eject from the mouth, and cf. Spatter.

spouse.etymology: OF. espous, espos, fem. espouse, F. époux, épouse, fr. L. sponsus, sponsa, prop. p.p. of spondere, sponsum, to promise solemnly, to engage one's self. Cf. Despond, Espouse, respond, Sponsor.

spout.etymology: Cf. Sw. sputa, spruta, to spout, D. spuit a spout, spuiten to spout, and E. spurt, sprit, v., sprout, sputter; or perhaps akin to E. spit to eject from the mouth.

sprag.etymology: Cf. Icel. spraka a small flounder.

sprain.etymology: OF. espreindreto press, to force out, F. épreindre, fr. L. exprimere. See Express, v. t., and cf. Spraints.

sprat.etymology: OE. sprot, sprotte, D. sprot; akin to G. sprotte.

sprawl.etymology: OE. spraulen; cf. Sw. sprattla to sprawl, dial. Sw. spralla, Dan. spælle, sprælde, D. spartelen, spertelen, to flounder, to struggle.

spread.etymology: OE. spreden, AS. sprædan; akin to D. spreiden, spreijen, LG. spreden, spreen, spreien, G. spreiten, Dan. sprede, Sw. sprida. Cf. Spray water flying in drops.

spree.etymology: Cf. Ir. spre a spark, animation, spirit, Gael. spraic. Cf. Sprack.

sprig.etymology: AS. sprec; akin to Icel. sprek a stick. Cf. Spray a branch.

spring.etymology: AS. springan; akin to D. & G. springen, OS. & OHG. springan, Icel. & Sw. springa, Dan. springe; cf. Gr. Springe, Sprinkle.

springbok.etymology: D. springbok; springen to spring, leap + bok a he-goat, buck.

springbuck.etymology: D. springbok; springen to spring, leap + bok a he-goat, buck.

sprinkle.etymology: OE. sprenkelen, freq. of sprengen to sprinkle, to scatter, AS. sprengan, properly, to make to spring, causative of springan to spring; akin to D. sprenkelen to sprinkle, G. sprengen. See Spring, v. i., and cf. Sprent.

sprit.etymology: Akin to G. spritzen, sprützen. See Sprit, v. i.

sprite.etymology: OE. sprit, F. esprit, fr. L. spiritus. See Spirit, and cf. Sprightly.

sprout.etymology: OE. sprouten, spruten; akin to OFries. spr, AS. spreótan, D. spruiten, G. spriessen, Sw. spruta to squirt, to spout. Cf. Sprit, v. t. & i., Sprit a spar, Spout, v. t., Spurt.

spruce.etymology: OE. Spruce or Pruse, Prussia, Prussian. So named because it was first known as a native of Prussia, or because its sprouts were used for making, spruce beer. Cf. Spruce beer, below, Spruce, a.

spry.etymology: Cf. dial. Sw. sprygg lively, skittish, and E. sprag.

spumy.etymology: L. spumosus, spuma foam: cf. F. spumeux.

spunk.etymology: Gael. spong, or Ir. sponc, tinder, sponge; cf. AS. sponge a sponge (L. spongia), spon a chip. Cf. Sponge, Punk.

spurn.etymology: OE. spurnen to kick against, to stumble over, AS. spurnan to kick, offend; akin to spura spur, OS. & OHG. spurnan to kick, Icel. spyrna, L. spernere to despise, Skr. sphur to jerk, to push. sq. root171. See Spur.

spurt.etymology: Written also spirt, and originally the same word as sprit; OE. sprutten to sprout, AS. spryttan. See Sprit, v. i., Sprout, v. i.

sputter.etymology: From the root of spout or spit to eject from the mputh. Cf. Splutter.

sputum.etymology: L., from spuere, sputum, to spit.

spy.etymology: OE. spien, espien, OF. espier, F. épier, OHG. speh, G. spähen; akin to L. specere to see, Skr. spa(Espy, v.t., Aspect, Auspice, Circumspect, Conspicuouc, Despise, Frontispiece, Inspect, Prospect, Respite, Scope, Scecimen, Spectacle, Specter, Speculate, Spice, Spite, Suspicion.

squab.etymology: Cf. dial. Sw. sqvabb a soft and fat body, sqvabba a fat woman, Icel. kvap jelly, jellylike things, and and E. quab.

squabble.etymology: Cf. dial. Sw. skvabbel a dispute, skvappa to chide.

squad.etymology: F. escouade, fr. Sp. escuadra, or It. squadra, (assumed) LL. exquadrare to square; L. ex + quadra a square. See Square.

squadron.etymology: F. escadron, formerly also esquadron, or It. squadrone. See Squad.

squalid.etymology: L. squalidus, fr. squalere to be foul or filthy.

squall.etymology: Cf. Sw. sqval an impetuous running of water, sqvalregn a violent shower of rain, sqala to stream, to gush.

squalor.etymology: L., fr. squalere to be foul or filthy.

squander.etymology: Cf. Scot. squatter to splash water about, to scatter, to squander, Prov. E. swatter, Dan. sqvatte, Sw. sqvätta to squirt, sqvättra to squander, Icel. skvetta to squirt out, to throw out water.

square.etymology: OF. esquarre, esquierre, F. équerre a carpenter's square (cf. It. squadra), fr. (assumed) LL. exquadrare to make square; L. ex + quadrus a square, fr. quattuor four. See Four, and cf. Quadrant, Squad, Squer a square.

squat.etymology: OE. squatten to crush, OF. esquater, esquatir (cf. It. quatto squat, cowering), perhaps fr. L. ex + coactus, p. p. cogere to drive or urge together. See Cogent, Squash, v. t.

squaw.etymology: Massachusetts Indian squa, eshqua; Narragansett squâws; Delaware ochqueu, and khqueu; used also in compound words (as the names of animals) in the sense of female.

squeak.etymology: Probably of imitative origin; cf. Sw. sqväka to croak, Icel. skvakka to give a sound as of water shaken in a bottle.

squeal.etymology: Of Scand. origin; cf. Sw. sqväla, Norw. skvella. Cf. Squeak, Squall.

squeamish.etymology: OE. squaimous, sweymous, probably from OE. sweem, swem, dizziness, a swimming in the head; cf. Icel. svemr a bustle, a stir, Norw. sveim a hovering about, a sickness that comes upon one, Icel. svimi a giddiness, AS. swimi. The word has been perhaps confused witrh qualmish. Cf. Swim to be dizzy.

squeeze.etymology: OE. queisen, AS. cwesan, cwysan, cwisan, of uncertain origin. The s- was probably prefixed through the influence of squash, v.t.

squelch.etymology: Cf. prov. E. quelch a blow, and quel to crush, to kill.

squib.etymology: OE. squippen, swippen, to move swiftky, Icel. svipa to swoop, flash, dart, whip; akin to AS. swipian to whip, and E. swift, a. See Swift, a.

squiggle.etymology: Cf. Prov. E. swiggle to drink greedily, to shake liquor in a close vessel, and E. sqig.

squilla.etymology: L., a sea onion, also, a prawn or shrimp. See Squill.

squint.etymology: Cf. D. schuinte a slope, schuin, schuinisch, sloping, oblique, schuins slopingly. Cf. Askant, Askance, Asquint.

squire.etymology: OF. esquierre, F. équerre. See Square, n.

squirm.etymology: Cf. Swarm to climb a tree.

squirrel.etymology: OE. squirel, OF. esquirel, escurel, F. écureuil, LL. squirelus, squirolus, scuriolus, dim. of L. sciurus, Gr. si`oyros; skia` shade + o'yra` tail. Cf. Shine, v. i.

squirt.etymology: Cf. LG. swirtjen to squirt, OSw. sqvätta, E. squander.

stab.etymology: Cf. OD. staven to fix, fasten, fr. stave, staff, a staff, rod; akin to G. stab a staff, stick, E. staff; also Gael. stob to stab, as n., a stake, a stub. Cf. Staff.

stability.etymology: L. stabilitas; cf. F. stabilité. See Stable, a.

stable.etymology: OE. estable, F. stable, fr. L. stabilis, fr. stare to stand. See Stand, v. i. and cf. Establish.

staccato.etymology: It., p.p. of staccere, equivalent to distaccare. See Detach.

stack.etymology: Icel. stakkr; akin to Sw. stack, Dan. stak. Sf. Stake.

staddle.etymology: AS. stathol, srathul, a foundation, firm seat; akin to E. stand. *163. See Stand, v. i.

staff.etymology: AS. stæf a staff; akin to LG. & D. staf, OFries stef, G. stab, Icel. stafr, Sw. staf, Dan. stav, Goth. stabs element, rudiment, Skr. sthapay to cause to stand, to place. See Stand, and cf. Stab, Stave, n.

stag.etymology: Icel. steggr the male of several animals; or a doubtful AS. stagga. Cf. Steg.

stage.etymology: OF. estage, F. étage, (assumed) LL. staticum, from L. stare to stand. See Stand, and cf. Static.

stagger.etymology: OE. stakeren, Icel. stakra to push, to stagger, fr. staka to punt, push, stagger; cf. OD. staggeren to stagger. Cf. Stake, n.

stagnant.etymology: L. stagnans, -antis, p.pr. of stagnare. See Stagnate.

stagnate.etymology: L. stagnatus, p.p. of stagnare to stagnate, make stagnant, from stagnum a piece of standing water. See Stank a pool, and cf. Stanch, v. t.

stair.etymology: OE. steir, steyer, AS. st, from to ascend, rise. sq. root164. See Sty to ascend.

stake.etymology: AS. staca, from the root of E. stick; akin to OFries. & LG. stake, D. staak, Sw. stake, Dan. stage. See Stick, v. t., and cf. Estacade, Stockade.

stale.etymology: OE. stale, stele, AS. stæl, stel; akin to LG. & D. steel, G. stiel; cf. L. stilus stake, stalk, stem, Gr. stall, stalk, n.

stalk.etymology: OE. stalke, fr. AS. stæl, stel, a stalk. See Stale a handle, Stall.

stall.etymology: OE. stal, AS. steall, stall, a place, seat, or station, a stable; akin to D. & OHG. stal, G. & Sw. stall, stallr, Dan. stald, originally, a standing place; akin to G. selle a place, stellen to place, Gr. stand. Stand, and cf. Apostle, Epistle, Forestall, Install, Stale, a. & v. i., 1st Stalk, Stallion, Still.

stallion.etymology: OE. stalon, OF. estalon, F. étalon, fr. OHG. stal a stable. See Stall, n.

stalwart.etymology: OE. stalworth, AS. stælwyrth serviceable, probably originally, good at stealing, or worth stealing or taking, and afterwards extended to other causes of estimation. See Steal, v. t., Worth, a.

stamen.etymology: L. stamen the warp, a thread, fiber, akin to Gr. stand. See Stand, and cf. Stamin, Stamina.

staminate.etymology: L. staminatus consisting of threads, fr. stamen thread: cf. F. staminé.

stammel.etymology: OF. estamel; cf. OF. estamet a coarse woolen cloth, LL. stameta a kind of cloth, the same as staminea, and OF. estame a woolen stuff. See Stamin.

stammer.etymology: OE. stameren, fr. AS. stamur, stamer, stammering; akin to D. & LG. stameren to stammer, G. stammeln, OHG. stammal, stamm, Dan. stamme, Sw. stamma, Icel. stama, stamma, OHG. & Dan. stam stammering, Icel. stamr, Goth. stamms, and to G. stemmen to bear against, stumm dumb, D. stom. Cf. Stem to resist, Stumble.

stamp.etymology: OE. stampen; akin to LG. & D. stampen, G. stampfen, OHG. stanpf, Dan. stampe, Sw. stampa, Icel. stappa, G. stampf a pestle and E. step. See Step, v. i., and cf. Stampede.

stampede.etymology: Sp. estampida (in America) a stampede, estampido a crackling, akin to estampar to stamp, of German origin. See Stamp, v. t.

stanch.etymology: OF. estanchier, F. étancher to stpo a liquid from flowing; akin to Pr., Sp., & Pg. estancar, It. stancare to weary, LL. stancare, stagnare, to stanch, fr. L. stagnare to be or make stagnant. See Stagnate.

stanchion.etymology: OF. estanson, estançon, F. étançon, from OF. estance a stay, a prop, from L. stans, stantis, standing, p.pr. of stare to stand. See Stand, and cf. Stanza.

stand.etymology: OE. standen; AS. standan; akin to OFries. stonda, stan, D. staan, OS. standan, stan, G. stehen, Icel. standa, Dan. staae, Sw. stå, Goth. standan, Russ. stoiate, L. stare, Gr. stha. *163. Cf. Assist, Constant, Contrast, Desist, Destine, Ecstasy, Exist, Interstice, Obstacle, Obstinate, Prest, n., Rest remainder, Soltice, Stable, a. & n., State, n., Statute, Stead, Steed, Stool, Stud of horses, Substance, System.

standard.etymology: OF. estendart, F. étendard, probably fr. L. extendere to spread out, extend, but influenced by E. stand. See Extend.

stannic.etymology: L. stannum tin: cf. F. stannique.

stanza.etymology: It. stanza a room, habitation, a stanza, i. e., a stop, fr. L. stans, p.pr. of stare to stand. See Stand, and cf. Estancia, Stance, Stanchion.

stapelia.etymology: NL. So named after John Bodæus a Stapel, a physician of Amsterdam.

staple.etymology: AS. stapul, stapol, stapel, a step, a prop, post, table, fr. stapan to step, go, raise; akin to D. stapel a pile, stocks, emporium, G. stapela heap, mart, stake, staffel step of a ladder, Sw. stapel, Dan. stabel, and E. step cf. OF. estaple a mart, F. étape. See Step.

star.etymology: OE. sterre, AS. steorra; akin to OFries. stera, OS. sterro, D. ster, OHG. sterno, sterro, G. stern, Icel. stjarna, Sw. stjerna, Dan. stierne, Goth. staírno, Armor. & Corn. stern, L. stella, Gr. star; perhaps from a root meaning, to seater, Skr. st, L. sternere (cf. Stratum), and originally applied to the stars as beingstrewn over the sky, or as beingscatterers or spreaders of light. *296. Cf. Aster, Asteroid, Constellation, Disaster, Stellar.

starboard.etymology: OE. sterbord, AS. steórbord, i.e., steer board. See Steer, v. t., Board of a vessel, and cf. Larboard.

starch.etymology: AS. stearc stark, strong, rough. See Stark.

stark.etymology: OE. stark stiff, strong, AS. stearc; akin to OS. starc strong, D. sterk, OHG. starc, starah, G. & Sw. stark, Dan. stærk, Icel. sterkr, Goth. gastaúrknan to become dried up, Lith. strëgti to stiffen, to freeze. Cf. Starch, a. & n.

starling.etymology: OE. sterlyng, a dim. of OE. stare, AS. stær; akin to AS. stearn, G. star, staar, OHG. stara, Icel. starri, stari, Sw. stare, Dan. stær, L. sturnus. Cf. Stare a starling.

start.etymology: OE. sterten; akin to D. storten 8hurl, rush, fall, G. stürzen, OHG. sturzen to turn over, to fall, Sw. störa to cast down, to fall, Dan. styrte, and probably also to E. start a tail; the original sense being, perhaps, to show the tail, to tumble over suddenly. *166. Cf. Start a tail.

starve.etymology: OE. sterven to die, AS. steorfan; akin to D. sterven, G. sterben, OHG. sterban, Icel. starf labor, toil.

roots.meaning: A noun suffix, commonly having a diminutive or a depreciatory force; as in duck-ling, dosling, hireling, fosterling, firstling, underling.

state.etymology: OE. stat, OF. estat, F. état, fr. L. status a standing, position, fr. stare, statum, to stand. See Stand, and cf. Estate, Status.

static.etymology: Gr. statique. See Stand, and cf. Stage.

station.etymology: F., fr. L. statio, from stare, statum, to stand. See Stand.

stationary.etymology: L. stationarius: cf. F. stationnaire. Cf. Stationer.

statistics.etymology: Cf. F. statistique, G. statistik. See State, n.

stative.etymology: L. stativus, fr. stare, statum, to stand.

statuary.etymology: L. statuarius, n., fr. statuarius, a., of or belonging to statues, fr. statua statue: cf. F. statuaire. See Statue.

statue.etymology: F., fr. L. statua (akin to stativus standing still), fr. stare, statum, to stand. See Stand.

stature.etymology: F. stature, OF. estature, from L. statura, originally, an upright posture, hence, height or size of the body, from stare, statum, to stand. See Stand.

statute.etymology: F. statut, LL. statutum, from L. statutus, p.p. of statuere to set, station, ordain, fr. status position, station, fr. stare, statum, to stand. See Stand, and cf. Constitute, Destitute.

stave.etymology: From Staff, and corresponding to the pl. staves. See Staff.

stay.etymology: AS. stæg, akin to D., G., Icel., Sw., & Dan. stag; cf. OF. estai, F. étai, of Teutonic origin.

stead.etymology: OE. stede place, AS. stede; akin to LG. & D. stede, OS. stad, stedi, OHG. stat, G. statt, stätte, Icel. staedhr, Dan. sted, Sw. stad, Goth. sta, and E. stand. *163. See Stand, and cf. Staith, Stithy.

steadfast.etymology: Stead + fast, that is, fast in place.

steady.etymology: Cf. AS. stedig sterile, barren, stæ, steady (in gestæ), D. stedig, stadig, steeg, G. stätig, stetig. See Stead, n.

steak.etymology: OE. steike, Icel. steik, akin to Icel. steikja to roast, stikna to be roasted or scorched, and E. stick, the steak being broiled on a spit. See Stick, v. t.

stealth.etymology: OE. staple. See Steal, v. t.

steam.etymology: OE. stem, steem, vapor, flame, AS. steám vapor, smoke, odor; akin to D. stoom steam, perhaps originally, a pillar, or something rising like a pillar; cf. Gr. stand.

steed.etymology: OE. stede, AS. steda a stud-horse, war horse, fr. stod a stud of breeding steeds; akin to G. stute a mare, Icel. stedda, sto, a stud. *163. See Stud of horses.

steel.etymology: AS. stel, styl, style; akin to D. staal, G. stahl, OHG. stahal, Icel. stal, Dan. staal, Sw. stål, Old Prussian stakla.

steelyard.etymology: So named from a place in London called the Steelyard, which was a yard in which steel was sold.

steep.etymology: OE. stepen, probably fr. Icel. steypa to cause to stoop, cast down, pour out, to cast metals, causative of stupa to stoop; cf. Sw. stöpa to cast, to steep, Dan. stöbe, D. & G. stippen to steep, to dip. Cf. Stoop, v. t.

steeple.etymology: OE. stepel, AS. stepel, st; akin to E. steep, a.

steer.etymology: OE. steer, AS. steór; akin to D. & G. stier a bull, OHG. stior, Icel. stjorr, , Sw. tjur, Dan. tyr, Goth. stiur, Russ. tur', Pol. tur, Ir. & Gael. tarbh, W. tarw, L. taurus, Gr. sth strong, stout, AS. stor large, Icel. storr, OHG. st, stiuri. *168. Cf. Stirk, Taurine, a.

steersman.etymology: Steer a rudder + man: cf. AS. steórman.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.

stellar.etymology: L. stellaris, fr. stella a star. See Star.

stellate.etymology: L. stellatus, p.p. of stellare to set or cover with stars, from stella a star. See Stellar.

steller.etymology: After Geo. W.Steller, a German naturalist.

stem.etymology: AS. stemn, stefn, stæfn; akin to OS. stamn the stem of a ship, D. stam stem, steven stem of a ship, G. stamm stem, steven stem of a ship, Icel. stafn, stamn, stem of a ship, stofn, stomn, stem, Sw. stam a tree trunk, Dan. stamme. Cf. Staff, Stand.

stench.etymology: AS. stenc a strong smell, fr. stincan. See Stink, v. i.

stencil.etymology: Probably from OF. estincelle spangle, spark, F. étincelle spark, L. scintilla. See Scintillate, and cf. Tinsel.

stenography.etymology: Gr. graphy: cf. F. sténographie, G. stenographie.

step.etymology: AS. stæppan; akin to OFries. steppa, D. stappen to step, stap a step, OHG. stepfen to step, G. stapfe a footstep, OHG. stapfo, G. stufe a step to step on; cf. Gr. Stamp, n. & a.

steppe.etymology: From Russ. stepe, through G. or F. steppe.

roots.meaning: A combining form meaning solid, hard, firm, as in stereo- chemistry, stereography.
A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.
A combining form meaning solid, hard, firm, as in stereo- chemistry, stereography.
A combining form signifying impressed form; stamp; print; type; typical form; representative; as in stereotype phototype, ferrotype, monotype.

sterile.etymology: F. stérile, L. sterilis, akin to Gr. stereo`s stiff, solid, stei^ros barren, stei^ra a cow that has not calved, Goth. stairo, fem., barren. See Stare to gaze.

sterling.etymology: OE. sterlynge, starling, for easterling, LL. esterlingus, probably from Easterling, once the popular name of German trades in England, whose money was of the purest quality: cf. MHG. sterlink a certain coin. Cf. East. "Certain merchants of Norwaie, Denmarke, and of others those parties, called Ostomanni, or (as in our vulgar language we tearme them), easterlings, because they lie east in respect of us." Holinshed. "In the time of . . . King Richard the First, monie coined in the east parts of Germanie began to be of especiall request in England for the puritie thereof, and was called Easterling monie, as all inhabitants of those parts were called Easterlings, and shortly after some of that countrie, skillful in mint matters and allaies, were sent for into this realme to bring the coine to perfection; which since that time was called of them sterling, for Easterling." Camden. "Four thousand pound of sterlings." R. of Gloucester.

stern.etymology: AS. stearn a kind of bird. See Starling.

sternutation.etymology: L. sternutatio, fr. sternutare to sneeze, intens. from sternuere.

stertorous.etymology: L. stertere to snore: cf. F. stertoreux.

roots.meaning: A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.

stevedore.etymology: Sp. estivador a packer, a stower, fr. estivar to pack, to stow, L. stipare to press, compress, probably akin to E. stiff. See Stiff, Stive to stuff.

steward.etymology: OE. stiward, AS. stiweard, stigweard, literally, a sty ward; stigu sty + weard warden, guardian, -- his first duty having been probably to attend to the domestic animals. *164. See Sty pen for swine, Ward.

stick.etymology: OE. sticke, AS. sticca; akin to stician to stab, prick, pierce, G. stecken a stick, staff, OHG. steccho, Icel. stik a stick. See Stick, v. t..

stickle.etymology: Probably fr. OE. stightlen, sti, to dispose, arrange, govern, freq. of stihten, AS. stihtan: cf. G. stiften to found, to establish.

stickleback.etymology: OE. & Prov E. stickle a prickle, spine, sting (AS. sticel) + back. See Stick, v. t., and cf. Banstickle.

stiff.etymology: OE. stif, AS. stif; akin to D. stijf, G. steif, Dan. stiv, Sw. styf, Icel. stifr, Lith. stipti to be stiff; cf. L. stipes a post, trunk of a tree, stipare to press, compress. Cf. Costive, Stifle, Stipulate, Stive to stuff.

stigma.etymology: L., a mark, a brand, from Gr. Stick, v. t.

stiletto.etymology: It., dim. of stilo a dagger, fr. L. stilus a pointed instrument. See Style for writing, and cf. Stylet.

still.etymology: OE. stille, AS. stille; akin to D. stil, OS. & OHG. stilli, G. still, Dan. stille, Sw. stilla, and to E. stall; from the idea of coming to a stand, or halt. Cf. Still, adv.

stilt.etymology: OE. stilte; akin to Dan. stylte, Sw. stylta, LG. & D. stelt, OHG. stelza, G. stelze, and perh. to E. stout.

stimulant.etymology: L. stimulans, p.pr.; cf. F. stimulant. See Stimulate.

stimulate.etymology: L. stimulatus, p.p. of stimulare to prick or goad on, to incite, fr. stimulus a goad. See Stimulus.

stimulus.etymology: L., for stigmulus, akin to L. instigare to stimulate. See Instigare, Stick, v. t.

sting.etymology: AS. sting a sting. See Sting, v. t.

stingy.etymology: Probably from sting, and meaning originally, stinging; hence, biting, nipping (of the wind), churlish, avaricious; or cf. E. skinch.

stink.etymology: AS. stinkan to have a smell (whether good or bad); akin to OHG. stinchan, G. & D. stinken to stink; of uncertain origin; cf. Icel. stökkva to leap, to spring, Goth. stigqan to push, strike, or Gr. Stench.

stint.etymology: OE. stinten, stenten, stunten, to cause to cease, AS. styntan (in comp.) to blunt, dull, fr. stunt dull, stupid; akin to Icel. stytta to shorten, stuttr short, dial, Sw. stynta to shorten, stunt short. Cf. Stent, Stunt.

stipe.etymology: L. stipes a stock, post, branch: cf. F. stipe.

stipend.etymology: L. stipendium; stips, gen. stipis, a gift, donation, given in small coin + pendere to weigh or pay out.

stipple.etymology: D. stippelen to make points, to spot, dot, from stippel, dim. of stip a dot, spot.

stipulate.etymology: L. stipulatus, p.p. of stipulari to stipulate, fr. OL. stipulus firm, fast; probably akin to L. stipes a post. Cf. Stiff.

stipule.etymology: L. stipula a stalk, stem, straw: cf. F. stipule. Cf. Stubble.

stir.etymology: OE. stiren, steren, sturen, AS. styrian; probably akin to D. storen to disturb, G. stören, OHG. storen to scatter, destroy. *166.

stirk.etymology: AS. stric, from steór a steer. See Steer a young ox.

stirrup.etymology: OE. stirop, AS. stigrap; stigan to mount, ascend + rap a rope; akin to G. stegreif a stirrup. *164. See Sty, v. i., and Rope.

stitch.etymology: OE. stiche, AS. stice a pricking, akin to stician to prick. See Stick, v. i.

stoat.etymology: OE. stot a stoat, horse, bullock; perhaps originally only of male animals, and akin to D. stooten to push, E. stutter; cf. Icel. st a bull, Sw. stut a bullock. Cf. Stot.

stock.etymology: AS. stocc a stock, trunk, stick; akin to D. stok, G. stock, OHG. stoc, Icel. stokkr, Sw. stock, Dan. stok, and AS. stycce a piece; cf. Skr. tuj to urge, thrust. Cf. Stokker, Stucco, and Tuck a rapier.

stockade.etymology: F. estacade stockade, boom (confused in French with estocade; see 1st Stoccado); fr. It. steccata a palisade (influenced by OF. estach, estaque, a stake, post), or from Sp. estacada a palisade; both of German origin, and akin to E. stake, stick; cf. G. stecken stick, OHG. steccho. See Stake, n., Stick, n. & v. t., and cf. Estacade, Stacket.

stocking.etymology: From Stock, which was formerly used of a covering for the legs and feet, combining breeches, or upper stocks, and stockings, or nether stocks.

stoic.etymology: L. stoicus, Gr. stoïque. See Stoic, n.

stoical.etymology: L. stoicus, Gr. stoïque. See Stoic, n.

roots.meaning: A suffix denoting the art, process, or science, of measuring; as, acidmetry, chlorometry, chronometry.

stoke.etymology: OE. stoken, fr. D. stoken, fr. stok a stick (cf. OF. estoquier to thrust, stab; of Teutonic origin, and akin to D. stok). See Stock.

stolon.etymology: L. stolo, -onis: cf. F. stolon. Cf. Stole a stolon, 1st Stool.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying bearing, producing, yielding; as, auriferous, yielding gold; chyliferous, producing chyle.

stomach.etymology: OE. stomak, F. estomac, L. stomachus, fr. Gr. sto`machos stomach, throat, gullet, fr. sto`ma a mouth, any outlet or entrance.

roots.meaning: A suffix used in medical terms to denote an inflammatory disease of; as, arthritis; bronchitis, phrenitis.
A combining form or suffix from Gr. poy`s, podo`s, foot; as, decapod, an animal having ten feet; phyllopod, an animal having leaflike feet; myriapod, hexapod.

stone.etymology: OE. ston, stan, AS. stan; akin to OS. & OFries. sten, D. steen, G. stein, Icel. steinn, Sw. sten, Dan. steen, Goth. stains, Russ. stiena a wall, Gr. Steen.

stop.etymology: OE. stoppen, AS. stoppian (in comp.); akin to LG. & D. stoppen, G. stopfen, Icel. stoppa, Sw. stoppa, Dan. stoppe; all probably fr. LL. stopare, stupare, fr. L. stuppa the coarse part of flax, tow, oakum. Cf. Estop, Stuff, Stupe a fomentation.

stopple.etymology: Cf. G. stöpfel, stöpsel. See Stop, n. & v. t.

store.etymology: OE. stor, stoor, OF. estor, provisions, supplies, fr. estorer to store. See Store, v. t.

storm.etymology: AS. storm; akin to D. storm, G. sturm, Icel. stormr; and perhaps to Gr. s to flow, to hasten, or perhaps to L. sternere to strew, prostrate (cf. Stratum). *166.

story.etymology: OF. estoré, estorée, built, erected, p.p. of estorer to build, restore, to store. See Store, v. t.

stout.etymology: D. stout bold (or OF. estout bold, proud, of Teutonic origin); akin to AS. stolt, G. stolz, and perh. to E. stilt.

stove.etymology: D. stoof a foot stove, originally, a heated room, a room for a bath; akin to G. stube room, OHG. stuba a heated room, AS. stofe, Icel. stofa a room, bathing room, Sw. stufva, stuga, a room, Dan. stue; of unknown origin. Cf. Estufa, Stew, Stufa.

stover.etymology: OE. estoveir, estovoir, necessity, provisions, properly an inf., "to be necessary." Cf. Estovers.

stow.etymology: OE. stowen, fr. stowe a place, AS. stow; cf. Icel. eldstoa fireplace, hearth, OFries. sto, and E. stand. *163.

straddle.etymology: Freq. from the root of stride.

straggle.etymology: Freq. of OE. straken to roam, to stroke. See Stroke, v. t.

straight.etymology: OE. strei, properly p.p. of strecchen to stretch, AS. streht, p.p. of streccan to stretch, to extend. See Stretch.

strait.etymology: OE. straight, streyt, streit, OF. estreit, estroit, F. étroit, from L. strictus drawn together, close, tight, p.p. of stringere to draw tight. See 2nd Strait, and cf. Strict.

strand.etymology: Probably fr. D. streen a skein; akin to G. strähne a skein, lock of hair, strand of a rope.

strange.etymology: OE. estrange, F. étrange, fr. L. extraneus that is without, external, foreign, fr. extra on the outside. See Extra, and cf. Estrange, Extraneous.

stranger.etymology: OF. estrangier, F. étranger. See Strange.

strangle.etymology: OF. estrangler, F. étrangler, L. strangulare, Gr. string, n. Cf. Strain, String.

strangulation.etymology: L. strangulatio: cf. F. strangulation. See Strangle.

strap.etymology: OE. strope, AS. stropp, L. stroppus, struppus, perhaps fr. Gr. Strophe). Cf. Strop a strap, a piece of rope.

strappado.etymology: It. strappata a pull, the strappado, from strappare to pull, from Prov. G. strapfen: cf. G. straff tense, stretched.

stratagem.etymology: F. stratagème (cf. Sp. estratagema, It. stratagemma), L. strategema, Gr. Stratum) + Agent.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.
A suffix denoting the art of writing or describing; also, the writing or description itself; a treatise; as, calligraphy, biography, geography.

stratocracy.etymology: Gr. -cracy, as in democracy: cf. F. stratocratie.

stratum.etymology: L., from sternere, stratum, to spread; akin to Gr. Strew, and cf. Consternation, Estrade, Prostrate, Stratus, Street.

stratus.etymology: L. stratus a spreading out, scattering, from sternere, stratum, to spread.
