straw.etymology: OE. straw, stre, stree, AS. streáw, from the root of E. strew; akin to OFries. stre, D. stroo, G. stroh, OHG. stro, Icel. stra, Dan. straa, Sw. strå. *166. See Strew.

strawberry.etymology: AS. streáwberige; streáw straw + berie berry; perhaps from the resemblance of the runners of the plant to straws.

stray.etymology: OF. estraier, estraer, to stray, or as adj., stray, fr. (assumed) L. stratarius roving the streets, fr. L. strata (sc. via) a paved road. See Street, and Stray, a.

stream.etymology: AS. streám; akin to OFries. stram, OS. strom, D. stroom, G. strom, OHG. stroum, str, Dan. & Sw. ström, Icel. straumr, Ir. sroth, Lith. srove, Russ. struia, Gr. sru. *174. Cf. Catarrh, Diarrhea, Rheum, Rhythm.

street.etymology: OE. strete, AS. str, fr. L. strata (sc. via) a paved way, properly fem. p.p. of sternere, stratum, to spread; akin to E. strew. See Strew, and cf. Stratum, Stray, v. & a.

strelitzia.etymology: NL., named after Charlotte, Princess of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, and queen of George III of Great Britain.

strength.etymology: OE. strengthe, AS. streng, fr. strang strong. See Strong.

stress.etymology: Abbrev. fr. distress; or cf. OF. estrecier to press, pinch, (assumed) LL. strictiare, fr. L. strictus. See Distress.

stretch.etymology: OE. strecchen, AS. streccan; akin to D. strekken, G. strecken, OHG. strecchen, Sw. sträcka, Dan. strække; cf. AS. stræck, strec, strong, violent, G. strack straight; of uncertain origin, perhaps akin to E. strong. Cf. Straight.

strew.etymology: OE. strewen, strawen, AS. strewian, streówian; akin to Ofries. strewa, OS. strewian, D. strooijen, G. streuen, OHG. strewen, Icel. stra, Sw. strö, Dan. ströe, Goth. straujan, L. sternere, stratum, Gr. st. *166. Cf. Stratum, Straw, Street.

strict.etymology: L. strictus, p.p. of stringere to draw or bind tight, to strain. See Strain, and cf. Strait, a.

stricture.etymology: L. strictura a contraction, from stringere, strictum, to draw tight: cf. F. stricture. See Strict.

stride.etymology: AS. stridan to stride, to strive; akin to LG. striden, OFries. strida to strive, D. strijden to strive, to contend, G. streiten, OHG. stritan; of uncertain origin. Cf. Straddle.

strident.etymology: L. stridens, -entis, p.pr. of stridere to make a grating or creaking noise.

stridor.etymology: L., from stridere to make any harsh, grating, or creaking sound.

strike.etymology: OE. striken to strike, proceed, flow, AS. strican to go, proceed, akin to D. strijken to rub, stroke, strike, to move, go, G. streichen, OHG. strihhan, L. stringere to touch lightly, to graze, to strip off (but perhaps not to L. stringere in sense to draw tight), striga a row, a furrow. Cf. Streak, Stroke.

string.etymology: OE. string, streng, AS. streng; akin to D. streng, G. strang, Icel. strengr, Sw. sträng, Dan. stræng; probably from the adj., E. strong (see Strong); or perhaps originally meaning, twisted, and akin to E. strangle.

stringent.etymology: L. stringens, -entis, p.pr. of stringere to draw or bind tight. See Strain.

strip.etymology: OE. stripen, strepen, AS. str in bestr to plunder; akin to D. stroopen, MHG. stroufen, G. streifen.

stripe.etymology: OD. strijpe a stripe, streak; akin to LG. stripe, D. streep, Dan. stribe, G. strief, striefen, MHG. striefen to glide, march.

stripling.etymology: Dim. of strip; as if a small strip from the main stock or steam.

strive.etymology: OF. estriver; of Teutonic origin, and akin to G. streben, D. streven, Dan. stræbe, Sw. sträfva. Cf. Strife.

strobile.etymology: L. strobilus a pine cone, Gr. strobole.

roots.meaning: A combining form usually signifying an instrument for viewing (with the eye) or observing (in any way); as in microscope, telescope, altoscope, anemoscope.

stroke.etymology: OE. strok, strook, strak, fr. striken. See Strike, v. t.

stroll.etymology: Cf. Dan. stryge to stroll, Sw. stryka to stroke, to ramble, dial. Sw. strykel one who strolls about, Icel. strj to stroke, D. struikelen to stumble, G. straucheln. Cf. Struggle.

strong.etymology: AS. strang, strong; akin to D. & G. streng strict, rigorous, OHG. strengi strong, brave, harsh, Icel. strangr strong, severe, Dan. streng, Sw. sträng strict, severe. Cf. Strength, Stretch, String.

structure.etymology: L. structura, from struere, structum, to arrange, build, construct; perhaps akin to E. strew: cf. F. structure. Cf. Construe, Destroy, Instrument, Obstruct.

struggle.etymology: OE. strogelen; cf. Icel. strj to stroke, to beat, to flog, Sw. stryka to stroke, to strike, Dan. stryge, G. straucheln to stumble. Cf. Stroll.

strum.etymology: Probably of imitative origin. Cf. Thrum.

strumpet.etymology: OE. strumpet, strompet; cf. OF. stupe debauchery, F. stupe, L. stuprare, stupratum, to debauch, stuprum debauchery, Gael. & Ir. striopach a prostitute.

strut.etymology: OE. struten, strouten, to swell; akin to G. strozen to be swelled, to be puffed up, to strut, Dan. strutte.

strychnine.etymology: L. strychnos a kind of nightshade, Gr. strychnine.

stubble.etymology: OE. stobil, stoble, OF. estouble, estuble, F. étuele, LL. stupla, stupula, L. stipula stubble, stalk; cf. D. & G. stopped, OHG. stupfila. Cf. Stipule.

stubborn.etymology: OE. stoburn, stiborn; probably fr. AS. styb a stub. See Stub.

stucco.etymology: It., fr. OHG. stucchi a crust, piece, G. stück piece; akin to AS. stycce. See Stock.

stud.etymology: OE. stod, stood, AS. stod; akin to OHG. stuota, G. stute a mare, Icel. sto stud, Lith. stodas a herd, Russ. stado, and to E. stand. The sense is properly, a stand, an establishment. *163. See Stand, and cf. Steed.

student.etymology: L. studens, -entis, p.pr. of studere to study. See Study, n.

studio.etymology: It. studio, properly, study. See Study.

studious.etymology: L. studious: cf. F. studieux. See Study.

study.etymology: OE. studie, L. studium, akin to studere to study; possibly akin to Gr. estudie, estude, F. étude. Cf. Etude, Student, Studio, Study, v. i.

stuff.etymology: OF. estoffe, F. étoffe; of uncertain origin, perhaps of Teutonic origin and akin to E. stop, v.t. Cf. Stuff, v. t.

roots.meaning: A suffix signifying to make, to form into, etc.; as, acetify, amplify, dandify, Frenchify, etc.

stumble.etymology: OE. stumblen, stomblen; freq. of a word akin to E. stammer. See Stammer.

stump.etymology: OE. stumpe, stompe; akin to D. stomp, G. stumpf, Icel. stumpr, Dan. & Sw. stump, and perhaps also to E. stamp.

stun.etymology: OE. stonien, stownien; either fr. AS. stunian to resound (cf. D. stenen to groan, G. stöhnen, Icel. stynja, Gr. stan to thunder, and E. thunder), or from the same source as E. astonish. *168.

stupe.etymology: L. stupa, or better stuppa, tow. Cf. Stop, v. t.

stupefy.etymology: F. stupéfier, fr. L. stupere to be stupefied + ficare (in comp.) to make, akin to facere. See Stupid, Fact, and cf. Stupefacient.

stupendous.etymology: L. stupendus astonishing, p. future pass. of stupere to be astonished at. Cf. Stupid.

stupid.etymology: L. stupidus, fr. stupere to be stupefied: cf. F. stupide.

stupor.etymology: L., from stupere to be struck senseless.

sturdy.etymology: OE. sturdi inconsiderable, OF. estourdi stunned, giddy, thoughtless, rash, F. étourdi, p.p. of OF. estourdir to stun, to render giddy, to amaze, F. étourdir; of uncertain origin. The sense has probably been influenced by E. stout.

sturgeon.etymology: F. esturgeon, LL. sturio, sturgio, OHG. sturjo, G. stör; akin to AS. styria, styriga.

stutter.etymology: Freq. of stut, OE. stoten; probably of Dutch or Low German origin; cf. D. & LG. stotteren, G. stottern, D. stooten to push, to strike; akin to G. stossen, Icel. stauta, Sw. stöta, Dan. stöde, Goth. stautan, L. tundere, Skr. tud to thrust. Cf. Contuse, Obtuse.

sty.etymology: AS. stigu, fr. stigan to rise; originally, probably, a place into which animals climbed or went up. *164. See Sty, v. i., and cf. Steward.

stylet.etymology: F., dim. of style; cf. It. stiletto. See Stiletto.

suasion.etymology: L. suasio, fr. suadere, suasum, to advise, persuade, fr. suadus persuading, persuasive; akin to suavis sweet: cf. OF. suasion. See Suave, and cf. Dissuade, Persuade.

suave.etymology: L. suavis sweet, pleasant: cf. F. suave. See Sweet, and cf. Suasion.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting that the ingredient (of a compound) signified by the term to which it is prefixed,is present in only a small proportion, or less than the normal amount; as, subsulphide, suboxide, etc. Prefixed to the name of a salt it is equivalent to basic; as, subacetate or basic acetate. [Obsoles.]

subaltern.etymology: F. subalterne, LL. subalternus, fr. L. sub under + alter the one, the other of two. See Alter.

subclavian.etymology: Pref. sub- + L. clavis a key. See Clavicle.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting that the ingredient (of a compound) signified by the term to which it is prefixed,is present in only a small proportion, or less than the normal amount; as, subsulphide, suboxide, etc. Prefixed to the name of a salt it is equivalent to basic; as, subacetate or basic acetate. [Obsoles.]

subdeacon.etymology: Pref. sub- + deacon: cf. L. subdiaconus.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting that the ingredient (of a compound) signified by the term to which it is prefixed,is present in only a small proportion, or less than the normal amount; as, subsulphide, suboxide, etc. Prefixed to the name of a salt it is equivalent to basic; as, subacetate or basic acetate. [Obsoles.]

subdivide.etymology: L. subdividere, sub under + dividere to divide. See Divide.

subdue.etymology: OE. soduen, OF. sosduire to seduce, L. subtus below (fr. sub under) + ducere to lead. See Duke, and cf. Subduct.

subjacent.etymology: L. subjacens, p.pr. of subjacere to lie under; sub under + jacere to lie.

subject.etymology: OE. suget, OF. souzget, sougit (in which the first part is L. subtus below, fr. sub under), subgiet, subject, F. sujet, from L. subjectus lying under, subjected, p.p. of subjicere, subicere, to throw, lay, place, or bring under; sub under + jacere to throw. See Jet a shooting forth.

subjection.etymology: L. subjectio: cf. OF. subjection, F. subjétion. See Subject, a.

subjoin.etymology: Cf. OF. subjoindre, L. subjungere. See Sub-, and Join, and cf. Subjective.

roots.meaning: A prefix denoting that the ingredient (of a compound) signified by the term to which it is prefixed,is present in only a small proportion, or less than the normal amount; as, subsulphide, suboxide, etc. Prefixed to the name of a salt it is equivalent to basic; as, subacetate or basic acetate. [Obsoles.]

subjugate.etymology: L. subjugatus, p.p. of subjugare to subjugate; sub under + jugum a yoke. See Yoke.

subjunctive.etymology: L. subjunctivus, fr. subjungere, subjunctum, to subjoin: cf. F. subjonctif. See Subjoin.

sublieutenant.etymology: Pref. sub + lieutenant: cf. F. sous- lieutenant.

sublimate.etymology: L. sublimatus, p.p. of sublimare to raise, elevate, fr. sublimis high: cf. F. sublimer. See Sublime, a., and cf. Surlime, v. t.

sublime.etymology: L. sublimis; sub under + (perhaps) a word akin to limen lintel, sill, thus meaning, up to the lintel: cf. F. sublime. Cf. Eliminate.

sublingual.etymology: Pref. sub + lingual: cf. F. sublingual.

sublunar.etymology: Pref. sub + lunar, or lunary: cf. F. sublunaire.

sublunary.etymology: Pref. sub + lunar, or lunary: cf. F. sublunaire.

subluxation.etymology: Pref. sub + luxation: cf. F. subluxation.

submerge.etymology: L. submergere, submersum; sub under + mergere to plunge: cf. F. submerger. See Merge.

submersed.etymology: L. submersus, p.p. of submergere. See Submerge.

submission.etymology: L. submissio a letting down, lowering: cf. F. soumission.

submit.etymology: L. submittere; sub under + mittere to send: cf. F. soumettre. See Missile.

subocular.etymology: Pref. sub + ocular: cf. L. subocularis.

subordinate.etymology: Pref. sub + L. ordinatus, p.p. of ordinare to set in order, to arrange. See Ordain.

suborn.etymology: F. suborner, L. subornare; sub under, secretly + ornare to furnish, provide, equip, adorn. See Ornament.

subpoena.etymology: NL., fr. L. sub under + poena punishment. See Pain.

subrogate.etymology: L. subrogatus, p.p. of subrogare. See Surrogate.

subscribe.etymology: L. subscribere, subscriptum; sub under + scribere to write: cf. F. souscrire. See Scribe.

subsequent.etymology: L. subsequens, -entis, p.pr. of subsequi to follow, succeed: cf. F. subséquent. See Sue to follow.

subserve.etymology: L. subservire; sub under + servire to serve. See Serve.

subside.etymology: L. subsidere; sub under, below + sidere to sit down, to settle; akin to sedere to sit, E. sit. See Sit.

subsidence.etymology: L. subsidens, -entis, p.pr. of subsidere. See Subside.

subsidiary.etymology: L. subsidiarius: cf. F. subsidiaire. See Subsidy.

subsidy.etymology: L. subsidium the troops stationed in reserve in the third line of battlem reserve, support, help, fr. subsidere to sit down, lie in wait: cf. F. subside. See Subside.

subsist.etymology: L. subsistere to stand still, stay, remain alive; sub under + sistere to stand, to cause to stand, from stare to stand: cf. F. subsister. See Stand.

substance.etymology: F., fr. L. substantia, fr. substare to be under or present, to stand firm; sub under + stare to stand. See Stand.

substitute.etymology: L. substitutus, p.p. of substituere to put under, put in the place of; sub under + statuere to put, place: cf. F. substitut. See Statute.

substrate.etymology: L. substratus, p.p. of substrahere. See Substratum.

substratum.etymology: L. substratus, p.p. of substernere to strew under; sub under + sternere to strew. See Stratum.

subsume.etymology: Pref. sub- + L. sumere to take.

subtend.etymology: L. subtendere; sub under + tendere to stretch, extend. See Tend.

subterfuge.etymology: F., from LL. subterfugium, fr. L. subterfugere to flee secretly, to escape; subter under + fugere to flee. See Fugitive.

subterranean.etymology: L. subterraneus; sub under + terra earth. See Terrace.

subterraneous.etymology: L. subterraneus; sub under + terra earth. See Terrace.

subtle.etymology: OE. sotil, subtil, OF. soutil, later subtil, F. subtil, L. subtilis; probably, originally, woven fine, and fr. sub under + tela a web, fr. texere to weave. See Text, and cf. Subtile.

subtlety.etymology: OE. sotelte, sutilte, OF. sotillete, L. subtilitas. See Subtle, and cf. Subtility.

subtract.etymology: L. subtractus, p.p. of subtrahere to draw from beneath, withdraw, remove; sub under + trahere to draw. See Trace, v. t., and cf. Substract.

subtraction.etymology: L. subtractio a drawing back. See Subtract, and cf. Substraction.

subtrahend.etymology: L. subtrahendus that is to be subtracted, p.fut.pess. of subtrahere. See Subtract.

suburb.etymology: L. suburbium; sub under, below, near + urbs a city. See Urban.

subvention.etymology: F., fr. LL. subventio, fr. L. subvenire to come up to one's assistance, to assist. See Souvenir, and cf. Subvene.

subversion.etymology: L. subversio: cf. F. subversion. See Subvert.

subvert.etymology: L. subvertere, subversum; sub under + vertere to turn: cf. F. subvertir. See Verse.

succade.etymology: L. succus, sucus, juice: cf. F. succade a sugarbox. Cf. Sucket.

succeed.etymology: L. succedere, successum; sub under + cedere to go, to go along, approach, follow, succeed: cf. F. succéder. See Cede, and cf. Success.

success.etymology: L. successus: cf. F. succès. See Succeed.

succession.etymology: L. successio: cf. F. succession. See Succeed.

successor.etymology: OE. successour, OF. successur, successor, F. successeur, L. successor. See Succeed.

succinct.etymology: L. succinctus, p.p. of succingere to gird below or from below, to tuck up; sub + cingere to gird. Cf. Cincture.

succor.etymology: OE. socouren, OF. sucurre, soucourre, secorre, F. secourir, L. succurrere, succursum, to run under, run to the aid of, help, succor; sub under + currere to run. See Current.

succotash.etymology: Narragansett Indian m'sickquatash corn boiled whole.

succuba.etymology: NL., fr. L. succubare to lie under; sub under + cubare to lie down; cf. L. succuba, succubo, one who lies under another.

succulent.etymology: L. succulentus, suculentus, fr. succus, sucus, juice; perhaps akin to E. suck: cf. F. succulent.

succumb.etymology: L. succumbere; sub under + cumbere (in comp.), akin to cubare to lie down. See Incumbent, Cubit.

succussion.etymology: L. succussio, from succutere: cf. F. succussion. See Succussation.

such.etymology: OE. such, sich, sech, sik, swich, swilch, swulch, swilc, swulc, AS. swelc, swilc, swylc; akin to OFries. selik, D. zulk, OS. sulic, OHG. sulih, solih, G. solch, Icel. slikr, OSw. salik, Sw. slik, Dan. slig, Goth. swaleiks; originally meaning, so shaped. *192. See So, Like, a., and cf. Which.

suck.etymology: OE. suken, souken, AS. s, s; akin to D. zuigen, G. saugen, OHG. s, Icel. s, sj, Sw. suga, Dan. suge, L. sugere. Cf. Honeysuckle, Soak, Succulent, Suction.

suckling.etymology: OE. sokeling. See Suck, v. t.

suction.etymology: L. sugere, suctum, to suck; cf. OF. suction. See Suck, v. t.

sudation.etymology: L. sudatio, fr. sudare to sweat: cf. F. sudation.

sudatory.etymology: L. sudatorius, fr. sudare to sweat: cf. F. sudatoire. See Sweat.

sudden.etymology: OE. sodian, sodein, OF. sodain, sudain, F. soudain, L. subitaneus, fr. subitus sudden, that has come unexpectedly, p.p. of subire to come on, to steal upon; sub under, secretly + ire to go. See Issue, and cf. Subitaneous.

sudorific.etymology: L. sudor sweat (akin to E. sweat) + facere to make.

suds.etymology: Akin to sodden, seethe. See Seethe.

sue.etymology: OE. suen, sewen, siwen, OF. sivre (pres.ind. 3d sing. il siut, suit, he follows, nous sevons we follow), LL. sequere, for L. sequi, secutus; akin to Gr. sac to accompany, and probably to E. see, v.t. See See, v. t., and cf. Consequence, Ensue, Execute, Obsequious, Pursue, Second, Sect in religion, Sequence, Suit.

suet.etymology: OE. suet, dim. fr. OF. seu, suif, F. suif, L. sebum. Cf. Soap, Sebaceous.

suffer.etymology: OE. suffren, soffren, OF. sufrir, sofrir, F. souffrir, (assumed) LL. sofferire, for L. sufferre; sub under + ferre to bear, akin to E. bear. See Bear to support.

sufferance.etymology: OE. suffrance, OF. sufrance, soufrance, F. souffrance, L. sufferentia, from sufferens, -entis, p.pr. of sufferre. See Suffer.

suffice.etymology: OE. suffisen, OF. soufire, F. suffire (cf. suffisant, p.pr.), L. sufficere to put under, to substitute, to avail for, to suffice; sub under + facere to make. See Fact.

sufficiency.etymology: L. sufficientia: cf. F. suffisance. See Suffice.

sufficient.etymology: L. sufficiens, -entis, p.pr. of sufficere: cf. F. suffisant. See Suffice.

suffix.etymology: L. suffixus, p.p. of suffigere to fasten on, to affix; sub under + figere to fix: cf. F. suffixe. See Fix.

suffocate.etymology: L. suffocatus, p.p. of suffocare to choke; sub under + fauces the throat. Cf. Faucal.

suffragan.etymology: F. suffragant, L. suffragans, p.pr. of suffragari to support with one's vote, to be favorable. See Suffrage.

suffrage.etymology: F., fr. L. suffragium; perhaps originally, a broken piece, a potsherd, used in voting, and fr. sub under + the root of frangere to break. See Break.

roots.meaning: A form of the prefix Sub-.

suffuse.etymology: L. suffusus, p.p. of suffundere to overspread; sub under + fundere to pour. See Fuse to melt.

sufi.etymology: From the name of a dynasty of Persian kings, Safi, Safavi; said to come from name Safi-ud-din of an ancestor of the family, confused with s pious.

sugar.etymology: OE. sugre, F. sucre (cf. It. zucchero, Sp. azúcar), fr. Ar. sukkar, assukkar, fr. Skr. çarkara sugar, gravel; cf. Per. shakar. Cf. Saccharine, Sucrose.

suggest.etymology: L. suggestus, p.p. of suggerere to put under, furnish, suggest; sub under + gerere to carry, to bring. See Jest.

suicide.etymology: L. sui of one's self (akin to suus one's own) + caedere to slay, to kill. Cf. So, adv., Homicide.

suit.etymology: OE. suite, F. suite, OF. suite, sieute, fr. suivre to follow, OF. sivre; perhaps influenced by L. secta. See Sue to follow, and cf. Sect, Suite.

sula.etymology: NL., fr. Icel. s the gannet. See Solan goose.

sulcate.etymology: L. sulcatus, p.p. of sulcare to furrow, fr. sulcus a furrow.

sulkiness.etymology: For sulkenness, fr. AS. solcen slothful, remiss, in asolcen, besolcen, properly p.p. of sealcan in asealcan to be weak or slothful; of uncertain origin.

sulky.etymology: See Sulkiness, and cf. Sulky, n.

sullen.etymology: OE. solein, solain, lonely, sullen; through Old French fr. (assumed) LL. solanus solitary, fr. L. solus alone. See Sole, a.

sully.etymology: OE. sulien, AS. sylian, fr. sol mire; akin to G. suhle mire, sich, sühlen to wallow, Sw. söla to bemire, Dan. söle, Goth. bisaulijan to defile.

sulphate.etymology: NL. sulphas, sulphatis, fr. L. sulphur, sulfur, brimstone, sulphur: cf. F. sulfate.

sulphur.etymology: L., better sulfur: cf. F. soufre.

sulphurous.etymology: L. sulphurosus, sulfurosus: cf. F. sulfureux.

sultan.etymology: F. sultan (cf. Sp. soldan, It. sultano, soldano), Ar. sultan sultan, dominion. Cf. Soldan.

sum.etymology: OE. summe, somme, OF. sume, some, F. somme, L. summa, fr. summus highest, a superlative from sub under. See Sub-, and cf. Supreme.

sumac.etymology: F. sumac, formerly sumach (cf. Sp. zumaque), fr. Ar. summaq.

sumach.etymology: F. sumac, formerly sumach (cf. Sp. zumaque), fr. Ar. summaq.

summation.etymology: Cf. F. sommation. See Sum, v. t.

summit.etymology: F. sommet, dim. of OF. som, sum, top, from L. summum, from summus highest. See Sum, n.

summon.etymology: OE. somonen, OF. sumundre, semondre, F. semondre, from (assumed) LL. summonêre, for L. summonere to give a hint; sub under + monere to admonish, to warn. See Monition, and cf. Submonish.

summons.etymology: OE. somouns, OF. sumunse, semonse, semonce, F. semonce, semondre to summon, OF. p.p. semons. See Summon, v.

sump.etymology: Cf. G. sumpf a sump in a mine, a swamp, akin to LG. sump, D. somp a swamp, Dan. & Sw. sump, and perhaps to E. swamp.

sumpter.etymology: OF. sommetier the driver of a pack horse; akin to OF. & F. sommier a pack horse, L. sagmarius, fr. sagma a pack saddle, in LL., a load, Gr. saj, sañj, to hang on. Cf. Seam a weight, Summer a beam.

sumptuary.etymology: L. sumptuarius, fr. sumptus expense, cost, fr. sumere, sumptum, to take, use, spend; sub under + emere to take, buy: cf. F. somptuaire. See Redeem.

sumptuous.etymology: L. sumptuosus, fr. sumptus expanse, cost: cf. F. somptueux. See Sumptuary.

sun.etymology: OE. sunne, sonne, AS. sunne; akin to OFries. sunne, D. zon, OS. & OHG. sunna, G. sonne, Icel. sunna, Goth. sunna; perh. fr. same root as L. sol. *297. Cf. Solar, South.

sunday.etymology: AS. sunnandæg; sunne, gen. sunnan, the sun + dæg day; akin to D. zondag, G. sonntag; -- so called because this day was anciently dedicated to the sun, or to its worship. See Sun, and Day.

sunder.etymology: OE. sundren, AS. sundrain (in asundrain, gesundrain), from sundor asunder, separately, apart; akin to D. zonder, prep., without, G. sonder separate, as prep., without, sondern but, OHG. suntar separately, Icel. sundr asunder, Sw. & Dan. sönder, Goth. sundro alone, separately.

sundry.etymology: OE. sundry, sondry, AS. syndrig, fr. sundor asunder. See Sunder, v. t.

sup.etymology: OE. soupen to drink, AS. s; akin to D. zuipen, G. saufen, OHG. s, Icel. s, Sw. supa, Dan. söbe. Cf. Sip, Sop, Soup, Supper.

superable.etymology: L. superabilis, from superare to go over, to surmount, fr. super above, over.

superabundant.etymology: L. superabundans, p.pr. of superabundare. See Superabound.

superannuate.etymology: Pref. super- + L. annus a year.

supersede.etymology: From Middle French superseder ( “ postpone, defer ” ) , from Latin supersedēre , from super ( “ over ” ) + sedēre ( “ to sit ” ) . supplant.etymology: F. supplanter, L. supplantare to trip up one's heels, to throw down; sub under + planta the sole of the foot, also, a sucker, slip, sprout. Cf. Plant, n.

supple.etymology: OE. souple, F. souple, from L. supplex suppliant, perhaps originally, being the knees. Cf. Supplicate.

supplement.etymology: F. supplément, L. supplementum, fr. supplere to fill up. See Supply, v. t.

suppliant.etymology: F., p.pr. of supplier to entreat, L. supplicare. See Supplicate, and cf. Supplicant.

supplicant.etymology: L. supplicans, p.pr. See Supplicate, and cf. Suppliant.

supplicate.etymology: L. supplicatus, p.p. of supplicare to supplicate; of uncertain origin, cf. supplex, supplicis, humbly begging or entreating; perhaps fr. sub under + a word akin to placare to reconcile, appease (cf. Placable), or fr. sub under + plicare to fold, whence the idea of bending the knees (cf. Ply, v. t.). Cf. Supple.

supply.etymology: For older supploy, F. suppléer, OF. also supployer, (assumed) LL. suppletare, from L. supplere, suppletum; sub under + plere to fill, akin to plenus full. See Plenty.

support.etymology: F. supporter, L. supportare to carry on, to convey, in LL., to support, sustain; sub under + portare to carry. See Port demeanor.

suppose.etymology: F. supposer; pref. sub- under + poser to place; -- corresponding in meaning to L. supponere, suppositum, to put under, to substitute, falsify, counterfeit. See Pose.

suspend.etymology: F. suspendre, or OF. souspendre (where the prefix is L. subtus below, from sub under), L. suspendere, suspensum; pref. sus- (see Sub-) + pendere to hang. See Pedant, and cf. Suspense, n.

suspension.etymology: Cf. F. suspension, L. suspensio arched work, imperfect pronunciation. See Suspend.

suspicion.etymology: OE. suspecioun, OF. souspeçon, F. soupçon, L. suspectio a looking up to, an esteeming highly, suspicion, fr. suspicere to look up, to esteem, to mistrust. suspicious.etymology: OE. suspecious; cf. L. suspiciosus. See Suspicion.

suspire.etymology: L. suspirare to breathe out, to sigh; sub under + spirare to breathe: cf. F. souspirer, OF. souspirer.

sustain.etymology: OE. sustenen, susteinen, OF. sustenir, sostenir, F. soutenir (the French prefix is properly fr. L. subtus below, fr. sub under), L. sustinere; pref. sus- (see Sub-) + tenere to hold. See Tenable, and cf. Sustenance.

[Obsoles.]

sustenance.etymology: OF. sustenance, sostenance, soustenance: cf. L. sustenentia endurance. See Sustain.

sustentation.etymology: L. sustentatio sustenance, maintenance, fr. sustentare to support, maintain, v. intens. fr. sustinere to sustain: cf. F. sustentation. See Sustain.

susurrant.etymology: L. susurrans, p.pr. from susurrare to whisper.

susurration.etymology: L. susurratio, fr. susurrare to whisper: cf. F. susurration.

sutler.etymology: D. zoetelaar, OD. soetelaar, a small trader, especially in camps, fr. soetelen to undertake low offices; cf. G. sudeln to do dirty work, to sully, soil, E. suds.

sutra.etymology: Skr. s a thread, a string of rules; an aphorism; fr. siv to sew.

suttee.etymology: Skr. sati a faithful wife, fem. of sant existing, real, true, good, p.pr. of as to be. Cf. Sooth.

suture.etymology: L. sutura, fr. suere, sutum, to sew or stitch: cf. F. suture. See Sew to unite with thread.

suzerain.etymology: F., formed fr. sus above, L. susum, sursum (fr. sub under + versum, p.p. of vertere to turn), after the analogy of souverain, E. sovereign. See Sub-, and Verse.

swad.etymology: Probably fr. AS. swe to bind.

swaddle.etymology: AS. swe, swe, fr. swe to bind. See Swathe.

swag.etymology: Cf. Icel. sveggja, sveigja to bend, to sway, Norw. svaga to sway. See Sway.

swage.etymology: Equiv. to suage, abbrev. fr. assuage.

swain.etymology: OE. swain, swein, Icel. sveinn a boy, servant; akin to Sw. sven, Dan. svend, AS. swan, OHG. swein.

swale.etymology: Cf. Icel. svalr cool, svala to cool.

swallow.etymology: OE. swalowe, AS. swalewe, swealwe; akin to D. zwaluw, OHG. swalawa, G. schwalbe, Icel. & Sw. svala, Dan. svale.

swamp.etymology: Cf. AS. swam a fungus, OD. swam a sponge, D. zwam a fungus, G. schwamm a sponge, Icel. svöppr, Dan. & Sw. swamp, Goth. swamms, Gr. somfo`s porous, spongy.

swan.etymology: AS. swan; akin to D. zwaan, OHG. swan, G. schwan, Icel. svanr, Sw. svan, Dan. svane; and perhaps to E. sound something audible.

swap.etymology: OE. swappen to strike; cf. E. to strike a bargain; perh. akin to E. sweep. Cf. Swap a blow, Swap, v. i.

sward.etymology: AS. sweard skin, covering; akin to OFries. swarge, D. zwoord, G. schwarte, Icel. svör skin, sward of the earth.

swart.etymology: OE. swart, AS. sweart black; akin to OFries, OS. & LG. swart, D. zwart, G. schwartz, OHG. swarz, Icel. svarir, Sw. svart, Dan. sort, Goth. swarts; cf. L. sordes dirt, sordere to be dirty. Cf. Sordid, Surd.

swash.etymology: Cf. Swash, v. i., Squash, v. t.

swath.etymology: AS. swa a track, trace; akin to D. zwaad, zwad, zwade, a swath of grass, G. schwad, schwaden; perhaps, originally, a shred. Cf. Swathe, v. t.

swathe.etymology: OE. swathen, AS. swe. See Swath, n., and cf. Swaddle.

sway.etymology: OE. sweyen, Icel. sveigja, akin to E. swing; cf. D. zwaaijen to wield, swing. See Swing, and cf. Swag, v. i.

swear.etymology: OE. swerien, AS. swerian; akin to D. zweren, OS. swerian, OHG. swerien, G. schwören, Icel. sverja, Sw. svärja, Dan. sværge, Icel. & Sw. svara to answer, Dan. svare, Dan. & Sw. svar an answer, Goth. swaran to swear, and perhaps to E. swarm. *177. Cf. Answer.

sweat.etymology: OE. sweten, AS. swætan, fr. swat, n., sweat; akin to OFries. & OS. swet, D. zweet, OHG. sweiz, G. schweiss, Icel. sviti, sveiti, Sw. svett, Dan. sved, L. sudor sweat, sudare to sweat, Gr. sveda sweat, svid to sweat. *178. Cf. Exude, Sudary, Sudorific.

sweep.etymology: OE. swepen; akin to AS. swapan. See Swoop, v. i.

sweet.etymology: OE. swete, swote, sote, AS. swete; akin to OFries. swete, OS. swoti, D. zoet, G. süss, OHG. suozi, Icel. sætr, soetr, Sw. söt, Dan. söd, Goth. suts, L. suavis, for suadvis, Gr. svadu sweet, svad, svad, to sweeten. *175. Cf. Assuage, Suave, Suasion.

swell.etymology: AS. swellan; akin to D. zwellen, OS. & OHG. swellan, G. schwellen, Icel. svella, Sw. svälla.

sweltry.etymology: See Swelter, Swelt, v. i., and cf. Sultry.

swerve.etymology: OE. swerven, AS. sweorfan to wipe off, to file, to polish; akin to OFries. swerva to creep, D. zwerven to swerve, to rope, OS. swerban to wipe off, MHG. swerben to be whirled, OHG. swerban to wipe off, Icel. sverfa to file, Goth. swaírban (in comp.) to wipe, and perhaps to E. swarm. Cf. Swarm.

swift.etymology: AS. swift; akin to swapan to sweep, swipu a whip; cf. swifan to move quickly, to revolve. See Swoop, v. i., and cf. Swivel, Squib.

swig.etymology: Cf. D. zwelgen to swallow, E. swallow, v.t.

swill.etymology: OE. swilen to wash, AS. swilian.

swim.etymology: AS. swimman; akin to D. zwemmen, OHG. swimman, G. schwimmen, Icel. svimma, Dan. swömme, Sw. simma. Cf. Sound an air bladder, a strait.

swindler.etymology: G. schwindler, fr. schwindlen to be dizzy, to act thoughtlessly, to cheat, fr. schwindel dizziness, fr. schwinden to vanish, to disappear, to dwindle. See Swim to be dizzy.

swine.etymology: OE. swin, AS. swin; akin to OFries. & OS. swin, D. zwijn, G. schwein, OHG. swin, Icel. svin, Sw. svin, Dan. sviin, Goth. swein; originally a diminutive corresponding to E. sow. See Sow, n.

swing.etymology: OE. swingen, AS. swingan to scourge, to fly, to flutter; akin to G. schwingen to winnow, to swingle, oscillate, sich schwingen to leap, to soar, OHG. swingan to throw, to scourge, to soar, Sw. svinga to swing, to whirl, Dan. svinge. Cf. Swagger, Sway, Swinge, Swink.

swinge.etymology: OE. swengen, AS. swengan to shake, causative of swingan. See Swing.

swingletree.etymology: So named in allusion to its swinging. See Swingle, v. i., and cf. Swingtree.

swirl.etymology: Akin to Norw. svirla to whirl, freq. of sverra to whirl, Dan. svirre, G. schwirren to whiz, to buzz. *177. See Swarm, n.

swiss.etymology: F. Suisse, of German origin. Cf. Switzer.

switch.etymology: Cf. OD. swick a scourage, a whip. Cf. Swink, Swing.

swivel.etymology: AS. swifan to move quickly, to remove; akin to Icel. sveifla to whirl, shake, svifa to ramble, to turn. See Swoop, and cf. Swift a reel, Swift, a.

swoon.etymology: OE. swounen, swoghenen, for swo, fr. swo to sigh deeply, to droop, AS. swogan to sough, sigh; cf. geswogen senseless, swooned, geswowung a swooning. Cf. Sough.

swoop.etymology: OE. swopen, usually, to sweep, As. swapan to sweep, to rush; akin to G. schweifen to rove, to ramble, to curve, OHG. sweifan to whirl, Icel. sveipa to sweep; also to AS. swifan to move quickly. Cf. Sweep, Swift, a. & n., Swipe, Swivel.

sword.etymology: OE. swerd, AS. sweord; akin to OFries. swerd, swird, D. zwaard, OS. swerd, OHG. swert, G. schwert, Icel. sver, Sw. svärd, Dan. sværd; of uncertain origin.

sycamore.etymology: L. sycomorus, Gr. sycomore. Cf. Mulberry.

sycophant.etymology: L. sycophanta a slanderer, deceiver, parasite, Gr. sycophante. The reason for the name is not certainly known. See Phenomenon.

syllepsis.etymology: L., fr. Gr. sy`llhpsis a taking together, from syllable, n.
